When the first reports about a diverted flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv came through on Wednesday, it appeared to have been caused by a tussle between two pilots.

Early claims even suggested one was Russian and the other Ukrainian.

But, in the age of social media, the true chaos aboard the Flydubai flight FZ1073 quickly came to light. Footage and images sent from the plane by blood-covered passengers showed them overpowering the co-pilot, who it later emerged was an Omani national.

The plane, a Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, was carrying over 170 people when it plunged more than 17,000ft in two minutes as the fight broke out. An emergency alert was sent out and the plane changed course towards Jordan, eventually landing in Saudi Arabia.

open image in gallery Passengers onboard the Flydubai flight revealed what was happening in bloody social media posts ( Social media )

Aviation experts told the BBC that the rapid descent led to damage pictured on the plane’s rudder, adding that the incident could easily have led to the plane breaking up in mid-air.

Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was identified as the victim of the attack, while his arrested co-pilot was identified as Hamam al-Hammami on Saturday by sources cited in CNN and Reuters.

The motive for the incident is still being determined but Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration suggested early on that it was a suspected terror attack.

open image in gallery Capt Smit Machchhar was attacked by his co-pilot – both are pictured covered in blood ( Social media )

‘Blood everywhere’

Nina Manes, a six-year-old girl on her way to the toilet accompanied by her mother, was the first to raise the alarm when the pair heard shouting coming from the cockpit, prompting cabin crew to rush to the blood-spattered scene.

“There was blood all over the cockpit and very, very sharp fighting moves,” Nina’s mother, Tali Manes, told Israel’s Channel 12.

“I screamed, ‘He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!’ People looked at me and didn’t understand.”

Her husband, Tzvika Manes, said: “The shrieks of my daughters when the plane nose-dived [are still with me]. They said, ‘Dad we don’t want to die.’ [Their cries] were the triggers that caused me to run inside the cockpit.”

open image in gallery The flight had been heading from Dubai to Tel Aviv but was diverted to Saudi Arabia ( Flightradar24.com )

One passenger recorded the incident on his phone and later shared the footage to social media. With blood dripping down his face, he declared that the passengers had “subdued the terrorists”. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” he added.

On Saturday, UAE prosecutors said Capt Machchhar had been attacked by a “crash axe” – a tool kept in the cockpit in case of emergencies, bypassing stringent security protocols.

Yaniv Hayun, a 50-year-old owner of a sewage plumbing company, was travelling on the plane with his wife and two daughters.

In his blood-spattered T-shirt, he was hailed as a hero by Mr Netanyahu who personally thanked him for helping to subdue the attacker and to prevent the plane from crashing.

Along with Tzvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan, he broke into the cockpit to intervene. By mimicking gestures he said he had see on television, Mr Hayun “grabbed the controls and started pulling back the handles”. He said he had learned the techniques from watching Air Crash Investigation.

open image in gallery Six-year-old Nina Manes played a crucial role in preventing disaster when she asked to go to the toilet at the same time as the attack was taking place ( Channel 12 )

He said it took 20 to 25 minutes to fully subdue and bind the pilot using cords from headphones linked to the plane’s entertainment system.

Mr Hayun was helped by a dentist, Dr Shota Musayev, who administered “life-saving medical treatment” to Capt Machchhar, including treating him for severe wounds to his head and cuts to his fingers. He helped to successfully stop the bleeding and to stabilise his blood pressure before emergency surgery.

All five are expected to receive Israel’s Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, president Isaac Herzog said on Thursday.

Both pilots have been transferred to the UAE for further investigations and for medical treatment.

‘Suicidal and indoctrinated’

Mr Netanyahu told Fox News that the attacker was “suicidal” and called out to the crew “Kill me, kill me!” after he was subdued.

“It’s clear he was suicidal, that’s not a question,” he added. The Israeli leader said that he had undergone a “Islamist radical indoctrination” and promised to reveal whether he had connections to Iran in the coming days.

The prime minister said those onboard managed to “prevent a 9/11 disaster, because that's what it looks like was happening”, claiming that the intent may have been to crash the plane.

A regional official familiar with the Flydubai investigation told the Associated Press that investigators in Saudi Arabia were working with authorities from the UAE, US, Oman and Israel, and that “all possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into”.

“Nothing is ruled out for now,” the official said.

open image in gallery Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, tells Indian prime minister Narendra Modi about the ordeal on a video call ( Reuters )

Al-Hammami was banned from flying last year over concerns that he had radical ideological views, according to Saudi state media.

Two Israeli security officials said that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, according to their initial assessments. He was arrested by Saudi security forces after the plane landed in Tabuk, northwest Saudi Arabia, and was being questioned by investigators.

On Saturday, the UAE prosecutor general said that al-Hammami had attempted to carry out a “terrorist” attack, according to the country’s state news agency WAM.

Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.

Mr Netanyahu said: “It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane. The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue.”

open image in gallery Benjamin Netanyahu meets Yaniv Hayoun, Or Fradilov, Dr Shota Musayev and his wife Sigalit, who the Israeli PM described as ‘heroes’ for helping prevent disaster ( Reuters )

Warnings and questions over security

Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said on Wednesday that politicians had been warned in a national security briefing the night before that Israel’s enemies could attack in the run-up to the country’s elections that are due to take place on 27 October.

A ban on pilots from states without formal relations to Israel was not enforced appropriately, according to a report cited by the Times of Israel.

Under the law, pilots from nations including Oman, which does not have formal ties with Israel, were banned from flying but airlines and security agencies did not enforce the rule.

open image in gallery Assaf Regavim, who helped to overpower the pilot ( Getty )

Furthermore, Israel’s security agency, Shin Bet, had raised concerns about flights from the UAE for months before the incident.

Shin Bet director David Zini had reportedly clashed with Israeli airlines over restrictions on flights to the UAE, reasoning that security measures at Emirati airports were insufficient, according to Israel’s N12 News.

Israeli authorities were concerned with possible missile attacks or attacks at an airport, the outlet reported on Thursday. A scenario like Wednesday’s hijacking attempt was “not raised in any discussion”, they said.

Country singer Zach Bryan wore a “Free Palestine” shirt during his concert at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium Friday night, just weeks after the New England Patriots owner barred Macklemore from performing at his venue over his pro-Palestine remarks.

Bryan, 30, wore a black T-shirt with white lettering that said “Free Palestine.” The shirt also featured a pine tree flag and the words “Appeal to heaven,” which are references to an American Revolutionary campaign.

Guitarist Noah Le Gros wore a Palestine soccer jersey onstage alongside Bryan, and later shared a picture of himself in the shirt standing in front of a Kraft Sports and Entertainment sign at the Massachusetts stadium.

It comes weeks after billionaire stadium owner Kraft barred Macklemore from performing at his stadium for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. tour after the rapper delivered a pro-Palestine speech onstage during an earlier concert. The Independent has contacted representatives for Robert Kraft for comment.

“Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners,” Macklemore said in a statement at the time. “And collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.”

open image in gallery Country singer Zach Bryan wore a ‘Free Palestine’ shirt during his concert at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium Friday night ( X via @hollley )

When Sheeran addressed the fallout in a statement, he said he would not be drawn into public debate about the war in Gaza but insisted he was “not complicit.”

The situation drew significant backlash across the music industry, and Sheeran’s other opening acts, including Irish singer Aaron Rowe and American producer Finneas, withdrew from the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. Protesters gathered outside Sheeran’s first concert without Macklemore last week.

Macklemore responded to the situation by announcing a tour of his own, with proceeds from the shows in Paris, London and Dublin going to organizations supporting Palestinians. He is calling it the Free Palestine tour.

Sheeran addressed the fallout onstage at a solo concert at Lincoln Financial Field on September 19, and said he was “so sorry” for disappointing his fans.

“I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics,” he said.

open image in gallery Robert Kraft barred Macklemore from performing at his Gillette Stadium over the rapper’s pro-Palestine comments ( Getty )

open image in gallery Macklemore was dropped from Ed Sheeran’s US tour over his calls for a ‘Free Palestine’ onstage ( Getty )

He clarified his own stance on the Israel-Palestine conflict, saying, “What happened in Israel, and at the music festival on October 7th was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate.”

On 17 September, Kraft addressed the controversy surrounding the tour, saying: “I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people. I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting.”

He also referenced the fact that Macklemore, who donated his entire $1m fee for Sheeran’s tour to support organizations supporting Palestinians, had asked Kraft to match the donation. Sheeran had also got in touch asking Kraft to match his $2m donation to Palestine.

“Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges,” continued Kraft. “In addition, I’d like the people who are speaking in support of the Palestinian people to know that for decades, I have supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians and have brought young Palestinians and Israelis together to build business, create jobs and forge relationships.”

An estimated 10,000 schoolchildren currently struggle with chronic fatigue, pain in their limbs and mobility issues as they navigate juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) – yet most teachers remain unaware of its prevalence.

JIA is the most common type of arthritis among children and teenagers, and typically causes inflammation in the hands, knees, ankles, elbows and wrists. However, given that arthritis is an autoimmune disease usually associated with old age, the warning signs are often ignored.

In Jessica Ward’s case, she was just six years old when her parents became increasingly concerned in the year after she developed blood poisoning following appendicitis, when she continued to have swelling in her joints.

For 14 months, she was a regular visitor at the hospital, enduring countless blood tests and appointments and suffering from instability and pain in her knees.

Upon being referred to the rheumatology department at Alder Hey children’s hospital in Liverpool, one of the few in the country, she was diagnosed within minutes of walking through the door.

open image in gallery Ms Ward found both primary and high school difficult as her teachers struggled to understand her condition ( Supplied )

“They knew immediately from the way I walked,” she said. “It’s not as well taught or heard of unless you’re a specialist working in this area with children.”

While her parents were relieved she had finally received a diagnosis, the following years became increasingly difficult to navigate as her school teachers in Wirral struggled to understand her condition. This included struggling to write due to hand pain and needing crutches and adapted shoes to walk.

“I didn’t have the greatest time in primary or high school, it was the denial factor of everybody,” she said. “In school, I found it extremely difficult due to my trauma response to hospital, which meant I missed a lot of school. In high school, there was a change in my medication and my immune system was completely battered. I struggled with friends, and I remember one day, my nan had to carry me home as my knees were that bad.

“People found that quite entertaining, some students and kids can be cruel. It wasn’t pleasant and it wasn’t great. I just don’t think teachers got it.

I did have a lot of instances of being bullied for not being able to be included in things.”

On one occasion, nursing staff from Alder Hey even visited her school to give a talk on juvenile arthritis, to help students and staff understand.

As a result of changes to her medication during her GCSE years, she became unwell and struggled to achieve the grades she wanted, despite passing all of her exams.

open image in gallery She has since become a teacher and helps other students with educational and physical needs ( Supplied )

After moving to a different sixth form and prioritising vocational work, her grades improved and she decided that she wanted to become a teacher.

Now aged 27, she works in a primary and a high school supporting students with physical and special educational needs.

“To be completely honest, being a teacher myself now, and trying to explain arthritis, it is still not understood,” she said.

“There’s never a one size fits all. Not everybody has the same condition, not all of them are the same. It may be a case of asking more questions, my biggest problem in school was having to repeat myself constantly to the same teachers.

“Feeling believed and understood is the biggest thing. You can’t see arthritis and it is hard.”

JIA is an autoimmune condition, where the immune system mistakenly attacks the body. While there is no cure, there are a number of different treatements available to manage symptoms, such as painkillers, steroids, and disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs.

While some children enter remission and outgrow the condition, others suffer with inflammation throughout their life, which can cause joint damage and disability.

In Ms Ward’s case, she has recently had to take several weeks off work after suffering with a recent flare up.

Arthritis UK are hoping to raise awareness of the condition within educational settings, and are encouraging schools to become aware of the side effects and to show compassion for missed classes.

Methotrexate is a drug commonly given to children with arthritis yet can make pupils feel nauseous and exhausted, often resulting in school absences.

Lynne Woolley, head of young people and families at Arthritis UK, said: “Going through school is one of the most important aspects of a young person’s life and we know that not getting the right support when living with arthritis can make many aspects of school life very difficult.

“Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is an often invisible and unpredictable condition. Learning to manage appointments, medication side effects, pain, and the impact on your mental health can be challenging alongside learning and being a young person!

“Jessica’s story is like many we have heard before, but just like she suggests there are several ways that school staff can help.

“Staff can take the time to understand their individual needs, working closely with them and their families can make a huge difference. Creating a safe, supportive and understanding environment encourages open communication and helps the school provide the right support as their needs change.

“We want schools to feel confident to open up the conversation with young people with JIA and their families. Often, relatively simple adjustments can prevent children from missing school and make an enormous difference to their wellbeing, confidence and ability to thrive. Arthritis UK’s website has free resources such as Individual Healthcare Plan (IHP) templates, films, teacher guides and a webinar for school staff which all can help.”

In a commercial kitchen outside Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns spreads a blue-green goo into a gridded mold, making one of his company’s signature products: potent THC gummies, featuring the primary intoxicating compound found in marijuana.

It’s a business he might soon have to give up. America’s multibillion-dollar market for impairing hemp products — from THC seltzers sold at some Target stores to smokable cannabis flowers — faces potential elimination after Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that has allowed it to flourish.

Advocates for the industry, along with some lawmakers, are fighting to save it. The short-term government-funding bill signed by President Donald Trump last month delayed the effective date of the “hemp THC ban” from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, giving Congress more time to consider regulating the products rather than banning them.

“It’s such a weird spot to be in,” said Hohns. “You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.”

Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in the hemp law he championed

Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. “Rope, not dope” was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp.

To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill.

But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole. Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high.

Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country, including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana’s THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned.

The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal.

Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products.

McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history.

The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn’t take effect for a year.

An industry tries to save itself

The ban “threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,” according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market.

The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds.

The owners of Kentucky’s Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that’s what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said.

“If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it’s gone,” Zipperle said.

They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year.

The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable.

Some consider other work

Hohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what's available in states that have.

“When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry,” Hohns said. “No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope.”

That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business.

Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin' Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production. Co-founder Matt Swanson took himself off the payroll on Thursday.

“There’s just so much uncertainty,” Swanson said. “I'm actively looking for employment.”

Allies and opponents line up

Among those who have come to the defense of the hemp industry are alcohol retailers, including Total Wine & More. Sales of cannabis seltzers have helped offset falling alcohol sales.

Opponents include people who say the products are dangerous.

“I have sympathy for people losing their jobs, but I also have sympathy for the many, many more people whose lives are affected by this,” said Kevin Sabet, CEO of Smart Approaches to Marijuana.

The regulated legal marijuana industry, which sees hemp THC as unfair competition, also supports the ban. Cory Harris, a lobbyist for state-legal cannabis operators, suggested that dire predictions about its effect on the intoxicating hemp industry are overstated.

While the ban would end interstate sales of products like THC seltzers and gummies, some could find a home in legal in-state markets, he said. It's possible THC drinks could be sold at stores in the states where they were produced. States like North Carolina could adopt legal hemp programs.

“If you go from having virtually no rules to suddenly having an awful lot of rules, that’s a buzzkill,” Harris said. “Welcome to our world. But if you establish your whole business within a legally questionable loophole, that’s just sort of the risk you take.”

___

Associated Press reporters Allen G. Breed in Clayton, North Carolina, and Dylan Lovan in Louisville, Kentucky, contributed.

London is set to become the first battleground over Labour’s push to undo the damage caused by Brexit, with the likely Tory candidate for mayor Sir James Cleverly saying he is ready to fight plans to rejoin.

With Sir Sadiq focussing on Brexit and renewing his demands for the UK to rejoin at last week’s Labour Party conference – coupled by Mr Burnham signalling that rejoin could be in the next general election manifesto – Sir James insisted he was ready to front up the Tory position of supporting the status quo.

The London mayoral election is coming up in May 2028 and will be a dry run for a general election in 2029 if Mr Burnham sticks to his promise of not calling an early poll.

Sir James was a Brexiteer in the 2016 referendum but supported Theresa May’s attempts to compromise with the European Union. In the 2016 referendum, seven of the 10 areas with the highest share of the vote for Remain were in London, including Lambeth, Hackney and Haringey, all of which polled over 75 per cent to stay in the EU.

Speaking to The Independent ahead of the Conservative Party conference this week, Sir James, a former foreign secretary and home secretary, claimed any push to rejoin the EU would damage London’s interests.

open image in gallery James Cleverly wants to become London mayor ( The Independent )

He argued that restrictive EU regulation on artificial intelligence and tech would harm the capital.

“The UK is the world's third largest hub for AI development because we have a different regulatory regime to the EU,” he said. “So, if you're happy to basically kill off London's tech sector...”

Sir James also claimed Labour were taking a “contradictory” approach to Brexit.

“It's only a few weeks ago that John Healey said the UK’s accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) – the kind of the Asia Pacific trading bloc – was going to be one of the most transformational economic events.

“So, if we were to rejoin the EU, we would have to tear it up. Labour on one hand are saying ‘this is brilliant, this is transformational’... but then flirting with the idea of tearing up AI, for example.

“Now you can love it or you hate it – but it is a fact of life, and it is really important.”

Supporters of rejoin point out that the UK is losing billions in exports for being separated from its biggest trading partner.The Independent has led the campaign for Britain to rebuild its relationship with Brussels on the basis of clear evidence that it has damaged the economy and failed to deliver promised benefits on a wide range of issues including immigration.

Sir Tony Blair recently sparked a fresh debate calling for the UK rejoin in the next decade while a report by the respected Institute for Public Policy for the Regions (IPPR) said the UK was losing £6.5bn in exports alone to the EU because of a lack of mutual recognition on product testing.

open image in gallery Prime minister Andy Burnham wants a rethink on Brexit ( Reuters )

Logistics UK, which represents transporters of goods, has pointed to a shortfall in more than £11bn a year in exports because of Brexit.

But Sir James also raised questions over Labour’s ability to negotiate a good re-entry into the EU.

He claimed: “This Labour government has shown an inability to negotiate a good deal, quite out of all recognition.

“You look at the Erasmus student travel arrangement with the EU. The Labour government renegotiated that it was more expensive for fewer students, and almost all the benefit was for EU students rather than British students – and they regarded that as a great success.

“The point I'm making is that Andy Burnham is desperately trying to be popular. He is willing to say whatever he thinks he needs to say to harvest some short-term popularity.”

Mr Burnham said a year ago that he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU and then at the Labour Party conference warned Brexit had created “more harm than good” claiming it had led to “a decade of drift and division.”

open image in gallery Sadiq Khan wants the UK to rejoin the EU ( PA )

Speaking to the BBC he quoted an interview former Tory chancellor George Osborne gave to The Independent as a reason to change.

He said: “We could look at what (former Conservative chancellor) George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market – or we could go all the way.”

He later suggested it is “possible” Labour’s next election manifesto could include an in-out referendum or even a pledge to rejoin the EU.

Sir Sadiq has also signalled his willingness to make Brexit a London issue in the mayoral election.

Commenting on Mr Burnham’s leader’s speech in Liverpool in an article for The Guardian, he wrote: “Perhaps most encouraging of all was the prime minister’s promise to rethink Britain’s relationship with the EU.

“Burnham is right – and the reality of the vote’s impact on the UK is sobering. Research commissioned by City Hall in 2024 showed that London’s economy was £30bn smaller than it would have been without Brexit and that there were nearly 2m fewer jobs overall in the UK as a result of us leaving. Earlier this year, we set out new analysis showing that our country has grown more slowly than our comparable European counterparts since 2016.

“If that trend continues, our economy could be £250bn smaller than similar EU countries’ by 2030.”

But Sir James was dismissive of Sir Sadiq’s stance, claiming the mayor and Labour are using Brexit to distract from their own shortcomings.

He complained: “Sadiq Khan wants to keep rowing about an event from 10 years ago, because in the intervening 10 years, he's got nothing to be proud of.”

An intense, public outcry over a woman's account of being gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity house prompted New York's governor this week to angrily yank control of the investigation away from the local prosecutor who didn't initially see what happened as a crime.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said Cornell police omitted key information that could have affected his decision whether or not to pursue criminal charges.

Now, the task of unraveling the case will fall to the state's attorney general, Letitia James, who was appointed as a special prosecutor.

James, a Democrat best known for tangling with President Donald Trump, suggested at a news conference Friday that her investigation wouldn't be rushed. She described it as a monthslong process, with no predetermined outcome.

Here’s what we know and don’t know about the woman's allegations and the investigations that followed:

A lawsuit shone a fresh light on the woman's allegations

The woman sued Cornell and seven former students last month, alleging she was given ketamine and became completely incapacitated while members of the Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her at their campus residence in October 2024.

She reported the alleged assault to campus police about three weeks later, giving investigators a detailed account over two days. She also spoke with Cornell’s disciplinary investigators.

But Van Houten quickly declined to pursue charges or further investigation after reviewing a police summary of her interview.

After the victim filed her civil suit, Van Houten said it contained allegations he had never seen. He contended Cornell’s police had withheld key information, including a transcript of the woman’s interview where she explicitly said she was “100% confident” she was raped.

Van Houten said the materials suggested she had consented to some sex with multiple men, hadn't been forced into other acts, and was intoxicated, but not to the point of helplessness.

Under New York law, voluntary intoxication alone generally does not establish an inability to consent for purposes of rape charges. The law distinguishes that from being physically helpless or incapacitated by drugs administered without consent.

Van Houten later reopened the investigation. “Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” he said.

The school’s investigation produced conflicting accounts

Only a fraction of the evidence collected by the school has become public, but the portions that have provided a fuller — though disputed — timeline of events, as well as a glimpse at how the men responded to being accused.

According to the records, the woman had been invited to the fraternity by a member for whom she had long held strong romantic feelings. Cornell's disciplinary panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking drugs and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent.

Later, other men started coming into the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available.

The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body.

“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told investigators.

The records also show that she acknowledged that her memory of the night was spotty, due to her extreme inebriation, and had verbally acquiesced to some acts she later felt were sexual abuse.

Some of the accused men disputed her account when speaking to investigators, or said that the drug use and sexual activity were consensual.

Cornell hasn’t detailed the results of its investigation, but said it resulted in some students being expelled. The records show it also cleared at least some of the men of sexual assault allegations.

New York's governor was outraged by the police investigation

Hochul said she appointed James because she had lost faith in Van Houten's handling of the case. She said Van Houten should have asked Cornell for more information and interviewed the woman before deciding to close the case.

“This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable,” she said. “And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”

Van Houten said he supports James’ appointment but maintains that New York law didn’t allow him to prosecute based solely on the woman’s allegations that she was too incapacitated to consent.

The case reverberated beyond Cornell

The case has roiled Cornell, with some students calling for greater transparency and accountability in the handling of the case, stronger sexual assault prevention efforts and changes to Greek life.

The presidents of every fraternity in Cornell’s Interfraternity Council voted unanimously to cancel social events this weekend in response to the allegations, according to reporting by Cornell's student newspaper.

The case has also renewed scrutiny of a New York sexual assault law that makes it more difficult to prosecute cases involving people too intoxicated to consent. New York is one of 19 states with such laws.

Hochul said Friday that she supports changing the law.

News.title: Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying
News.content:
The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

News.title: Bath complete revenge mission on Exeter despite imperious Feyi-Waboso
News.content:
Bath held off a furious comeback from Exeter, led by the irrepressible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, to avenge their Gallagher Prem semi-final defeat here in June.

It felt as if lightning might strike Bath twice. Once again Exeter overturned a 26-10 half-time deficit, to manufacture a second-half lead thanks to a pair of blistering finishes by Feyi-Waboso. Four months ago, Bath failed to take a drop goal in the closing stages, but this time with the reassuring presence of Finn Russell at fly-half, they kept their cool.

The Scotland playmaker twice sent penalties deep into the Exeter 22 from where Stephen Varney conceded a yellow card and penalty try before Bath replacement Ted Hill powered through a thicket of Exeter tacklers.

“Finn is one of the best 10s in the world and I thought he had a very good game,” Johann van Graan, the Bath head of rugby, said. “His decision making is above most players in the world and I thought that came through tonight.”

Despite the appearance of yet another high-scoring shoot-out, both teams defended with real bite, although Bath struggled to lay a finger on Feyi-Waboso who ended up in a scrap with a fan in the stands here when he was a spectator in May. He exacted a measure of revenge beating eight defenders and carried for 132 metres.

“Manny still needs game time,” Rob Baxter, the Exeter director of rugby, said. “When he’s on the ball, you see something incredible, but it is his ability to get on the ball again. He is just getting his game minutes and match fitness up.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco, which is placed between the cheek and lower gum, is particularly popular in south Asia. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Eight tips for improving your laptop’s performance (and save your sanity)
News.content:
MacBooks and Windows laptops both have modes intended to maximise battery life. Low Power Mode (Mac) and Power Saver (Windows) should be avoided if you want peak performance.

On a Mac, you’ll find the Low Power Mode switch in Settings > Battery. For the best experience, set this to Never, but remember to change it back if you need your MacBook to last longer.

On a Windows laptop, there are two controls you need to consider. Both are found in Settings > System > Power & Battery.

Energy Saver mode uses multiple tactics to reduce battery consumption, including lowering maximum power. Switch this off, and you have access to Power Mode controls.

Your options are Best Power Efficiency, Balanced and Best Performance. While Balanced is the default, I was able to unlock up to 33 per cent more power by playing around with these settings using my own laptop.

To make matters more complicated, some laptops have their own performance modes. Many Asus laptops have MyAsus or Armory Crate, for example. Lenovo has the Vantage app, Dell has MyDell, and MSI laptops have MSI Center.

3. Stop applications from opening on start-up

If your laptop is slow when it first starts up, it may be because a whole bunch of apps have been given the green light to wake up with it.

Some applications such as antivirus software are critical, but most can be toggled off. As an example, I make sure apps such as Spotify, Steam and WhatsApp don’t open on startup; I only launch them when I need them.

On a MacBook, you can see which apps have this permission in Settings > General, under Open at Login. Select an app entry and click the “minus” button to remove it.

On a Windows laptop, you’ll find the list of start-up apps in Settings > Apps > Startup. Each entry has a little on/off slider.

4. Free up storage space

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

Sports.title: He never took his eyes off me, says Man City and BBC Sport host Natalie Pike as she opens up on stalker hell
Sports.content:
Next

NATALIE PIKE has opened up about her stalking hell after a man showed up to the Etihad while she was broadcasting pitchside.

The broadcaster instantly recognised it was the man who had been tormenting her and the ordeal led to her having a panic attack in the announcer’s room.



Speaking to The Telegraph, she said: “I stood in a corner, burst out crying, and I just couldn’t catch my breath.”

Just eight days earlier, the former FHM model was on a spa day with a friend when she noticed lots of missed calls from her hairdressers and the school her son Reggie, 8, attends.



The salon said two men had turned up in a van and demanded to know where Natalie was as they knew she was a customer.

The hairdresser quickly alerted Reggie’s school which was just down the road.



Natalie said she just turned white, adding: “I had no idea what it could mean. So I did what we tend to do as women, and I started investigating myself.”

Looking back through her Instagram messages she noticed a lot of messages from one account.



She said: “They began in the usual way: ‘Happy birthday’, ‘You’re beautiful’, that kind of thing. Then they started deteriorating.

“So I took a screenshot of this person’s profile, sent it to my hairdresser, and she instantly confirmed it was the same man she had seen.”

Just a week later, Natalie was pitchside presenting for City against Newcastle when she noticed a man hovering metres away.

“I just had a sense that something wasn’t right,” she said.

Natalie continued: “So I looked over my shoulder, and I instantly saw him – the man from the picture.



Panic set in and Natalie said she ran from the pitch and had her first ever panic attack.

Thankfully police pinpointed the man through CCTV and tracked him through the stadium as he made his way towards Natalie.

The presenter said the footage was “harrowing”, adding: “he never took his eyes off me.

“He came in at the back of the stand and then, over a 20-minute period, moved down and stopped several times until he was about a metre away from me.”

The suspect was arrested the next morning and police took Natalie’s full statement.



She said the investigation went “full steam” from there.

Detectives went to his house where they found photos of him sitting in the pub around the corner from her home and of her ex-husband’s car.

It was later revealed he had been messaging her best friend, husband and other people she knew.

He was handed a 12 month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, at the end of September bringing the eight-month ordeal to a close.



Natalie said she considers herself fortunate as only about six per cent of recorded offences end in a charge and under two per cent see a criminal conviction.

The pundit chose to forgo the option of a screen separating her from the stalker in the courtroom and instead delivered her victim impact statement directly to him.

She said: “I thought, ‘I don’t need to hide. I’ve got nothing to hide about’. Seeing him sentenced, and hearing the judge emphasise the seriousness of the case, I felt strong.

“And I felt an overwhelming relief that I could now get on with my life.”



This included spending time with her mum who has stage four bowel cancer.

When Natalie told her about the stalking, her mum collapsed and was in hospital for five weeks.

A stalking protection order was issued banning the man from the village Natalie lives in and the Etihad.

But Natalie still tried her best to be untraceable including changing her car number plate, avoiding local shops and switching her routes home.



She added: “One of the sad things about this is that it has really affected my enjoyment of going to the Etihad.”

Natalie was a fan of the Citizens during her youth and got her first season ticket to watch the club when she was 15.

She would head down to Maine Road to watch the club compete in the third tier of English football, well before the successful team that regularly picks up trophies in more recent times.

She juggled her love of football with a full-time modelling career for nine years, during which she won the FHM High Street Honeys competition.



The stadium “would always be my place of safety. I was there throughout my divorce, the pandemic, all the awful things that happen in life, and I could still be happy there. I feel like that has been taken away from me.”

After modelling for the 2008/2009 Manchester City kit she started as their in-house presenter.

Now she is recognised as the voice of the club’s Match Day Live alongside the City Square Live broadcasts and she has interviewed a host of famous faces.

This summer she broadcast Scotland‘s takeover of Boston for the World Cup.

Born in Edinbrough, Natalie said the opportunity restored her “faith in human nature”.



She continued: “It makes me emotional thinking about it, because it came at the perfect time, and it was such a release from everything else that was happening.”

In a post to Instagram today, Natalie revealed her experience and wrote: “This has been incredibly difficult to share, but I hope that by doing so it might help someone else.

“If you are experiencing stalking, please report it and seek specialist support. My experience of doing both has shown me just how important that can be.”

She directed people to the Suzy Lamplugh Trust National Stalking Helpline which she used for advice herself.

It is not the first stalking ordeal suffered by a high-profile female sports presenter in this country.

Last year Laura Woods described how she had been bombarded for three years by an obsessed female Liverpool fan, who would send her birthday cards that read: “Today’s the day you were born and tonight’s the night you’re going to die.”

The woman was later jailed for 14 months.

MAX DOWMAN was shown a straight red card for England Under-19s on Friday.

The Arsenal wonderkid was given his marching orders in the 73rd minute as the Young Lions took on their United States counterparts in Spain.



Dowman, 16, was sent off with England leading 2-1, giving his team a tough task to remain ahead in a tight affair with 17 minutes left to play.

England boss Ben Futcher brought on Dowman’s Arsenal teammate Ife Ibrahim to plug the gap and implement a defensive approach to keep hold of the lead.



The change paid off as England managed to come out of the other side victorious, maintaining their 2-1 advantage.

The fixture was played behind closed doors and there has been no confirmation of the reason for Dowman’s dismissal.

However, a handful of reports have claimed that the red card was given for “violent conduct.”

Dowman had impressed earlier in the game, setting up Reigan Heskey for the opening goal within the first minute of the clash.

The USA hit back when New York City FC prospect Maximo Carrizo converted an eighth-minute penalty.

But England regained the lead in the second half through Luca Williams-Barnett, ensuring they maintained a flawless record in the September and October international break.

Dowman is yet to play above U19 level for England despite his impressive exploits for the Arsenal first team.

England Under-21s chief Lee Carsley has said he is hoping to work with Dowman before he is called up to the Three Lions senior squad by Thomas Tuchel in future.

He said last week: “It’s important that players develop at their own pace. Max is an outstanding talent, the timing and the balance of when he comes to the U21s is inevitable.

“He’s going to the U21s because of his talent, but we have to make sure we do that at the right time.



We have to be patient and make sure that ultimately we want them to play for the senior team for a prolonged period.

“So we have to make sure that we get the time right with that. We had a similar issue a few years ago with Ethan Nwaneri.

“He was early and he made his debut and he’s done really well and there’s that tendency to push him on quickly.”

Lewis Hamilton says it will be important for Ferrari to focus on their own race for what is expected to be a challenging Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia but admits it would be "awesome" if they have the pace to stay with polesitter Max Verstappen from the front row.

​Hamilton produced "probably my best lap of the year" to claim second on the grid with his last attempt of qualifying at the Sepang International Circuit, his second front-row start of the year.

It will be the first time Verstappen and Hamilton, the grid's two-most successful drivers and the sport's biggest names, have started at the head of a Grand Prix together since July 2023, at that year's Hungarian Grand Prix.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli is just behind them in third, creating a mouth-watering head of the grid for lights out at 8am on Sunday live on Sky Sports F1 and Sky Sports Main Event.

Verstappen claimed pole, Red Bull's first of the season, by 0.298s and the Dutchman's form so far this weekend on F1's return to Sepang suggests he is the favourite to win too.

Indeed, Hamilton was staying cautious about Ferrari's chances of fighting for victory.

"I think I can be really happy with today," Hamilton told Sky Sports F1.

"I think in the last race we were not fast in the race so I don't know, pace wise, how we will be tomorrow.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of qualifying at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on the Sepang International Circuit

"What I do know is we carry this deficit of straight-line speed. What that ultimately means is I think we're slightly quicker through corners, particularly low-speed corners I think we're a little bit quicker than say the Red Bulls and some of the others, but then on the straights we lose a lot.

"What that means then for the race on a track like this where degradation is very, very high, tyres are getting so hot all the time, is we have to push more through corners to try and keep up and make up for the loses in the straights.

"So that's ultimately what we have to be careful of doing too much of tomorrow [Sunday] and degrading more in trying to hold on to them. So I think we just have to run our own race, whatever that be pace wise, and not be focusing on trying to over-push to hold on.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the thrilling end to qualifying at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia!

"I think he's got the pace generally to pull away but if that's different when we start the race and we're able to hold on and we're in the fight, that'd be awesome as well. But all we can do is do our best, so I'll give it everything tomorrow."

Grand Prix distance tipped to be 'completely different ballgame'

F1 has experienced typically hot and humid conditions on the sport's first return to Malaysia in nine years but the abrasiveness of an aged Sepang track surface has created additional unexpected challenges.

Multiple pit stops are predicted in Sunday's 56-lap race, with teams expected to adopt different tyre strategies and all three tyre compounds likely to be seen.

Hamilton said after qualifying: "I'm much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track - I mean, they're overheating from the get-go.

"Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you're going to go.

"I like to think we've got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I'll just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow."

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur told Sky Sports F1: "It's a good qualifying but the success is on Sunday, it's never on Saturday.

"On top, we know that this one will be a lot about degradation, about race pace, about tyre management much more than great position.

"But I prefer to have a good qualifying than not. Starting from the first and second row with Lewis and Charles [Leclerc] is a good start, but we have to now put all our focus on the race."

Verstappen eyes first 2026 win but ready for 'not straightforward' race

Verstappen's 49th career pole position was his first since the final race of last season in Abu Dhabi, also the scene of the Dutchman's most recent win.

He made clear his determination on his arrival at Sepang on Thursday to claim a victory before the 2026 campaign ended.

Speaking after qualifying first at Sepang, Verstappen told Sky Sports F1: "As a team, we want to win. We're here to win, we're not just here to grab podiums.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen reacts to 'special' pole at the Bahrian GP in Malaysia

"So, we are looking forward to it but we also know that it's not going to be that straightforward.

"There are so many things that we still need to see that have to work well, or in our favour, but we'll see tomorrow."

Verstappen won the last Malaysia Grand Prix in 2017 so is aiming for back-to-back triumphs at Sepang, albeit with an unusually-large nine year-gap in between and under different race titles.

Sports.title: Ten injured as car drives into crowd gathered to support NRL team
Sports.content:
An 18-year-old man has been arrested after a vehicle drove into a crowd of people who had gathered to support the Newcastle Knights NRL team in New South Wales on Saturday, as the side trained ahead of their Grand Final against Sydney Roosters

Newcastle Knights CEO Peter Parr has expressed his deep concern after a vehicle drove into a crowd of people supporting the NRL team on Saturday, as they prepared for their Grand Final against Sydney Roosters.

Police say 10 people were injured in the incident in Wallsend, New South Wales, including several children, while the 18-year-old man driving the vehicle has been arrested.

Thousands had been cheering the team on this week as they trained ahead of Sunday's Grand Final at Accor Stadium, Australian Associated Press reported.

Two of the injured, a five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, are in critical condition, and the other eight are in stable condition at a hospital, according to New South Wales Police.

Those in a stable condition included another five-year-old girl and a two-year-old girl.

In a statement on Newcastle Knights' website, Parr extended the club's support to those who have been affected by the incident.

"Our thoughts and prayers are first and foremost with everyone who has been injured, their families and loved ones, and everyone who witnessed what occurred this morning," Parr said.

"What was meant to be a special morning for our community, thousands of Novocastrians coming together to farewell our team and show their support ahead of the Grand Final, has understandably turned into a distressing morning.

"We want to thank our incredible fans for the passion and support they showed our team this morning. The scenes across Newcastle demonstrated once again what this football club means to our community.

"I want to particularly acknowledge the extraordinary response of our first responders. The speed and professionalism of NSW Police, NSW Ambulance and all emergency services at the scene was remarkable.

"We also extend our deepest thanks to the doctors, nurses and entire team at John Hunter Hospital who are caring for those injured.

"I would also like to personally acknowledge NSW Police Commissioner Malcolm Lanyon for his leadership and support.

"Newcastle is a strong community. We have seen that strength throughout this week, and today we need to draw on it again with compassion, care and support for those who need it most."

Assistant Commissioner David Waddell of New South Wales Police told reporters on Saturday: "The male has been arrested.

"There were two other persons in the car. We had to get the three of them out of there because the crowd did turn on them.

"We have taken that male for mandatory drug and alcohol testing. He has now been taken to the police station where he will be dealt with, and likely charged later today."

Waddell added the crash was not believed to be related to terrorism.

"There is no concerns other than this being a tragic incident where a young person has done the wrong thing and driven irresponsibly, driven erratically, and obviously lost control of the vehicle into the crowd. But there's no, no suggestion at all that it's targeted or any ill motive," Waddell said.

Sports.title: 'Three tenths backwards' - Wolff admits confusion over Mercedes upgrades
Sports.content:
Toto Wolff has admitted his surprise at Mercedes' major upgrade package for the Bahrain Grand Prix having appeared to take the team backwards, following an underwhelming qualifying display.

Despite dominating the 2026 season, Mercedes have brought far fewer upgrades than their rivals at the front of the grid, which meant anticipation had built around the addition of their first major package since May.

The Silver Arrows arrived in Malaysia, which is hosting the event due to ongoing conflict in the Middle East, off the back of three successive race victories, and most expected that streak to continue with the help of the upgrades.

Instead, Drivers' Championship leader Kimi Antonelli could only manage fourth, while his team-mate George Russell was eighth as Red Bull's Max Verstappen claimed a dominant pole. Both Mercedes drivers will move up a place on the grid as a result of third-placed Isack Hadjar having to serve a grid penalty.

Wolff told Sky Sports F1: "Very difficult to understand. We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we didn't see all year, but then you can say it's very hot and the tarmac is different to all the (other) tracks.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Toto Wolff explains Mercedes issues after big upgrade package at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia

"It looked really good this morning (in final practice). We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding.

"And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.

"It looks like we are very draggy, because it's the first time that we are losing a lot of time on the straights, especially to Max.

"And then through the low-speed, we are not able to turn the car. There's just too much understeer. So, overall, things we haven't seen this year."

Verstappen's first pole of the season was secured by an emphatic margin, with Antonelli half a second behind and Russell a further couple of tenths back.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player SkyPad analysis of Max Verstappen's first pole position in 2026

While the extreme heat and track surface at the Sepang International Circuit make for unique conditions, Wolff was still alarmed by the timesheet.

"Something else is going on, and we have to understand," he added. "This is now working through the data and putting our heads together, because we still believe that the upgrade works. We just need to understand why not here.

"It's so different (in Malaysia), but nevertheless, you're expecting three tenths to kick in, and it looks like three-four-five tenths backwards.

"It's odd, but I guess we will find a solution."

'Affecting us more than others'

Russell arrived in Malaysia full of confidence after producing the strongest weekend of the season to claim victory in Azerbaijan, but has been unable to reproduce that form.

The Brit's deficit to Antonelli was made more disappointing by the fact he had two runs to his team-mate's one in the final part of qualifying, after a track limits in Q2 forced the Italian to use up an extra set of fresh tyres.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell and Kimi Antonelli react to Mercedes' qualifying at Bahrain GP in Malaysia

Russell told Sky Sports F1: "From the first practice we seemed to be ok, but we've just not really made any improvements since.

"It's a very demanding circuit on the tyres, the tarmac is all broke up, it's extremely rough, it's so hot out there and the tyres are going through hell.

"And, for whatever reason, it seems to be affecting us far more than others."

Antonelli was disappointed with his Q2 error but felt the incident had only potentially cost him one position on the grid given he felt Verstappen was out of reach, while Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton took second.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the thrilling end to qualifying at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia!

Antonelli told Sky Sports F1: "It's a shame for the mistake, but all in all, I think with a clean qualifying without the track limit, maybe P2, P3 on the road would have been possible, because obviously with only one set in Q3 it's never easy, especially with the track cooling down.

"But Max did an incredible job and was very quick. And also Ferrari, they made a huge a step compared to FP3.

"All in all, we have to be happy because it could have been much worse. We'll focus on tomorrow."
