Sports.title: Decline and fall: who will believe in Raheem Sterling now?
Sports.content:
In another world, where careers broke in different directions, Raheem Sterling would be in this England squad now, playing for the manager, Thomas Tuchel, who made him the No 1 target of the new Chelsea era after the Todd Boehly-Clearlake Capital takeover.

He is 16 months younger than Harry Kane, who continues to break records as England’s captain and hit a personal high of 73 goals last season. Sterling, meanwhile, is without a club and awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty at Basingstoke magistrates court to dangerous driving and possession of nitrous oxide after an incident that witnesses feared might kill someone.

How have their careers diverged so starkly? Why is Kane thriving while Sterling lives through such a sad and public decline?

Multiple sources, who asked not to be named to protect relationships, paint a complicated picture of Sterling. One describes him as a “lost soul”. Another believes he has been “hopelessly misguided” in his life and career. To understand his fall, it is pertinent to remember the magnitude of his rise.

Those who saw Sterling’s ascent – from the boy helping his mum on cleaning jobs in Stonebridge to the outrageously gifted footballer in Queens Park Rangers’ academy, to Liverpool’s first team at 17 – recall a player who seemed perfectly calibrated for success.

“Raheem was confident,” says Mark Anderson, the Liverpool youth scout who convinced the club to make him one of the most expensive 15-year-olds. “He played with passion and desire. From the first time I saw him, I thought he had the ingredients to become an international prospect.”

Sterling was quickly training with Liverpool’s first team, where players were stunned that this slight teen possessed a natural strength beyond many adults. He was rarely seen in the gym, yet held his own against Martin Skrtel, Mamadou Sakho and Kolo Touré, who towered over him.

View image in fullscreen Raheem Sterling scores his first senior goal for Liverpool against Reading at Anfield in 2012. Photograph: Allstar/Alamy

“Raheem was much tougher mentally than some people might have imagined,” Steven Gerrard wrote in his book, My Story, admitting that he and Jamie Carragher did not go easy on him in training.

Sterling’s resilience was tested when he rejected a £100,000-a-week contract and became engulfed in a public storm. It marked a turning point in how he was perceived: from England’s brightest prospect to arrogant young footballer – fair or not.

Sterling gave an interview to the BBC insisting he was not a “money-grabbing 20-year-old”. Liverpool-supporting pundits turned on him. Matters worsened when his then-agent, Aidy Ward, told the Evening Standard that Sterling wouldn’t sign a new deal even if they offered close to £1m per week. Liverpool sold him to Manchester City for an initial £44m that summer.

Public sentiment had begun to shift – from England’s fifth-youngest debutant to the player who told Roy Hodgson he was too tired for a game against Estonia – and the first images of Sterling inhaling from a balloon allegedly filled with nitrous oxide emerged in 2015. Leaving Liverpool darkened the mood, and the reputation has since haunted him. Particularly with England, where he became the scapegoat for the Euro 2016 last-16 exit to Iceland, the abuse so toxic that Sterling branded himself #TheHatedOne on Instagram. He was 21.

View image in fullscreen Sterling poses for a portrait for the Guardian at Manchester City’s training complex in 2015. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

Within two years he was the victim of a racially motivated attack outside Manchester City’s training ground and was racially abused by Chelsea supporters during a match at Stamford Bridge.

At his peak, he was spectacular. In 2019, he won a domestic treble with City, scored two goals in the FA Cup final and the winning penalty in the League Cup final shootout and secured the Football Writers’ Association’s footballer of the year award. A year later, Xavi Hernández claimed Sterling was “winning [the] race” to replace Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. The street footballer tamed by Pep Guardiola’s brilliantly rigid systems. By 2021, he had twice finished in the top 15 of Ballon d’Or voting.

This was a player who kept producing when it mattered as England reached the Euro 2020 final: two winners the only goals of England’s group stage, the opener against Germany in the last 16 and winning the penalty that led to the decisive goal against Denmark in the semi-final. But even his attempts to do good seemed to turn some against him.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City won the FA Cup final 6-0 against Watford in 2019, Sterling scoring twice. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

He became a central figure calling out racism in society, particularly his own depictions in the media after criticism for buying his mother a house. In 2020, he recorded an anti-racism video declaring “I will never tire of being black”, texting the contributors including Kevin De Bruyne, David Alaba and Jordan Henderson, to ask them to take part. He received an MBE a year later. If anything, it made some who did not know Sterling personally more fervently opposed to him.

One source who worked closely with Sterling describes him as “polite and charming”, saying: “He doesn’t come across as arrogant or having an attitude. He’s a nice guy, shy – quite bashful.”

In some quarters, there has been a degree of glee in the way Sterling’s career declined sharply after he joined Chelsea. He had won almost everything and, at 27, was entering the years when many players peak.

View image in fullscreen Sterling reacts after scoring England’s opener against Germany at Euro 2020. Photograph: Catherine Ivill/Getty Images

Sterling was the player Tuchel told Boehly to prioritise – the American billionaire captivated by the prospect of making a forward fresh from winning his fourth Premier League title in five years their marquee signing. Sterling signed a five-year contract on £325,000 a week.

Tuchel was sacked seven weeks later. In the years that followed, Sterling played under Graham Potter, Frank Lampard, Mauricio Pochettino and Enzo Maresca. One source questioned whether leaving the rigid structures of Brendan Rodgers at Liverpool and Guardiola at Manchester City for the chaos at Chelsea was damaging. From posting extraordinary numbers at City – 23 goals and 14 assists in 2017-18, 25 and 16 in 2018-19, 31 and 10 in 2019-20 – his output dwindled.

A collective decision at Chelsea in summer 2024 to sell him was made based on his personal life and ability to play in the team. In a particularly brutal week, two days before the start of the 2024-25 season, Maresca told Sterling he was not part of his plans and left him out of the squad for the game against Manchester City and a Conference League tie with Servette in which Pedro Neto wore his No 7 shirt. Sterling was forced to train away from the first team.

View image in fullscreen Looking dejected for Chelsea, where Sterling’s form dropped off amid a rapid turnover of managers. Photograph: Joe Prior/Visionhaus/Getty Images

It seems he was not entirely innocent here. The Guardian was told he was known to turn up late for training when he was supposed to set an example, though sources close to Sterling say he never faced a recorded disciplinary at Chelsea. His treatment ultimately was harsh, though it is understood Maresca assessed his wingers during friendlies until a final call was made.

Sterling made clear he wanted to stay in London for his family, and Chelsea reluctantly sanctioned a loan to Arsenal. He scored once, in a Carabao Cup game against League One club Bolton on 25 September 2024, his most recent professional goal.

When he returned, sources say he was told to stay away from the main facilities at Cobham, though a Chelsea source denied this was the case. Sterling declined loan interest from Juventus, but by January, after six months without playing, needed to move for the sake of his career.

The club agreed to buy him out of the remaining 18 months of his contract at a reduced fee. Their statement announcing his departure was 23 words long.

View image in fullscreen In action for Feyenoord, where Sterling chose to rebuild his career under Robin van Persie. Photograph: Wart Brinkerhof/MTB/Alamy

Sterling chose to rebuild under Robin van Persie at Feyenoord. It was disastrous: ruthlessly mocked on social media by the club’s fans, laughed at in the stadium.

One source who worked with Sterling compared his career trajectory with Michael Owen’s – two teen prodigies whose speed was their greatest asset, and whose careers faded as that diminished. Owen played his final season at Stoke, making eight Premier League appearances from the bench, and retired at 33. Sterling will be 32 in December. Another source questioned whether winning so much and earning vast sums had dulled the desire required to stay at the top.

Sterling returned home from the Netherlands and, 11 days later, drove his Lamborghini for more than an hour on motorways during rush hour while inhaling nitrous oxide from balloons, it seemed like a cry for help. He admitted to officers, when arrested in May, that he had a “problem” with nitrous oxide – a stark admission from an athlete with hopes of playing again.

“It’s sad to see that someone struggles, because he was a devoted father for his children and he was a family guy, a nice guy to be around,” Tuchel said on Friday. “It just seems that he goes through a difficult period. I’m not sure how much is his fault; sometimes you just enter a strange spiral in your life, a downward spiral. Thoughts are with him of course. The belief is always that he can turn it around.”

View image in fullscreen Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty to dangerous driving in September. Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PA

Standing in the dock in court dressed in black last month, while Liverpool were preparing for a League Cup game against Tottenham, Sterling learned he faces the real prospect of prison when the court reconvenes in November.

“Before he was Raheem Sterling the international footballer, the Premier League player and the name everybody knew, he was simply a young boy with a football who somebody had to believe in,” Anderson says.

Will anyone still believe in him now?

Sports.title: The football horse that Andy Burnham rode in on is now bucking his vibe | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
It’s coming for you. It’s coming for you. Oh Andy Burnham, the hugely problematic relationship between principle and realpolitik in post-cash Britain. It’s coming for you. We are going all in on football chat these days, aren’t we? Football populism, football blokeyness, the stylings of the football everyman. That was certainly the horse the prime minister rode in on a few months ago. And right now it’s a horse that’s still very much snorting around the cabinet room, and threatening to run right over the top of him.

Also: fresh plot twists. Previous governments have been thrown into early-term crisis by things such as war, sex scandals and economic meltdown. But never, and historians will have time to pore over this in the coming decades, by the urgent need to overpay for Jack Grealish. “The ramifications of this are MASSIVE,” the man on the radio said on Thursday morning. And he was right. There are ramifications here. And the ramifications, well, Clive, they’re massive. In this case the man on the radio was discussing the United Kingdom’s multilayered geopolitical meltdown through the prism of whether this means Spurs are less or more likely to get relegated. And to be fair there are very few global events that can’t be better understood through a Spurs-in-crisis lens.

The Arctic ice shelf is about to collapse. Chinese military scientists have worked out how to land three successive nuclear warheads in exactly the same spot, thereby causing not only standard mass destruction but disturbing the Earth’s crust at a tectonic level. Sounds bad. But break it down for me. Does this mean Spurs are more likely to be relegated or less likely to be relegated? Zombie apocalypse. People eating pine cones in bunkers. Yes, fine. But is there any upside here for Roberto De Zerbi’s troubled north London tenure?

Football has always loved a ramification, loved it when things are huge and sweeping, parcelled out in scrolling headlines and graphics that go whoosh. But this week there is a genuine sense of scaling up. When it comes to Burnham and Manchester City, football is not providing an analogy for politics. It is politics. The singularity has happened. We are the ramification. Football is the captain now. It’s in the room, taking the big chair, digging its great, dripping, bloody fingernails right into the key faultline in Burnham’s political persona.

There is a wild and vengeful irony in this, because football is so tightly stitched into Burnham’s own story. Abu Dhabi provided the seed capital for his political point of difference, the Manchesterism energy that carried him into Downing Street. Football gave him his lingua franca, the refreshingly relatable vibe, which is a fairly low bar given Burnham’s immediate predecessor addressed the public in the manner of a deeply disappointed human-sized water vole that is only now realising, as it stands at its lighted plinth, that it’s not actually supposed to be able to talk.

But football is also fire from the gods. Be wary of this thing. Nothing has cut through like this, but nothing has the same wild popular energy. And like the government of the United Arab Emirates, it will also come looking for its pound of meat in return.

View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham makes a point to the Manchester City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, at Vincent Kompany’s testimonial in 2019. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

Personally, I like Burnham and want him to succeed. I like that someone is talking about altering fundamentally the way the nation feels, not just its level of economic activity, acknowledging that the current version of net human happiness has fallen short, that we have created a country that sold itself off by the pound, outsourcing its social fabric to a series of shell companies in Panama.

I like the fact the person having this grand-scale vision is not called Ramsey Fartington-Smythe, but Andy Burnham, which sounds like the name of a mid-90s deep house DJ in a northern club called Flesh, or Paper, currently popping up on leaflets stapled to lamp-posts underneath people like DJ Flexxxx and MC Deathface (“plus Andy Burnham”). This Andy Burnham wants to change the country. Good. He’s right. At which point, enter football, and the deeper problem of whether the things Burnham says and the things he is required to do, as expressed perfectly in the football-centred culture that got him here, can actually exist in the same space.

double quotation mark He could, for example, stop thanking the UAE so profusely. What does he think this is, a favour? It’s a business deal

Burnham gave two speeches this week. One of them was kind, soft, generous, seductive. This was chimney-sweep Andy, talking about restoring balance to society and control to our lives, little person versus big person, about chatbot life, waiting-list culture, the move away from living in a country that makes a good show of openly hating the people who live there. Then he said some other things, words that have now been toned down and walked back by Downing Street, but which seemed to express a bizarre degree of cognitive dissonance. “I would be really concerned to lose them,” the prime minister of the United Kingdom said, expressing sympathy for an oppressive monarchical regime throwing money at an effort to escape the rules that bind everyone else.

He went on to say it would be “wrong” to “jump to a conclusion” here. Which, to be clear, would be a conclusion based on the application of English law by an independent judicial panel, with the potential for far more serious sanctions. Andy, you’re the actual prime minister. This isn’t an Everton message board. It’s an issue of deep public and regulatory concern. There is no place here for tribal gripes or pub-level football chat. Finally Burnham said the quiet thing out loud. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester.”

Here you have the spectacle of a man trying to live two ideological lives simultaneously. What is Manchesterism anyway? In its base form, it’s the same as Londonism. Many other things have contributed and taken this on. Political devolution. Local talent. Tech companies. The Intelligence Economy. But Abu Dhabi’s investment was the big fast-forward after the 2008 financial crisis.

This was nine years before Burnham became mayor. But he benefited hugely, politically and personally, from the investments of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the same people pumping money into Nolito, who were also putting a billion into the New Islington transformation, another billion into the Manchester Campus, a place on the Manchester tram map that is now literally called Etihad, with all the talk of locals being moved out, unaffordable housing, civic leaders shying away from the human-rights record of their partners.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Follow the money and you never know where you might end up. Look at this from a certain angle and Abu Dhabi basically gave us downtown Andy Burnham. He’s another Etihad academy graduate, the Phil Foden of Downing Street. And this is a living, breathing channel to power.

One of Burnham’s first calls as prime minister was to Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, president of the UAE. Who is of course the brother of Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, owner of Manchester City. And who also employed as a key aide one Jaber Mohamed, said to be personally responsible for payments through Etisalat that form part of the alleged cooking of the Premier League books. When Burnham says he is bringing the great Manchester success story to government, this is an umbilical part of what he’s describing.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans thank Sheikh Mansour with a banner, but they’re already thanking him by promoting his brand. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

This is, of course, not a problem of Burnham’s own making. He has to live in the world as it is, required by the job to cosy up to investors whose behaviour is a perfectly realised example of the overclass billionaire-ism he sets himself against.

But Burnham also has a choice to make. He could, for example, stop thanking the UAE so profusely. What does he think this is, a favour? It’s a business deal, with something very clearly going back in return. It brings to mind the “Thank You Sheikh Mansour” banner at the Etihad Stadium. What is this for exactly? You’re already thanking him by promoting the brand, cheering the soft power, allowing him to own the streets beneath your feet.

In the end what we have here is not an analogy for modern Britain, a parable of loss of control and alienation, of being hostage only to power. It is instead these things being enacted right in front of us. The wider choice for Burnham, and also for Manchester City’s fans, is: what do you want to have, what do you want to be? Billions will come and go. There will be hard economic consequences if the UAE takes its ball away. But the rule of law, not rolling over in the face of power, retaining your sovereign assets. Do these things feel good too? And in a way that money can’t actually buy? Isn’t this exactly what Burnham No 1 was talking about?

The alternative, as we have now discovered, is being pushed around in a bath chair and made to dance for cash. This is all right there in the cabinet room as we speak, asking what you want to stand for. Realpolitik? Or some sort of stab at real things, real principles? Even, in some glorious reconditioned future, Spurs being relegated of their own sovereign, self-governing accord.

Sports.title: Etihad’s statements on funding appear to contradict Manchester City’s defence
Sports.content:
Manchester City’s defence in their appeal against the independent commission’s guilty verdict in more than 100 charges of financial rule breaches appears to be contradicted by previous statements made by their main sponsor, Etihad Airways, to the US government.

A key element of City’s appeal, which was confirmed by the club on Friday, is understood to be based on their claim that commercial contracts, which the commission concluded were part-funded by their owner, were in fact paid for by the Abu Dhabi government.

In a 2015 submission to the United States’ department of commerce, transportation and state as part of investigation into state-owned airlines, Etihad described suggestions that the government paid for its sponsorship of the club as “false”.

Etihad, the state-owned national airline of the United Arab Emirates, has been City’s principal shirt sponsor since 2009 and was the main source of the initial transformation of their revenue that followed their purchase by Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group (Adug) the previous year.

In 2011 City announced a 10-year naming rights deal worth £400m for the Etihad Stadium, which was extended on improved terms in 2021.

The Etihad submission to the US department of commerce said: “The assertion that the Abu Dhabi government paid for Etihad’s sponsorship of English Premier League football club Manchester City is false. In 2011, Etihad and Manchester City entered into a 10-year sponsorship agreement, which included naming rights for Manchester City’s stadium. Etihad funded this sponsorship from its own liquidity.

“We are government-owned and have been since our founding. We are and have always been clear that we do not receive any subsidies from the Abu Dhabi government, and that we are financed through a combination of equity, shareholder and commercial loans.

“Our shareholder [the Abu Dhabi government]’s equity and loans are not subsidies under any applicable definition; they are the means by which the Abu Dhabi government has sensibly invested in a successful business model.”

City’s argument is also a departure from the position the club took in their successful appeal against Uefa’s charges of breaching financial fair play rules at the court of arbitration for sport in 2020, when they maintained that all their sponsorship income was provided by their commercial partners.

The commission dismissed City’s argument as “untrue” in its core decision published on Tuesday. Paragraph 77 of the judgment states: “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme.” City submitted their appeal on Thursday evening and insist they have “a body of irrefutable evidence” that will prove the commission’s findings to be untrue.

The Football Association has confirmed it has powers to take disciplinary action against City and key individuals at the club. The FA said the independent commission’s decision on City had “significant implications for the integrity of the game” and that it “will take action where appropriate”.

The FA will wait until the appeal process has concluded – which based on the Premier League’s rule book should be by the end of January – before deciding whether to take action but said it was monitoring the case closely.

The FA has powers to take action against individuals proved to have broken rules and/or acted dishonestly, which the commission concluded had been the case. The names of those involved were redacted in the 40-page core judgment published this week but the FA could ask the Premier League for an unredacted version.

“The Independent Commission’s decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game,” the FA statement read. “We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.

Quick Guide How do I 

“As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely.”

The FA’s standard practice is to wait for disciplinary proceedings conducted by leagues, such as the Premier League or EFL, to run their course before taking action.

In July the FA fined Chelsea £10m and imposed a suspended two-window transfer ban after the club admitted 74 breaches of its agent regulations, four months after the Premier League fined them £10.75m for the same offences, which related to unlawful payments to players and agents. The FA has additional powers to take action against individuals, although did not do so in the Chelsea case because those involved are no longer working in football.

The FA charged Southampton’s manager, Tonda Eckert, with misconduct for his role in the so-called Spygate saga involving Middlesbrough in May, with a disciplinary hearing taking place last month that could result in the German being given a lengthy ban from football.

Sports.title: Thrown in with Giggs and Beckham: how Manchester United tried to get Billy Kenny
Sports.content:
“So this is the scouser ya been goin’ on aboot then …” My face turned Manchester United red. Scanning the room full of smiles and staring eyes, I identified the mystery Scottish voice as the man who’d just become the first player to score more than 20 league goals for the club since George Best in the 1960s. “Good answer,” replied Brian McClair after following up on my smile and nod by asking whether I supported Everton or Liverpool. “Ye’ll dee well ’ere laddie.”

Brian Kidd had just introduced me to the Man United first team by silencing the room to draw attention to my presence. “Lads, this is Billy from up the road,” he said. I was still starstruck from seeing all these famous faces as my chauffeur for the day, Eric Harrison, pulled up in the car park at The Cliff a few minutes earlier. Paul McGrath. Mark Hughes. Bryan Robson. Kevin Moran. Norman Whiteside. I ticked them all off in my head. Thank fuck I was developing an ear for everyday Glaswegian because after a bit of piss-taking from the first-teamers about being a scouser, I found myself standing in an office at the end of a short and narrow corridor, shaking hands with another one.

“This is ma boy, this is ma boy …” Alex Ferguson leapt up from his chair to give me a hug. Just like Dalglish at Liverpool, Ferguson made me feel special. I’ve no idea how he knew about it, but he inquired about my trip with Liverpool to Wembley for the cup final. Then he told me all about watching 20 minutes of me playing for Liverpool schoolboys against Salford after Eric Harrison had watched me a few times. After I told him how made up I was to be there, he ordered me to go out and enjoy myself. Which is exactly what happened.

The few dozen trialists all got split up and mixed in with the lads who had signed schoolboy forms already, all kitted out in gleaming Manchester United training kit. Brian Kidd told me I could keep the kit, which was sound. I already had my eye on it, so I didn’t need to risk making the wrong impression. Although there were kids from all over the show – Brazil, Argentina, Ghana – I struck up an instant rapport with a lad from Scotland.

Tommy Harrison is unforgettable. I think he was captain of Scotland schoolboys and came to United with a big reputation. We got on like a house on fire, trading nicknames. I confused him at first by shouting “rock on, Tommy” every time I saw him. We worked out that his diet of Scottish telly left him in the dark about the catchphrases of TV comics Cannon and Ball. Wee Jimmy Krankie was more his scene.

I looked Tommy up a few years back online and found he didn’t go on to make a long career at the peak of the game. For whatever reason, he turned down United and signed for Hearts. I think he played lower leagues in Scotland for a few clubs but back in 1988 I would have put serious money on him getting into the United first team. But there are a million and one ways to fall away. I just hope he’s happy and healthy whatever he’s doing today.

On the pitch, I recall getting put in centre-mid in all the games, a slight departure from my right-midfield role in the Liverpool schoolboys games and a bit of a surprise given that’s where they’d seen me in action. I loved it. Not just because it suited my restless, obsessive, compulsive nature. More headers, tackles, touches of the ball. Bang at the centre of things. There’s another big reason I liked it so much: Ryan Wilson. The name might not mean much to many readers. But once I explain that he later changed his surname to Giggs, it all makes sense. I’d played against him several times in fierce clashes with Salford schoolboys. We were direct rivals. The outcome of our ding-dong battle on the wing always decided the result. So I was made up to play in the same team as him for the first time during the trial.

View image in fullscreen Billy Kenny (third left in the front row) with Liverpool schoolboys. Photograph: Courtesy of Billy Kenny

I recognised a fair few lads there from Salford and Manchester schoolboys teams and enjoyed the buzz of playing with them all for a change. Despite the scouse-Manc thing, I got on well with all those lads.

The first few days of training were great. Me and Tommy settled into a nice routine, enjoying the intensity and quality of the games then filling our bellies with boss scran. At the start of the second week, we both noticed a crowd building near a pitch where younger kids played. As we wandered over, we felt a crackle of excitement as parents and coaches gathered on the sideline. One kid kept drawing gasps of astonishment from adults watching. Every pair of eyes seemed drawn to him. He didn’t say much, but I noticed what sounded like a cockney accent. Small, skinny, with spiky blond hair, he looked like a baby. But every time he got the ball he’d do something mad. His touch, technique, balance and range of passing were unreal. It turns out me and Tommy were getting our first glimpse of David Beckham.

He must have been about 12 or 13 but played like a seasoned professional. I could say exactly the same about my enemy/teammate Ryan Wilson, by the way. But they were very different players. Ryan was lightning quick and almost impossible to stop. Baby-faced Beckham was about stupidly good technique and total control of the football. I’m so pleased no one can ever try to claim that either of them failed to fulfil their huge potential. Mixing with exceptional young players in this environment did wonders for my self-belief.

View image in fullscreen Eric Harrison with players including Ryan Giggs (second left) and David Beckham (fourth left) at Manchester United. Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty Images

But it wasn’t without problems. I recall feeling massively homesick in about week three. I’d not heard a scouse accent for weeks – apart from the shite ones when other lads tried to take the piss. I know it was only Manchester but it might as well have been Madagascar for all I cared. It just wasn’t home.

Brian and Eric knew I was struggling. Brian took me to his home for my tea one night. He fed me steak and chips, talked about my daa and told me just how perfect Man United would be for me to develop into a footballer. The attention to my welfare continued throughout the trial. In the final week, Eric pulled me aside to tell me “the boss” and all the staff were made up with me. So much so that they’d invited my daa over for the last day to talk about my future.

“The boss” and Brian Kidd greeted us like kings when we walked into his office. Ferguson told me how they had loads of great kids already signed up and that I was exactly what they needed in a central midfielder. He knew I was in demand. If I chose United, I’d be guaranteed “the security” of a three-year pro contract, he said. With those words, all the crippling insecurities seemed to disappear. I knew instantly that I had the ability to make it as a footballer.

Sports.title: Nations League: Italy earn draw against 10-man France, Northern Ireland stun Ukraine
Sports.content:
Zinedine Zidane’s first home game in charge of France ended with a 1-1 draw against Italy in the Nations League on Friday. Visiting keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma produced a string of saves to frustrate fans at Stade de France, while the hosts ended the game with 10 men after Dayot Upamecano’s late dismissal.

Michael Olise put France ahead in the 55th minute with a curling shot that went in off the crossbar, following a short free-kick taken by Rayan Cherki. But poor defending midway through the second half allowed Italy defender Alessandro Bastoni to run through and clip a low shot inside the right post.

Moise Kean missed a close-range chance early on for Italy, shooting straight at goalkeeper Mike Maignan. Donnarumma made a double save from Ousmane Dembélé and Désiré Doué early in the second half, then produced a brilliant low save to deny Adrien Rabiot moments after Italy’s equaliser.

Upamecano was sent off late in the game for picking up a second yellow card, but the hosts kept pushing for a winner, and Donnarumma had to claw away Eduardo Camavinga’s shot in stoppage time to preserve a point.

“We would have liked to win for our fans tonight but I was obviously really touched and delighted to be back at the Stade de France,” Zidane said afterwards. “I am happy with the performance albeit not with the result. We had chances to score a second goal and we didn’t do it. But I am really proud of my players.”

The Italy manager, Roberto Mancini, was pleased with his side’s efforts. “I think this was a great performance tonight against one of the best teams in the world, with very positive aspects to it,” he said. “We are on the right road, and we need to keep playing this way.”

France stay top of Group A1, a point clear of Belgium who eased to a 3-0 home win over bottom side Turkey in Liège. The two neighbours meet again on Monday at the Stade de France, while Italy host Turkey in Bologna.

View image in fullscreen Kevin De Bruyne celebrates after scoring one of his two goals for Belgium in Liège. Photograph: Virginie Lefour/Belga/Shutterstock

Kevin De Bruyne, in his 127th match for the Red Devils, scored the opening goal with a cool finish from the edge of the box, after a nice one-two with Dodi Lukebakio. Turkey posed the greater attacking danger after the Napoli midfielder’s opener but could not find a leveller and were punished just before the hour mark.

De Bruyne claimed his second goal in the 59th minute, curling a ball from the edge of the box past Turkey goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir into the top corner. Romelu Lukaku, Belgium’s all-time record goalscorer, added a third in the 76th minute, skewing the ball home from Charles De Ketelaere’s low cross.

In League B, Northern Ireland stunned Ukraine 3-0 in Slovakia to go clear at the top of their group and boost their hopes of promotion to the top tier.

Ciaron Brown, the only player in Michael O’Neill’s starting lineup over the age of 24, scored twice either side of Isaac Price’s goal in Trnava. The away win puts Northern Ireland on seven points from three games, and they are still yet to concede going into Monday’s clash with Georgia in Belfast.

Northern Ireland’s positive start was quickly rewarded as Kieran Morrison floated a corner to the back post where Ruairi McConville headed it back for Brown, earning his 33rd cap, to prod home despite the desperate efforts of Illia Zabarnyi on the line.

View image in fullscreen Ciaron Brown (left, No 22) celebrates his second goal of the night in Trnava. Photograph: Dénes Erdős/AP

Georgiy Sudakov was the first Ukraine player to get a sight of goal but his 19th-minute effort was straight at keeper Pierce Charles, and moments later the hosts were 2-0 down. Morrison’s first-time ball into the box was met powerfully by Price at the back post – earning Morrison an assist in his first competitive international.

Brown’s second came in bizarre fashion just after the hour – the 28-year-old Oxford defender went up to flick on Pierce Charles’ free-kick from inside the Northern Ireland half, and Ukraine goalkeeper Dmytro Riznyk let the bouncing ball slip through his legs to wrap up a remarkable result.

“It’s a great result for us, a great performance,” O’Neill said. “The early goal helps settle us into the game. The second goal was a brilliant goal. We worked it the length of the pitch. We were patient. We could have crossed it early but that allowed us to get more men in the box and it’s a brilliant header from Isaac.

“The third goal is fortuitous but it’s a mistake by the opposition, so we have to capitalise on that, but I thought throughout our performance was brilliant,” the Northern Ireland manager added. “We limited the opposition to crosses and shots from outside the box and I thought we defended brilliantly.”

The Liverpool full-back Milos Kerkez scored the only goal in the other Group B2 tie to earn Hungary a 1-0 win over Georgia, moving the Magyars level with Ukraine in second place with four points from three games.

Edin Dzeko brought the curtain down on his international career during Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 1-1 draw with Sweden. The 40-year-old was withdrawn after 63 minutes of his 152nd appearance, with the hosts trailing after Viktor Gyökeres had scored two minutes earlier. Kerim Alajbegovic ensured the spoils would be shared with an 80th-minute effort.

In the group’s other game, Poland thumped Romania 6-0 with Robert Lewandowski hitting a hat-trick. Radu Dragusin was sent off in the 22nd minute for bringing Lewandowski down in the area, and the veteran striker got up to convert the penalty. Lewandowski struck again in the 47th and 86th minutes, with Piotr Zielinski, Jan Bednarek and a Virgil Ghita own goal completing the scoring in Warsaw.

View image in fullscreen Robert Lewandowski scores from the penalty spot to kick off Poland’s 6-0 rout of Romania. Photograph: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

The Faroe Islands earned an impressive 1-1 home draw with Group C3 leaders Slovakia, Adrian Justinussen’s second-half goal cancelling out a Gunnar Vatnhamar own goal before the break. Moldova moved up to second in the group with a 2-1 away victory over Kazakhstan.

Elsewhere in the third tier, Vasilije Adzic scored twice as Group C2 leaders Montenegro won 2-1 in Latvia, while Cyprus beat Armenia 2-0 despite a second-half red card for Kostas Pileas.

Sports.title: Slegers feels support from Arsenal hierarchy despite dismal run but biggest test looms
Sports.content:
Renée Slegers says she has felt the full support of Arsenal’s board and praised her senior players for showing “monumental leadership” this week as she vows to find solutions to recent poor form before Sunday’s pivotal trip to Manchester City.

One win in five matches has put Slegers under mounting pressure. Arsenal let slip a two-goal lead to draw at Paris FC in the Women’s ­Champions League on Wednesday and in the WSL they have slipped seven points behind City, the ­leaders and defending champions, having scored only twice in their four league games.

Slegers was in a determined mood on Friday, speaking of a “strong togetherness” at the club. Asked whether she felt the full support of the board, she replied: “Yes, that’s what I felt. That’s been positive and that’s helped me. The club’s leadership has been really good and positive for me in this moment because everyone thinks this is a difficult time and this is not something that we want for the team and for the club.

“But the leadership from Clare [Wheatley, the director of football], Rich [Garlick, CEO], James [King, director of football operations], Jodie [Taylor, technical director] has been superb. So I want to give everything back to the club.

“There’s been a lot of contact, of course. There’s a strong ­togetherness and I’ve really felt their support and they’re here with us, which I’m very grateful for, of course, because I care so much for the team, for the club. I believe in the potential that we ­possess. I believe we can come out of this.”

The 37-year-old Dutchwoman began with an apology to the media for her no-show after Wednesday’s game, when Arsenal conceded a bizarre penalty after Leah Williamson was penalised for handling the ball in the area when she thought she was taking a goal-kick. Slegers’s assistant Aaron D’Antino stepped in.

“After the game there was emotion from my end,” Slegers said. “[I] make the decision to be with the team instead.” She said that had felt important but added: “I will be there next time. I said to the team: ‘I’m angry, I’m really angry, and let’s try to use the emotions that we’re feeling and let it fuel us moving forward, so that’s definitely part of what I hope [to see] and what I believe is going to help us in the right direction.”

Sunday presents a huge challenge against a side who have a 100% record in the WSL this season and have won all their home league matches since Andrée Jeglertz took over as head coach in the summer of 2025.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Slegers praised her squad for their response since Wednesday, saying her “players have been brilliant – I’ve seen the best sides of them”.

“What the group has shown, it’s something I haven’t seen before,” she said. “The captains in the team they’ve been monumental; it’s the strongest leadership I’ve seen so far working within football, they’ve been amazing. They’re very calm, composed, solution-orientated and laser-focused. It was a great moment and I think vital for us moving forward.

“It’s strange because I have to be finding a solution, so I have to be calm, I have to give direction, I have to lead now. But at the same time, what I also feel is gratitude for how everyone is responding and how together we are and how the session on the pitch was today. It was really, really good.”

Sports.title: Alex Iwobi lands unexpected managerial role alongside Fulham contract
Sports.content:
Fulham midfielder Alex Iwobi has taken up a managerial role in Baller League with his new Project 17 team.

The 30-year-old has started all five of the Cottagers’ league games this season, proving he is still a key figure for the club.



3 Alex Iwobi's new role will see him combine playing and managerial duties Credit: Getty

However, the Nigerian has one eye on his off-the-pitch projects with his Baller League commitments now set to take centre stage alongside his Fulham contract.

Iwobi is the latest high profile figure to come into the indoor football league led by YouTube sensation KSI.

The star joins Micah Richards, Daniel Sturridge, Chloe Kelly, Ian Wright and Jens Lehmann on the touchline.



Iwobi, who had previously expressed an interest in Baller League, has never hidden his ambitions to explore other avenues away from football.

Iwobi's other ventures

“I’m not just a footballer, I like to express myself in many different ways, whether that’s music, fashion, charity. Anything really,” Iwobi said.



“Of course, yes I’m a footballer first and foremost. I like to show people who I am and everyone knows I like to play fireballs, I like to play street football, so it’s a part of me.

“So if I can get involved in Baller League, all my boys know, the team knows, Project 17 knows that I’ll be down.”



He also provided an insight into his managerial philosophy, claiming his style would be an ‘entertaining’ one.

“Alex Iwobi the manager, he’s probably going to be the same as a player. Very chilled, very entertaining, very passionate. Wants his team to win,” he added.

“All about excitement. I just want my players to enjoy their football. That’s the advice I’ve been given as a kid.

3 KSI serves as the president of the UK Baller League Credit: Getty



3 Iwobi joins a host of recognisable names in the dugout in this season's Baller League Credit: Getty

“When I’m managing a team I’m gonna tell them, “Look, of course we’re going to have tough times, tough games, but enjoy the craft, enjoy the challenge.

“People that are watching are going to see me enjoy the difficult times as well as the exciting and the winning times.

“Baller League is entertaining. I like small-sided games. Even when I’m training, that’s probably one of the most exciting things I look forward to.



“I’ve come from playing street football in cages, power league fireball. It’s something I’m very passionate about. Sometimes I enjoy it more than the actual games.”

Iwobi began his career at Arsenal, playing 149 times for the club before securing a £34million switch to Everton in 2019.

The Nigerian clocked up 140 appearances for the Merseyside club before moving to Fulham in 2023.

Sports.title: Man City given survival hope as financial expert predicts number of points to be deducted
Sports.content:
Man City given survival hope as financial expert predicts number of points to be deducted

Manchester City are not guaranteed to go down even if they are hit with a mammoth points deduction this season, financial expert Kieran Maguire believes.

The Premier League giants were recently dealt a seismic guilty verdict by an independent commission over 115 charges of financial wrongdoing.

3 City are fighting for their Premier League existence with any number of sanctions possible Credit: Getty

City, who have appealed against the decision and maintain their innocence, are adjudged to have inflated their revenue by more than £900million by disguising owner funding as sponsorship.

In what is now undoubtedly the biggest scandal in Premier League history, the breaches occurred over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018.

City won eight trophies during this period, including three top-flight titles.

talkSPORT understands the club intend to argue that sponsorship deals were propped up by the Abu Dhabi government, not Abu Dhabi United Group and consequently owner Sheikh Mansour.

However, this evidence was dismissed during the independent commission's investigation, while Etihad Airways have already denied receiving government funding in relation to their deal with City.

All this leaves City facing unprecedented sanctions unless the verdict can be overturned.

What could City's punishment be?

New Premier League regulations state that the appeal hearing must take place within 12 weeks.

With the hearing lasting a maximum of five days, a decision will then be given within 30 days.

If the verdict is upheld, the case will then move to a hearing over possible sanctions, with pressure from other clubs in the Premier League for punishment to be delivered this season.

Football finance expert Maguire outlined the precedents already in place for monetary and sporting punishments in the Premier League.

3 Chelsea were recently handed the biggest financial penalty in Premier League history but, unlike City, were credited for self-reporting and co-operating in full Credit: Getty

However, he stressed City's case far outweighs anything that has come before, including the scandals surrounding Chelsea, Everton, Leicester and Nottingham Forest.

Nevertheless, Maguire believes there is still a realistic scenario whereby City are punished this season and still manage to stay up.

"As far as the outcome is concerned, I think we've got to look at precedent," Maguire told talkSPORT.

"Chelsea were given significant fines from both the Football Association (and remember, the Football Association might take this up later) and from the Premier League for around £20m over their financial misdemeanours, not registering payments to unauthorised agents and so on.

"So you would expect that to be quite significant. Also, it was noticeable in the Chelsea claim that the club agreed to pay the Premier League legal costs, which were quite substantial. These are going to be far bigger.

"So we're probably talking about £50m-£60m in all probability, plus a substantial fine.

3 Everton and Forest have been handed significant points deductions over PSR breaches in recent years Credit: Getty

"Then, of course, we've got the precedent of Nottingham Forest, Everton, and Leicester City, all of whom breached the PSR limits and were given points deductions.

"Now, the logic behind that is that if you spend more money on players, it gives you an advantage on the pitch, and that advantage on the pitch should be punished with a punishment on the pitch in the form of a points deduction.

"Given that the Man City offences took place over a longer period of time, therefore it's multiple offences over multiple years, you would expect a multiple of the points deductions that we've seen.

"We don't know by how much Man City exceeded the PSR limits, and we're now working on the basis of reading some of the former reports that it works out as a three-point deduction to kick off with, plus one extra point per extra £6.5m over the limit. So that will form a rough basis.

"And then there's a further issue, have you assisted with the investigation? We'll suggest they probably haven't.

So that's called an aggregating factor, and the panel could subsequently give an additional points deduction on top of that.

"If all of those are proven post-appeal, my gut reaction is we would be looking for somewhere in the region of perhaps 50 to 60 points.

"If it's more than 70 points, they're effectively relegated.

"From a drama point of view, and I appreciate the commission's not interested in the drama, you give Man City a 50-point deduction, they go to minus 35, there's 33 matches left to play for, you've actually got a fantastic story.

"Because they could try and stay up. They could just about stay up. And I think the attitude of the players and everything would be fascinating.

"But that's a Hollywood story, rather than, is that appropriate?"

Sports.title: Tottenham made major mistake selling in-form star and keeping player who ‘no one likes’
Sports.content:
Tottenham made major mistake selling in-form star and keeping player who ‘no one likes’

Tottenham have been accused of making a huge howler by offloading academy prospect Troy Parrott.

The in-form Republic of Ireland international was on the books at Tottenham until he completed a permanent move to Dutch side AZ Alkmaar in 2024.

6 Troy Parrott is in a rich vein of form for club and country Credit: AFP

The move proved to be a fruitful one as Parrott took his game to another level, netting 51 goals in 97 games.

That earned him a summer switch to La Liga club Real Betis in a deal worth around £17million.

It didn’t take long for the club’s supporters to take Parrott to their hearts as the striker came off the bench to score the winner in a 1-0 win over Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid last month.

Then, in midweek Parrott scored one of the goals of the season in Ireland’s 2-2 Nations League draw against Austria to put himself further in the spotlight.

Meanwhile, Tottenham’s issues in front of goal have been laid bare this season.

Roberto De Zerbi’s men have scored just twice in five Premier League outings with Dominic Solanke out of form and Richarlison currently out of favour.

Discussing whether Spurs had made an error in allowing Parrott to leave the club following Harry Kane’s exit three years ago, Rory Jennings and Ade Oladipo believe Parrott would have been offered the time needed to develop into a first-choice striker.

Tottenham's big blunder

“I don’t know why clubs do this,” Jennings told talkSPORT. “Football fans are often seen as being quite demanding.

“I think football clubs are quite cynical and scornful about their own support.

“Do you know why Tottenham fans would have been so forgiving? They would have given him so much time, so much time to learn on the job.

6 Parrott netted his first Betis goal in the 1-0 win over Real Madrid last month Credit: Getty

“He would have been allowed to make his mistakes. He would have been given a forgiveness that would not have been extended to Richarlison.

“He would have bought the club some time.

“If they would have put Troy Parrott up front and the results were exactly the same, the support would have allowed him to develop.

“Chelsea fans were always like this. If a young player came in, whether it was Gael Kakuta or Charlie Colkett or whoever. You’re allowed to make your mistakes.

“If it’s a seasoned pro, a Brazilian international and someone who’s cost a lot of money, it’s like ‘mate, stick the ball in the back of the net before we get irate'.

“It’s a terrible decision.”

6 Parrott caught the eye during a successful two-year spell at AZ after Spurs' controversial decision to sell Credit: Getty

6 Meanwhile, Spurs fans have never been truly convinced by Richarlison and he has been omitted from De Zerbi's squad for this season Credit: Getty

Unpopular

Oladipo concurred with his broadcast colleague while claiming that Richarlison is universally disliked.

“There is something about homegrown players that come through the system that you want to see and give more time to,” the talkSPORT host said.

“Talking of Richarlison Let’s be honest, Spurs fans don’t really like him. Nobody really likes him.

“And Dominic Solanke, unfortunately, stops scoring goals.”

The discussion continued into Saturday morning with former Republic of Ireland striker Tony Cascarino providing a deeper insight into why Spurs allowed Parrott to leave the club.

Asked whether Tottenham should develop its academy stars rather than spend big,

6 Jose Mourinho was unconvinced by Parrott during the pair's time together at Tottenham Credit: AFP

Cascarino told the Weekend Sports Breakfast: “It’s a tough one.

“Let’s take Troy Parrott for example because [Harry] Kane left for Bayern Munich in 2023 and Troy was loaned out to Excelsior in the Netherlands.

“He played 25 games, scored ten goals and did reasonably well.

“He goes to AZ Alkmaar and Tottenham never chose to take him back and allowed him to leave the football club.

“Jose Mourinho said of Troy when he was about 18 that he wasn’t good enough.

“He didn’t feel Troy was ready and that was probably true at the time. What I would say is that since then, Troy has been unbelievable.”

Cascarino heaped praise on Parrott for his stunning midweek solo strike while labelling the goal the best in Irish football history.

6 Parrott scored a sensational solo goal in the midweek draw against Austria Credit: Getty

“He got the best goal I’ve ever seen any Irish player get in midweek,” Cascarino said.

“Confidence as a forward is a big thing and Troy just looks so much more of an improved player.

“He seems injury free and he looks like a quality player now. He’s 24 so he’s still young.

“I sort of get it that this happens sometimes at big clubs that you’re allowed to go. Will Lankshear was the same going to Middlesbrough.

“He might not be ready for the Premier League but they’re giving him the opportunity to play and prove.

Sports.title: Man City legend Riyad Mahrez lands new club, aged 35, three months after leaving Al Ahli
Sports.content:
Man City legend Riyad Mahrez lands new club, aged 35, three months after leaving Al Ahli

Riyad Mahrez is on the verge of signing for Qatari side Al Shamal SC, according to reports.

The Manchester City legend has been a free agent since leaving Saudi Pro League club Al Ahli in July.

3 Mahrez scored twice for Algeria at the 2026 World Cup before bidding farewell to the international game Credit: Getty

Mahrez showed his enduring class at the 2026 World Cup with two goals in four games for Algeria before they were eliminated in the round of 32.

He subsequently announced his retirement from international football.

Now, multiple reports claim the 35-year-old is making a return to domestic football in Qatar.

It is understood Al Shamal SC, who also boast ex-Arsenal defender Pablo Mari in their ranks, have verbally agreed a deal to sign Mahrez.

The move is expected to be confirmed imminently.

How did Mahrez perform in Saudi Arabia?

The five-time Premier League winner bagged 37 goals and 38 assists in 122 total appearances across all competitions for Al Ahli.

He joined from Man City in a deal worth £30million as part of the Saudi club's blockbuster recruitment drive in 2023.

Superstar talents Roberto Firmino, Edouard Mendy, and Franck Kessie also signed that summer, while Ivan Toney arrived in 2024.

Working under current Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle, Mahrez proved one of the most successful marquee signings in the Saudi Pro League.

The silky winger was highly influential as Al Ahli won the AFC Champions League Elite twice and the Saudi Super Cup.

3 Mahrez has five Premier League winners' medals to his name Credit: Getty

Mahrez will be reunited with his former club when they face Al Shamal in the AFC Champions League Elite later this season.

Paying tribute to the former Leicester star upon his exit earlier this year, Al Ahli said: “Three unforgettable years. Countless magical moments.

"A legacy that will forever live in the hearts of every Al Ahli fan."

Speaking at the time, Mahrez said: "To my teammates… thank you for everything we shared.

"I was fortunate to experience unforgettable moments with you, win trophies, write a chapter in the history of this club and build bonds that will always be stronger than football."

He added: "I am proud that I fought alongside you until the very end.

3 Mahrez played a core role in both AFC Champions League elite triumphs Credit: Getty

"I always tried to put the team, the coaching staff and the club first, sometimes even ahead of my own personal interests, because I truly believed in this project and in the people behind it.

"I leave with my head held high, knowing I stayed loyal to my teammates, the coaching staff, the club and its fans until the very end."

Sports.title: Harry Kane eyeing three-man England club that hasn’t had new member for 78 years
Sports.content:
Harry Kane eyeing three-man England club that hasn’t had new member for 78 years

Harry Kane has the opportunity to make more England history before he becomes the most-capped player for the Three Lions.

The Bayern Munich striker, who is already the country's all-time top scorer, netted his 87th international goal in the Czechia win.

3 England beat Czechia in Prague thanks to goals from Harry Kane and Anthony Gordon Credit: Getty

The 33-year-old bounced back from his miss from the spot against Spain to seal England's first Nations League victory on Tuesday.

His goal in Prague has meant Kane has now scored in each of his last five competitive England away matches.

Harry Kane close to another England record

Kane has scored in each of his last five away England appearances, with only three players scoring in six in a row for the Three Lions.

James Windridge (6, March – June 1908), Tom Finney (7, September 1946 – May 1948) and Stan Mortensen (6, May 1947 – October 1948).

Kane's run started with his second-half winner away in Andorra during World Cup qualifying in June 2025.

The former Tottenham star then netted in each of England's three away trips last autumn in Serbia, Latvia, and Albania.

Kane did make seven appearances under Thomas Tuchel at the World Cup, with a further two outings in the pre-tournament friendlies.

While his seven goals in total came on foreign soil, the matches are not classed as 'away' games for England and are instead neutral - including against Mexico at the host's Azteca home Stadium.

This means that the Czechia win was Kane's first competitive away contest for his country since beating Albania last November.

3 Kane scored England's second with a clinical finish into the bottom corner Credit: Getty

Harry Kane's last five England away games Czechia 0-2 England (One goal) - September 2026 Albania 0-2 England (Two goals) - November 2025 Latvia 0-5 England (Two goals) - October 2025 Serbia 0-5 England (One goal) - September 2025 Andorra 0-1 England (One goal) - June 2025

Tom Finney's seven-game away scoring run

England's trip to Croatia on Saturday, live on talkSPORT, is their last away match of this international break.

Tuchel's men then have back-to-back home games, the return fixture against Slaven Bilic's side - which comes after facing Czechia again.

Should Kane score in Rijeka, he would become only the fourth player - and first for 78 years - to score in each of his last six away England appearances.

Only Preston North End icon Finney has ever managed to do so in seven straight matches on the road.

The 76-cap hero's historic run began on his international debut against Ireland in Belfast in 1946 and stretched over 20 months.

3 Finney scored 30 England goals in 76 caps and was briefly the country's all-time record scorer Credit: Getty

Finney then found the net in Dublin, Lisbon, Brussels, Cardiff, Glasgow and finally finished with his seventh strike away in Turin.

Kane, meanwhile, would have the chance to equal that feat in Atletico Madrid's Metropolitano Stadium against Spain on November 15.

Tuchel says it's impossible for England to find another Kane

Kane, who is just two caps away from becoming England's joint-most appearance holder, is among the favourites to win the Ballon d'Or.

"You will not get another Harry Kane, first of all," Tuchel said.

"He is the first one to push everyone, and that is his mindset, and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills. He is a complete package.

"We look for different options and solutions. We finished the game with Jude [Bellingham] up front as a number nine.

"There will be someone else, but it will not be Harry or a copy of Harry.

"We will find a solution when it comes to it, but maybe not me. It might be another 10 years."

Sports.title: Unai Emery makes shock claim over Premier League rivals after Man City verdict
Sports.content:
Unai Emery appears to have hinted that other Premier League clubs inflate their budgets following the guilty verdict on Manchester City.

In one of football's biggest-ever stories, City have been found guilty by an independent commission on all of their charges in relation to Premier League financial rule breaches.



3 City have officially launched an appeal after being found guilty on all charges over Premier League finance rule breaches Credit: AFP

They are said to have arranged 'sham contracts' to artificially inflate revenue and reduce costs between the 2009/10 and 2017/18 seasons, with other charges being for noncooperation in the investigation.

City announced on Friday that they have launched an appeal against the verdict as they face the prospect of huge sanctions, which remain undecided, including a heavy points deduction and stripped titles.

It's a monumental case that could affect the past, present and future of the English top flight, as well as the reputations of managers and players involved at the club during the investigated period of time.



However, Aston Villa boss Emery has suggested that City are not the only club that have gone against financial regulations.

Speaking to Diario de Sevilla on the verdict, via Mundo Deportivo, he said: "It's an issue that was already known.



"Because we all have our restrictions, we have to sell players to comply with Financial Fair Play; we have to figure out how to draw up contracts with new players.

"Fair Play seeks financial balance so that what is generated is spent, and there is no inflation.



"Yes, many other clubs have inflated their budgets, and now it's coming to light, and naturally there's a decline."

Emery added: "That's something the courts and those in charge will have to decide.

"I feel sorry for how that team played. With (Pep) Guardiola, there were times when they were unbeatable."

3 Emery has suggested that other clubs have inflated budgets in what is a shock claim amid the recent verdict Credit: Getty



What is the latest on City and their charges?

Now that City have appealed, an appeal process is set to follow, and as per Premier League rules, a hearing must be held within 12 weeks.

This can only last five days, and then a decision will be due within 30 days of its conclusion.

As talkSPORT reported, City will argue that the so-called 'tagged sponsorship payments', which totalled £830million, came from the Abu Dhabi Government, not owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

This applies to state-controlled entities such as Etihad Airways and Etisalat, yet the former previously refuted funding from the Abu Dhabi Government as "false".



But this defence has been contradicted by their title sponsor, Etihad.

In 2015, a lobbying coalition formed by American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines called the 'Partnership for Open and Fair Skies' wrote to the United States departments of Commerce, Transportation and State.

3 City face serious sanctions for the charges that span across a period of nine seasons Credit: Getty

They argued that Etihad had gained a competitive advantage by receiving huge sums from the Abu Dhabi Government.



A 2010 internal report that was written for Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahya, the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, is cited, which does in fact claim that the Abu Dhabi Government, which was phrased as 'Executive Council', did cover the sponsorship of City.

City may be able to use this to their advantage during their appeal, but Etihad's response was to flatly deny any government funding in relation to their deal with the club.

"The assertion that the Abu Dhabi Government paid for Etihad's sponsorship of English Premier League football club Manchester City is equally false," Etihad argued.

"In 2011 Etihad and Manchester City entered into a 10-year sponsorship agreement, which included naming rights for Manchester City's stadium. Etihad funded this sponsorship from its own liquidity. It is not uncommon for airlines to have sponsorships with sports teams and their venues…



"We are government-owned and have been since our founding. We are and have always been clear that we do not receive any subsidies from the Abu Dhabi government, and that we are financed through a combination of equity, shareholder and commercial loans.

"Our shareholders' equity and loans are not subsidies under any applicable definition; they are the means by which the Abu Dhabi government has sensibly invested in a successful business model."

Sports.title: Son of Ballon d’Or winner joins non-league club after spells with Chelsea and Tottenham
Sports.content:
Son of Ballon d’Or winner joins non-league club after spells with Chelsea and Tottenham

Andriy Shevchenko’s son Kristian has joined non-league side Sholing FC ahead of their FA Cup third-round qualifying match this weekend.

The 19-year-old, who was born and raised in London, has spent his youth career in the academies of Chelsea, Tottenham, and Watford.



3 Andriy Shevchenko's son Kristian could make his FA Cup debut this weekend Credit: Getty

The teenager, who is the second of the 2004 Ballon d'Or winner's four sons, is eligible to play for England at international level.

However, the right winger is already following in his father's footsteps by being capped at Under-19 and Under-20 level with Ukraine.

Kristian Shevchenko joins Sholing FC

The attacker began his football journey in Chelsea’s academy, the club where his dad, Andriy, spent three years from 2006 until 2009.



He then joined their London rivals, Tottenham, in December 2022, where he worked under ex-Manchester City midfielder Yaya Touré.

Eight months later, Shevchenko moved to Watford, where he spent the next two years progressing through the Hornets' youth ranks.



The Ukrainian signed a professional contract with the Championship outfit in July 2025 but never made a senior appearance.

He has now taken the next step in his career by joining Sholing, who currently sit 16th in the Southern League Premier Division South.



The Boatmen are only five points above the bottom of the table, having won just three of their eight league fixtures this season.

Shevchenko's Sholing debut, however, could come in FA Cup third-round qualifying action this Saturday.

3 Shevchenko was involved in FA Youth Cup action for Watford but never made a senior appearance Credit: Getty

3 He also represented Ukraine at the 2025 FIFA U20 World Cup Credit: Getty



Paul Doswell's men beat Tiverton Town and Andover New Street to earn a match-up with National League South side Ebbsfleet United.

Should Sholing shock the team one step above them in the pyramid, then they will receive £5,625 from the competition’s prize fund.

The Boatmen, who would still bag £1,875 with a defeat, have only ever reached the Fourth Qualifying Round once before in their history.

Sholing, who won three of their last five games across all competitions, lost at that stage to Torquay United in 2020/21.



Shevchenko is not the only new face in the door at the Mortgage Decisions Stadium, with Jonas Mukuna also joining the club.

His famous father, Andriy, meanwhile, won the FA Cup as a player during his time at Chelsea, scoring 22 goals in 77 appearances.

Sports.title: 'If you play for your country, there's no way you can behave like that': ECB chief RICHARD THOMPSON on England's booze culture, why he was desperate to keep Brendon McCullum and why the 18 counties are stronger than ever before
Sports.content:
It would be wrong to say there’s a spring in Richard Thompson’s step as he ticks off another lap of Lord’s to raise money for the Alzheimer’s Society. After all, it’s been only two weeks since he had knee surgery, and medics have told him to divide the 100 laps between clockwise and anti-clockwise, to ease pressure on the joint.

But the ECB chairman is feeling more chipper than he did during a summer in which English cricket was at times going in one direction only – round and round in circles, and getting absolutely nowhere.

We are speaking the day after the season ended with England’s one-day series win against Sri Lanka at the Oval and the last gasps of the County Championship, decided 24 hours earlier in Warwickshire’s favour. When Thompson says ‘it’s been a rollercoaster’, he isn’t joking.

The overall headline, he believes, is positive: the English game is better placed at the end of the season than it was at the start. After losing the Test series to New Zealand, triggering the retirement of Ben Stokes and the sacking of Brendon McCullum, England won their remaining five series across the three formats, and appear to have placed the right men in the right jobs: McCullum in charge of an increasingly impressive white-ball set-up, and Stephen Fleming set for the Test role.

Thompson speaks admiringly of the ‘alchemy’ between McCullum and Harry Brook, the limited-overs captain – under them, the T20 side have won 23 games out of 26 – and says Fleming is ‘very committed to doing a role that he’s always wanted to do’.

But it’s fair to say the path to clarity has been strewn with chaos and confusion – even carnage – as drinking escapades elbowed runs and wickets off the back pages. The charge sheet is now part of history: Brook in Wellington, Ben Duckett in Noosa, Stokes and Gus Atkinson in the Rex Rooms, Brydon Carse in Derby. And while Thompson has forgiven, he can’t entirely forget.

‘We’re through the worst of it,’ the ECB chairman Richard Thompson says of the England cricket team's rollercoaster summer. ‘But there was behaviour that was totally unacceptable'

Thompson, with radio presenter Jamie Theakston, completes 100 laps of Lord's to raise money for the Alzheimer’s Society

‘We’re definitely through the worst of it now,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘But I think the point is that there was behaviour that was just totally unacceptable. If you play for your country, there’s no way you can behave like that.

'You’re measured by a far higher standard. We certainly want to learn, and I think the changes we’ve made demonstrate that.’

Has the penny finally dropped? ‘As much as I hope it can. Something that happened three years ago that we don’t know about could suddenly blow up.

'But, culturally, when you’ve got a new captain and a new coach, it provides an automatic reset, and that’s now happened. The way Joe (Root) spoke in particular about the more recent issues could not have articulated it any better.’

Thompson says suggestions that McCullum should have been removed from the Test job immediately after the Ashes were impractical, since England were heading straight to Sri Lanka for a white-ball tour, followed by the T20 World Cup.

And he dismisses the argument that the ECB erred in making him all-format coach as ‘hindsight’. More important, he says, is where England have ended up: ‘We’ve retained Baz. If we had lost him completely, that would have been a real loss, because we still knew he had so much to offer.’

All the while, the Hundred embarked on its first season under part-private ownership, and with concerns mounting among the 11 non-host counties that they will eventually be left behind – despite the £25million windfall guaranteed each club by the sale of the eight franchises.

Thompson insists that a gap has always existed between the ‘haves and the have-nots’ of the county game. But he points to Northamptonshire’s victory in the T20 Blast as a reminder that the smaller clubs continue to pack a punch on the field. Indeed, in the last 20 years, only Derbyshire among the 18 first-class counties have failed to win one of three main trophies.

‘We’ve retained Baz (McCullum, right). If we had lost him completely, that would have been a real loss, because we still knew he had so much to offer'

'Nothing’s ever perfect, but I don’t think the 18-county structure has ever been more financially secure,’ Thompson says of the domestic game

‘Prior to the Hundred, you could say, well, are the 18 counties safe?’ he says. ‘And, arguably, I would say I’m not sure. Since we’ve done the Hundred deal, they absolutely are, and I always have been an 18-county advocate.’

At a time when football is threatening to be torn apart by the Manchester City scandal, Thompson is proud of cricket’s relative stability.

‘All the counties are completely underwritten, all toxic debt has been taken out. We’re the only sport in the country that isn’t held back by debt and spurious owners or other issues that are causing tension.

‘Our game is driven principally by its members. It’s far more transparent in its leadership and its ownership structures. Nothing’s ever perfect, but I don’t think the 18-county structure has ever been more financially secure.’

Thompson says speculation about a separate TV deal for the Hundred, driven by private investors keen to recoup their expenditure, is ‘not happening any time soon’, and says the investors are ‘very happy’ about the way the first year went, despite concerns about ticket pricing.

And he stresses that it is the ECB who are still in control of the competition – pre-empting the argument that the board have given up the prime month of August to foreign businessmen.

‘There was a suggestion that Pakistani players would not be picked up,’ he says. ‘It was a scurrilous rumour that should never have circulated in the first place, and we soon made sure that was never going to be the case.

'But it showed that the ECB still provide that influence around the tournament. The team owners recognise their role, and where the boundary exists between owning a team and running a competition.’

Thompson says private investors are ‘very happy’ about the way the first year of the revamped Hundred, won by Manchester Super Giants (above), unfolded

Thompson speaks admiringly of the ‘alchemy’ between McCullum and Harry Brook

Thompson, who is excited about the future of the English game, talks tactics with pace bowler Jofra Archer

Thompson, who turns 60 this month, will be in the chair until the end of the 2028 season, by which time he will have served six years in the role.

They have not been dull, encompassing the rise and fall of Bazball, the partial privatisation of the home summer, off-field headaches, even the return of Kevin Pietersen.

With about 75 laps to go, Thompson still has the energy to exude optimism: ‘Both on and off the field, despite the challenges we’ve had, I think we’ve managed them as best we can, and we’ve come out of it stronger.’

He may be right. But few would care to predict where the rollercoaster goes next.
