The Masters 1000 event runs from Wednesday to October 18 and features a ⁠strong field, led by four-time champion Novak Djokovic along with Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Daniil Medvedev, Ben Shelton, Felix Auger-Aliassime and defending ⁠champion Valentin Vacherot.

Sinner won the Shanghai title in 2024, defeating Djokovic in ⁠the final.

Sinner’s absence could boost Zverev’s ⁠push to finish the season as the world number one. The German, who was the French Open and US Open champion this year, has emerged as ‌the Italian’s closest challenger.

Zverev can move to the top of the rankings for the first time if he ‌wins ‌both the China Open in Beijing and the Shanghai Masters.

World.title: The double standards of a failed execution
World.content:
Had Christa Pike faced the death penalty in the Middle East, there would be relentless outrage and condemnations.

Let’s pretend that the Islamic Republic of Iran had undertaken to execute a 50-year-old woman for a crime committed when she was an 18-year-old.

Let’s say the crime was murdering a fellow female student. Let’s also say that the woman slated for execution had suffered rape and sexual abuse since she was a toddler and had been diagnosed with mental illness, later admitting: “It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I’d done.”

A fair amount of international uproar would presumably ensue, alleging Iran’s barbarity in choosing to kill a woman with such a troubled past. The United States would no doubt be at the helm of the criticism.

And yet no such uproar has transpired since Wednesday’s attempted execution in the US state of Tennessee of 50-year-old Christa Pike, to whom all of the above details pertain in reality.

Pike was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee since 1820 – lest anyone assume US society was advancing rather than regressing. However, the executioners failed in their task, and, when Pike remained alive after being injected with all manner of lethal drugs, the operation was called off and she was rushed to hospital.

Fearing the pain that would attend death by injection, Pike had initially requested to be killed by firing squad – one of various civilised options provided to death penalty victims in some US states. The request had been denied.

According to Pike’s lawyers, the failed execution amounts to “chemical torture”. The degree of brain damage Pike may have sustained due to oxygen deprivation remains to be seen.



Again, one can only imagine the sort of self-righteous denunciations that would be occasioned had Iran not only tried to execute a mentally ill woman but royally messed up the killing, potentially leaving her half-dead instead.

Of course, Iran would not be the only country that would come under fire for such a stunt; plenty of other countries in the Middle East and Africa would be similarly denounced for such savagery.

But it’s all in a day’s work in the US, where the death penalty is legal in more than half of the country’s 50 states.

Among the myriad problems with the death penalty, of course, is the frequency with which innocent folks end up being murdered. The Death Penalty Information Center reported that, “since 1973, at least 203 people who were wrongly convicted and sentenced to death in the U.S. have been exonerated.”

Recalling that capital punishment “served as a tool for controlling Black populations and discouraging rebellion” during the era of slavery in the US, the organisation noted the enduring racialised nature of state killing in the country with Black people “currently comprising 40% of the death row population despite only being 12% of the U.S. population”.

To be sure, it’s hardly shocking that the racist classism that passes for democracy in the US is reproduced in death as well as in life.

After all, what better way to uphold the capitalist hierarchy and maintain elite social control than by disproportionately incarcerating and legally murdering people of colour and the poor?

And while Pike is not Black, her attempted murder still serves the mechanism of control by reminding the nonelite of their dispensability and the ultimate arbitrariness of their fate.

Call it capitalist punishment.

Meanwhile, the state’s monopoly on killing means that many cold-blooded murderers get off scot-free – as in the case of Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who fatally shot Renee Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in January.

Ross, it so happens, is a veteran of the war on Iraq, where over the years the US has also engaged in a great deal of killing with impunity. And as in other locations that have had the misfortune to be in the US’s crosshairs, mass slaughter has been cast as just and civilised as long as the US is the one doing the slaughtering.

Indeed, whether it’s committing state-sanctioned execution at home or the extrajudicial killing of fishermen in the Caribbean, the US has yet to be adequately taken to task for barbarism that would have had the US itself up in arms if the tables were turned.



The prevailing double standard goes something like this: When Iran executes people, it’s a moral abomination and a crime. When the US executes people, it’s a legitimate exercise in domestic criminal justice.

As Pike remained unconscious in a Tennessee hospital, the state has paused executions for the remainder of the year as the powers that be ponder what the hell happened during the execution-that-wasn’t.

For his part, President Donald Trump – who ramped up executions during his first term and is busy replicating the feat in his second – reasoned that “it shouldn’t be very difficult” to kill someone by injection, notwithstanding what happened in Tennessee.

But as the US keeps up the killing spree at home and abroad, one can’t help but think that it shouldn’t be that easy.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
World.content:
The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.

The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.

Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.

Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

A crash axe is usually kept âin the cockpit in case of emergencies.

The weapon used has been a key question for investigators, given the stringent security on such a sensitive route. Early reports from passengers on board had suggested it might have been a knife.

The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.

The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. There has been no official confirmation of this.

While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.

He completed a three-year distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!"

The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidalâ¦ It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."

He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".

The UAE has begun investigating whether the "incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.

Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.

The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.

"I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.

World.title: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv
World.content:
A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko has said, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.

The attack on Saturday morning injured two people, and damaged the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge, Klitschko said, causing traffic jams.

It comes after the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones this week, with Klitschko warning that "the enemy is tearing Kyiv apart".

Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo. Moscow again urged foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.

The two Kyiv bridges across the Dnipro River link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday.

The Russian strikes have severed road, rail and trolleybus links across the wide river. The ongoing drone threat means restrictions on other routes, bringing traffic jams to the city's roads for a second day - though Friday's gridlock has not been repeated to the same level.

Many of the city's residents - which number about three million - rely on the metro to travel across the city every day. The fear is this new Russian tactic will result in sustained attacks which could effectively cut the city in two.

World.title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
World.content:
Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to get emergency housing legislation through parliament on Friday.

About 50 planned marches are taking place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona .

"There is a lot of anger in the streets," said a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union, where a demonstration has already started. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.

The measures put forward by Pedro SÃ¡nchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.

Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.

Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.

His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.

World.title: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
World.content:
The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.

It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement.

The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months.

Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports, there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members.

The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.

Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.

On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."

His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".

Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing."

"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said.

"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."

Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.

Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

World.title: US murderer Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after failed execution, lawyers say
World.content:
Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her botched execution.

Hospital staff are working to save her life and clear the drug used, pentobarbital, from her system, the filing states.

During the execution attempt, prison officials tried to start intravenous (IV) lines by using at least seven needles on Pike, according to her lawyers.

At one point, Pike herself offered guidance of where they could try.

"One needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed," the filing states.

While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee ordered an independent review into Pike's botched execution and he halted all executions in the state for the year.

The state's department of correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".

Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have not not offered any explanations about what went wrong.

World.title: Women given shorts at Oktoberfest to prevent upskirting
World.content:
The operator of a popular amusement ride at the Munich Oktoberfest has been handing out free cycling shorts to women, after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.

Some videos showing women on the Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, have been viewed millions of times. One is said to have made thousands of euros for a woman who posted it online.

The Teufelsrad is one of the oldest attractions at the Oktoberfest, the annual beer festival which comes to an end this weekend after 16 days. Its circular platform rotates faster and faster until its riders fall off, and the motion and speed often make skirts fly up.

Filming under skirts is illegal in Germany, and carries a two-year sentence in jail.

However, critics believe the law does not go far enough, and the videos of women on the Teufelsrad in their traditional dirndl dresses often show their underwear. Sometimes, the images have been digitally altered to show them naked, according to local broadcaster BR.

World.title: Kim wins Asian Games gold to secure military exemption
World.content:
Asian Games - final round

-18 T Kim (Kor); -15 K Higa (Jpn), W Ding (Chi), S Kaewkanjana (Tha); -11 W-H Wang (Tpe)

Tom Kim won gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military.

The 24-year-old led going into the final round and produced a brilliant six-under-par 64 to finish 18 under and claim victory by three strokes.

There were signs of nerves with a bogey on the 17th but, after five birdies and an eagle prior to that, Kim had the margin for error and tapped in for par on the last before letting out a roar, his relief clear to see.

Able-bodied South Korean males are usually required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of military service before the age of 28.

However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal-winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.

Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier.

Kim rushed from the Presidents Cup in the United States to tee off at the Kasugai Country Club in Japan, having to manage on just six hours of sleep and a 14-hour time difference.

His efforts were worth it as the world number 32 can now continue his career, in which he has already won four PGA Tour titles and triumphed at the Scottish Open in July, with minimal disruption.

Kim had previously come close to securing an exemption at the Paris Olympics in 2024, finishing day one tied for third before ultimately finishing eighth.

However, his compatriot SH Kim, 28, missed out on a military exemption as South Korea could only win silver in the team event, alongside Tom Kim and Mun Do-yeob, who has already completed his service.

World.title: UK-Iranian dual national bailed after RAF Fairford incident arrest
World.content:
A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.

Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.

Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

World.title: Non-communicable diseases caused 74% of global deaths in 2023 – WHO
World.content:
Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as heart disease, diabetes and dementia accounted for 74 per cent of global deaths in 2023, up from 58 per cent in 2000, according to the latest estimates released by the World Health Organisation (WHO).

The findings, contained in the WHO’s latest Global Health Estimates released on Friday, show that although global life expectancy has largely recovered from the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the world’s disease burden is increasingly shifting towards chronic illnesses and mental health conditions.

According to the report, global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023, almost returning to the 73.4 years recorded in 2019 before the pandemic. However, healthy life expectancy, which measures the number of years people live in good health, recovered more slowly, reaching 62.8 years in 2023, still 0.4 years below its pre-pandemic level.

The WHO noted that eight of the world’s 10 leading causes of death were NCDs in 2023, highlighting a long-term global shift away from communicable diseases.

Cardiovascular diseases remain leading killer

The report identified cardiovascular diseases as the leading cause of death and disease burden worldwide.

It said ischaemic heart disease alone caused approximately 9.5 million deaths and 210 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in 2023. DALYs measure years of healthy life lost due to illness, disability or premature death.

While many parts of the world have made significant progress in reducing the burden of ischaemic heart disease since 2000, the WHO reported rising individual-level risks in the Western Pacific and South-East Asia regions, highlighting persistent inequalities in cardiovascular health outcomes.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The organisation also reported substantial increases in the burden of other chronic diseases.

According to the report, the risk of dying from diabetes has risen considerably since 2000, particularly in South-East Asia.

Alzheimer’s disease and dementia have also become more prominent.

Dementia rose from the 19th leading cause of death globally in 2000 to the fifth in 2023, while deaths linked to the condition tripled during the period.

Mental health concerns

The WHO also highlighted the growing impact of mental health conditions on global health.

Between 2019 and 2023, the global age-standardised DALY rate increased by approximately 20 per cent for depressive disorders and nearly 45 per cent for anxiety disorders.

Together, depression and anxiety accounted for an estimated 110 million years of healthy life lost through premature death and disability in 2023.

The report further showed changing patterns in drug use disorders across regions.

Between 2000 and 2023, the WHO Region of the Americas recorded the largest increases in mortality risk and healthy life loss associated with drug use disorders, while the Western Pacific region experienced substantial declines.

Need for stronger health data systems

Speaking further on the findings, Alani Labrique, Director of WHO’s Department of Data, Digital Health, Analytics and AI, described rising life expectancy as one of public health’s greatest achievements.

However, Mr Labrique noted that the next challenge is ensuring that the additional years people live are spent in good health, while health systems adapt to the changing needs of ageing populations and the growing burden of chronic diseases.

He said the estimates provide countries with evidence on how patterns of death and disease burden are changing over time, helping governments shape health policies, strengthen digital and data infrastructure, and improve their ability to generate insights needed for targeted health interventions.

World.title: Wike attacks Amaechi, says 24 years in top positions produced ‘nothing’ for Rivers
World.content:
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, has accused his predecessor, Rotimi Amaechi, of failing to deliver meaningful development to Rivers State despite spending 24 years in top political positions.

Mr Wike said Mr Amaechi served as speaker of the Rivers State House of Assembly for eight years, governor for eight years and a federal minister for another eight years, but could not point to any significant development he brought to the state during that period.

He challenged residents of the Evo Kingdom in Obio Akpor Local Government Area of Rivers State to identify projects or other developments attracted to the area by Mr Amaechi during his years in public office.

Mr Wike made the remarks on Friday during an interactive session with leaders and stakeholders of the Evo Kingdom, according to a statement issued by his Senior Special Assistant on Media and Public Communications, Lere Olayinka.

“Someone was speaker of the House of Assembly for eight years, governor for eight years, and minister for eight years. That is 24 years in top leadership positions,” Mr Wike said.

“Can anyone point out what has been done to Evo Kingdom or Rivers State in all those 24 years? Nothing, not one single thing.”

Mr Wike contrasted Mr Amaechi’s record with his own tenure as Minister of State for Education, saying he could identify projects he attracted to Rivers State while serving in that capacity.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I was Minister of State for Education and I can count the projects I attracted to Rivers. But he was speaker, governor and a full minister for eight years in a lucrative ministry, yet brought nothing home,” he said.

“After 24 years in power without empowering his people, how can he now say he loves them?”

Mr Wike also reiterated his earlier pledge to resign as FCT minister if President Bola Tinubu loses Rivers State and the FCT in the 2027 elections.

He made the declaration at a strategic consultative meeting with stakeholders in Akpor Kingdom, where he rallied Rivers State’s political structure behind Mr Tinubu.

“My interest in Rivers State is for God to use me as a vessel to help our people. I am back not for what I will get, but for what I can do to uplift my people,” he said.

The former Rivers governor also defended his decision to maintain an open-door policy towards former political opponents, saying political actors should focus on collective interests rather than personal animosity.

“There is no permanent enemy in politics, only permanent collective interest. It is about the interest of our people. The more united we are, the stronger we become,” he said.

Mr Wike urged political actors in Rivers State not to be distracted by criticism on social media over his engagement with former critics.

He said electoral politics was ultimately about building a broad political structure capable of mobilising voters.

The minister called for an inclusive campaign structure in Obio/Akpor, urging politicians and community leaders across the area to participate.

“Whether you are a politician, traditional ruler, pastor or native doctor, I need everyone on board,” he said.

“When it comes to voting and elections, we must bring everyone together.”

World.title: Why NASS will continue to partner Tinubu’s administration – Akpabio
World.content:
The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, has said the National Assembly under his leadership will continue to partner with the administration of President Bola Tinubu, despite the legislature’s constitutional responsibility to scrutinise the executive arm.

Mr Akpabio stated this on Friday when he led a delegation of National Assembly members to visit Mr Tinubu in Lagos as part of activities marking Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary.

He said the decision of the National Assembly to partner with the executive, rather than act solely as a watchdog, was in the interest of Nigerians.

“On the part of the National Assembly, we want to continue to remain worthy partners to the administration of President Bola Tinubu. And we believe that what we are doing is in the interest of all Nigerians,” he said.

The relationship between Nigeria’s executive and legislative arms of government is based on separation of powers, checks and balances, rather than the legislature serving as a partner of the executive in implementing government policies.

Section 4 of the 1999 Constitution vests legislative powers in the National Assembly, while Sections 88 and 89 empower both chambers to investigate the conduct of government ministries, departments and agencies and persons responsible for administering laws and public funds.

The Constitution specifically provides that the investigative powers of the National Assembly may be used to expose corruption, inefficiency or waste in the administration of laws and the disbursement or administration of public funds.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The legislature also exercises control over public spending through its power to consider and approve the executive’s budget proposals. This means that while the National Assembly can cooperate with the executive on legislation and policies, it is constitutionally expected to independently scrutinise the government’s actions.

The 10th National Assembly’s relationship with the Tinubu administration has always been seen as a contrast to the provision of the constitution.

Since its inauguration in June 2023, the Assembly has repeatedly been criticised by opposition politicians, civil society organisations and some lawmakers for its excessive cooperation with the executive. Critics have accused the lawmakers of approving several presidential requests with little scrutiny, prompting some to describe the legislature as a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

The criticism has followed the assembly’s handling of several major executive requests, including borrowing proposals, budget amendments and extensions, presidential nominations and other policy initiatives.

In April, Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) criticised the National Assembly for the hurried approval of President Tinubu’s request for $6 billion in foreign loans, arguing that the process did not demonstrate sufficient legislative scrutiny.

There have also been complaints from within the National Assembly itself. In November 2025, Edo North Senator, Adams Oshiomhole, a member of the ruling All Progressives Congress, accused the Senate leadership of rushing bills through the chamber without giving senators adequate time to examine their details.

He said lawmakers were not meant to “rubber-stamp” legislation. Following his complaint, the Senate leadership directed that bills should, where possible, be made available to senators at least two days before consideration.

The 10th Assembly’s leadership, however, has consistently rejected the description of the legislature as a rubber stamp. Mr Akpabio has repeatedly argued that lawmakers were not elected to fight the president but to work with the executive in the interest of Nigerians.

The approach of the 10th Assembly can be contrasted with periods in which previous National Assemblies had more visible disagreements with the executive.

Under Bukola Saraki as senate president, the 8th Senate frequently clashed with the Muhammadu Buhari administration over appointments, legislation and the budget. In March 2018, Mr Saraki said the Senate had rejected 13 of 240 executive nominees submitted by the late President Buhari over a period of more than two years, while confirming 227.

The period under former Senate President David Mark also produced significant instances of the legislature asserting itself in relation to the executive. In February 2010, the National Assembly invoked the controversial “doctrine of necessity” to recognise then-Vice President Goodluck Jonathan as acting president after President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua had been away from the country for an extended period without formally transmitting a letter transferring presidential powers.

Reviewing obsolete laws

Mr Akpabio said the partnership between the legislature and the executive had helped the National Assembly review and amend some outdated laws in the country.

He referenced reform of the tax system, including changes relating to stamp duties, as an example.

“You’ve seen already, in three years, we have been able to tinker with all the anachronistic and old laws that we met on the ground. You know very well that things like stamp duties were laws that were in 1939. And some of the laws were incorporated in 1901. And the laws of 1959 were incorporated into the Nigerian Constitution, the current one we are having. And many of them have not been changed.

Mr Akpabio said the National Assembly’s passage of four major tax laws was part of efforts to reform Nigeria’s economic system, adding that the laws were passed despite initial concerns from sections of the country over their possible implications.

“Stamp duties and so many others….. So you’ve seen the reform in the tax system. Let me use the word economic system, with four major tax laws brought into the country at one time. Very voluminous, all of them. And then, because we were able to digest them, we were able to do what we ought to do.

“And we were able to pass them in record time with the whole country in agreement. At the beginning, people were very sceptical and said, “What are they trying to do? Are they trying to make a law for one section or the other?” We say we are all for all Nigeria. It’s a people’s parliament and we are doing that,” he said.

Screening of presidential nominees

Mr Akpabio also defended the speed with which the National Assembly sometimes screens and confirms presidential nominees, describing it as part of its partnership with the executive.

“You’ve seen the speed with which we pass legislations that benefit Nigeria. You’ve seen the speed that we clear people who are coming to add value to the current administration. You’ve seen the partnership in terms of laws that definitely will change the paradigm of the Nigerian trajectory,” he sud.

The senate president said the National Assembly would continue to deepen its partnership with the executive.

“And so we will continue to do that. That’s our own contribution. We are elected for that and we partner with an administration which we believe is focused and which is determined to change the fortunes of Nigeria.

“Don’t forget, it’s easy to say with the mouth, but difficult to do. But in our own case, we are matching words with action. And so the government is going forward,” Mr Akpabio said.

World.title: Calypso: Enslaved African gift and its Mighty Sparrow, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
Slinger Francisco, better known as Mighty Sparrow, the “Calypso King of the World”, flew away on 27 September. He was ninety.

Calypso music was invented in the seventeenth century by African slaves in Trinidad who had mainly been taken from the Ibibio, Efik and Igbo peoples in present-day Nigeria and Congo. It is generally accepted that the name calypso originated from the Efik word “kaiso” (ka isu), which means “go on!”, and the Ibibio words “kaa iso”, meaning “continue, go on”. They were common words used by the slaves to urge somebody to go on or meet a challenge. Eventually, the word “cariso” emerged among Trinidadians. It meant “old-time” calypsos.

Calypso was not just music, but also a coded means of communication from which the colonial masters were excluded. It spread news among the enslaved, made fun of slave owners, advanced social commentary and allowed verbal competition, including insulting lyrics.

It was initially sung in French Creole because the masters who brought the slaves to the Trinidadian sugar plantations were French planters. But it was a Spanish colony which changed hands between the Courlanders from present-day Latvia, the Dutch, French and British. The latter fully took over the territory following ‘The Treaty of Paris’, signed on 30 May, 1814. This is how Calypso was eventually rendered more in English.

Calypso evolved with varied instruments, including guitar, congas, trombone, double bass, saxophone, piano and maraca. It was street music that became the famous Trinidad Carnival, which promoted competition, especially after the 1834 abolition of slavery.

The best-known calypso musicians adopted names that sounded bombastic, such as Roaring Lion; historical, like Attila the Hun; and, given British colonialism, royal titles like Duke and Lord. This might have given rise to the common name or title ‘Lord’, such as Lord Invader, Lord Melody, Lord Pretender, Lord Creator, Lord Brynner and, of course, Lord Kitchner, referred to as the “Grandmaster of Calypso”.

Mighty Sparrow explained how he earned his new name: “When I started singing, the bands were still using acoustic instruments and the singers would stand flat-footed, making a point or accusing someone in the crowd with the pointing of a finger, but mostly they stood motionless. When I sing, I get excited and move around, much like James Brown, and this was new to them. The older singers said, ‘Why don’t you just sing instead of moving around like a little sparrow?’ It was said as a joke, but the name stuck.” Later, he changed his name from Little Sparrow to Mighty Sparrow.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

His first public performance was the song “The Parrot and the Monkey” in 1954. The following year, he recorded “Missing Baby (Ruby)”, “High Cost of Living” and “Race Track”. Sparrow had been born a Grenadian, but at the age of one, his mother moved him to Trinidad and Tobago, T&T. His music explored the wide themes of calypso music.

In 1956, he celebrated the departure of United States troops from T&T with his famous song ‘Jean and Dinah’ or “Yankees Gone”. In it, he accused them of promoting prostitution. When T&T became independent on August 31, 1962, he released a song, ‘Our Model Nation’. He sang: “The whole population of our little nation Is not a lot But oh! what a mixture of races and culture That’s what we’ve got Still no major indifference Of race, color, religion or finance It’s amazing to you I’m sure.”

But there was a political crisis in the new nation, and Mighty Sparrow, in his album ‘Sparrow the Conqueror’, defended the Government of Dr Eric Williams. He sang that the actions of the opposition were senseless: “Come on, what is wrong with this island Poor Dr. Williams Come on, I said what’s wrong with this island Poor Dr Williams Everybody doing what they like Striking when they want to strike It appears that nobody cares About the island economy I tell you.”

He crooned that what was going on was anarchism: “No gas today, no phone tomorrow What next I don’t know No drain digging, no rubbish cleaning Only corbeaux working The island as you see suffering politically Because the present Government have some stupid opponent Oh Lord man they ignorant Because the present Government have some stupid opponent Not one is intelligent Some of them, them opposing So much crime they commit Some again have no education Is them does make the confusion Anything at all the Premier say They always standing in the way And like they suffering from a mental block Talking one set of sewerage talk I tell you.”

Mighty Sparrow was so fanatical in his support of the Williams administration, and so angry with those opposed to it, that he recommended the death penalty for the opposition: “The Premier cannot make a suggestion Without a big objection And some of them way want to object Really should have a rope ‘round they neck.”But Sparrow eventually fell out with the Williams administration. Part of his criticism is captured in the song “No, Doctor, No”.

Pan-Africanist Kwame Nkrumah strove in the late 1950s not just to mould Africa into a single country but also to strive for wider African-Diaspora unity. But it appeared the Caribbean was moving faster as it, in 1958, established the West Indies Federation, made up of ten British colonies, to jointly secure independence and build a united region with its capital in T&T. But disagreements over issues like leadership, power distribution and the choice of a capital surfaced. Jamaica sounded the death knell by holding a referendum in 1962, resulting in its exit and the collapse of the federation.

Sparrow was inconsolable. In a song that year titled ‘Federation’, he sang: “Whether you’re a damn Trinidadian (We are as one!) If they say you’re a smart Barbadian (We are as one!) Get away from me you crazy Grenadian (We are as one!) I don’t care if you’re a bad Jamaican (We are as one!) Let us join together and love one another (We are as one!) If you’re born in New York and your parents are West Indian (We are as one!)”

He had long stays in Britain and the US. In 1977, he went to West Africa on a music tour during which he was given a Yoruba chieftaincy, Omowale (the child has returned home) of Ikoyi. Sparrow settled in the US and, in 2008, released “Barack the Magnificent” in support of Barack Obama’s race to the White House.

In all, he had over 280 songs captured in more than seventy albums, straddling varied aspects of life, from love and politics to gospel. For over seven decades, Mighty Sparrow flew around the world, pollinating generations. Now, he has flown out into eternity.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: Nigeria’s business activity expands as household confidence weakens – CBN
World.content:
Nigeria’s business activity strengthened in September 2026, but households became more pessimistic about economic conditions, finances and prices, according to new reports by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN).

The CBN’s September Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) showed that overall economic activity expanded for the fourth consecutive month, with the Composite PMI rising to 53.0 points from 52.7 points in August.

The survey, conducted between 7 and 11 September among 1,900 purchasing and supply executives across the Industry, Services and Agriculture sectors, showed that 23 of the 32 subsectors surveyed recorded expansion, while nine declined.

The improvement was supported by stronger industrial activity, with the Industry PMI rising to 52.0 points in September from 50.6 points in August, marking a second consecutive month of expansion.

The sector’s Output Index also rose to 53.2 points, supported by increases in new orders and employment, while the Raw Materials Inventory Index returned to expansion at 51.1 points from 49.4 points in August.

The Services sector remained in expansion at 53.2 points, compared with 53.3 points in August, while the Agriculture PMI eased slightly to 53.1 points from 53.4 points.

The regulatory body said agriculture had now recorded 26 consecutive months of expansion.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, the improvement in business activity was accompanied by renewed pressure on input prices.

The Composite input price index increased by 0.8 points in September, while the output price index declined by 0.5 points.

CBN said the September PMI pointed to a “broadening recovery” in economic activity, although the renewed increase in input price pressures warranted close monitoring.

Household expectations

Meanwhile, the picture was less positive among households. In a separate report, CBN’s September Household Expectations Survey, it was revealed that the Overall Consumer Sentiments Index fell sharply to -18.7 points from -9.9 points in August, indicating increased pessimism about the economy.

The Economic Conditions Index stood at -21.5 points, while the Family Financial Situation Index was -23.9 points and the Family Income Sentiments Index stood at -10.5 points.

This indicates a pessimistic outlook on current economic conditions among households and regarding their family financial situation.

Also, the report showed that Nigerian households also reported stronger concerns about prices.

The average price sentiment index rose to 33.5 points from 23.0 points in August, indicating that respondents perceived prices as remaining high. Among the selected items, households reported the lowest perceptions of price changes for food and telecommunication services.

The Central Bank said households expected price pressures to remain elevated over the next three and six months, with the price outlook indices standing at 29.7 and 28.4 points, respectively.

Meanwhile, Nigeria’s headline inflation eased marginally to 15.39 per cent in August 2026 from 15.43 per cent in July, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), while month-on-month inflation fell more sharply to 0.71 per cent from 1.57 per cent.

CBN said the respondents’ cautious mood was also reflected in household spending intentions, with food remaining the dominant expenditure priority, followed by transportation, other household goods, education, and electricity and water.

It said households remained particularly reluctant to make major purchases. The sentiment indices for house purchases, motor vehicles, investments and consumer durables were all negative, at -68.2, -67.3, -50.7 and -49.5 points, respectively.

Buying conditions also remained weak, with the index for consumer durables at 24.8 points and that for motor vehicles and buildings and landed properties at 24.2 points, all below the 50-point threshold.

The survey further showed that 61.1 per cent of respondents believed faster price increases would weaken the Nigerian economy, while 62.2 per cent preferred lower lending rates.

However, 45.1 per cent favoured higher interest rates when they were presented as a means of containing inflation, while 44.8% preferred lower interest rates, even at the cost of rising inflation.

READ ALSO: CBN urges Nigerians to handle Naira with care

Despite the weak September sentiment, households expected confidence to improve gradually, with the Overall Consumer Sentiments Index projected at -8.7 points next month, -0.4 points over the next three months and 7.1 points over the next six months.

The contrasting findings suggest that while business conditions continued to improve in September, households remained under pressure from high prices, interest rates and concerns about their finances.

The regulatory body said households remained cautious during the month, with subdued buying conditions and purchase intentions pointing to persistent concerns about household finances and economic conditions.

World.title: 2027: Atiku open to opposition cooperation, campaign says amid G100 run-off report
World.content:
The campaign of African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar says the former vice-president remains open to discussions to strengthen cooperation among opposition parties ahead of the 2027 election.

Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communications of the Atiku Presidential Campaign Council, told PREMIUM TIMES on Friday that the campaign had not confirmed reports that Mr Abubakar rejected a proposal for opposition parties to rally behind a single presidential candidate.

He also said no agreement on a single candidate or cooperation in the event of a presidential run-off had been confirmed.

“I cannot confirm at this stage that His Excellency has rejected the proposal or that any agreement on a single candidate or run-off cooperation has been reached,” Mr Shaibu said.

He added that Mr Abubakar “remains open to discussions aimed at strengthening cooperation among opposition forces.”

Mr Shaibu said he was checking the details of the G100 proposal and Atiku’s response, including whether the group presented polling or electoral modelling to support its strategy.

“I also do not want to speculate about conditional endorsements or reciprocal commitments,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

G100 considers run-off option

His comments followed a report by Saturday PUNCH that the G100 opposition initiative was considering cooperation among opposition parties if the 2027 presidential election proceeds to a second round.

The PUNCH report, citing unnamed G100 sources, said consultations with Mr Abubakar and Nigeria Democratic Congress presidential candidate Peter Obi were continuing but that neither candidate had shown an inclination to accept a single-candidate

One unnamed source said a possible run-off was among the scenarios being considered if efforts to produce a common opposition candidate before the election failed.

Another source referred to unspecified “statistics” and “research” which, according to the report, suggested that no candidate might secure victory in the first round.

PREMIUM TIMES has not independently obtained the research referred to in the report.

Mr Shaibu said the Atiku campaign was checking whether any such polling or electoral modelling had been presented during the consultations.

Push for common opposition candidate

G100 has been canvassing cooperation among opposition parties ahead of the presidential election.

In August, PREMIUM TIMES reported that G100 and the Minority Caucus of the House of Representatives were pushing opposition parties towards a common presidential candidate.

The group subsequently convened an opposition summit in Abuja on 31 August, attended by representatives of the ADC, Allied Peoples Movement, NDC, a faction of the Peoples Democratic Party, Peoples Redemption Party and Social Democratic Party.

READ ALSO: Atiku govt will seek PIA amendment if law blocks production subsidy Amaechi

Atiku and Mr Obi did not attend the summit.

The participating groups agreed to establish committees and working groups to develop proposals on opposition unity, a national reform programme and a possible common presidential candidate. PREMIUM TIMES reported the outcome of the talks.

More recently, Kenneth Okonkwo, a spokesperson for the Atiku campaign, argued that opposition parties would need to pool their political structures and votes if they hoped to mount a stronger challenge to the ruling All Progressives Congress. PREMIUM TIMES reported his comments on 28 September.

World.title: Pete Edochie in Ghana, speaks on health challenges
World.content:
Veteran Nollywood actor Pete Edochie has spoken on his health condition, saying, “I’m not very well myself.”

The 79-year-old actor disclosed this while visiting his longtime friend, Ghanaian actor Emmanuel Armah, who has battled severe health challenges for almost 11 years in Accra.

The visit was part of Edochie’s engagements in Ghana, where he attended the launch of the Pete Edochie Legacy Project, an initiative established to honour his decades of contributions to African cinema, culture and storytelling.

The project’s launch was held as part of Accra Legacy Week, which celebrates individuals whose careers and influence have made significant contributions to African culture and the creative sector.

In a viral video on Friday, Edochie spoke about his condition and expressed hope that he would recover despite the physical difficulties he currently faces.

“I’m not very well myself. I’m not. Walking is a problem for me now, but I still have hope that I will recover, you know. Sometimes I get up, and parts of my body are swollen.

“And then after some time they go down again, like my hand is swollen and now my leg is. I just keep asking God, ‘You are the author of life’”, said the veteran actor.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Burden

Edochie said his prayer was that his health challenges would never make him a burden to his family.

The actor said: “Whenever you feel it is time for me to go, just take me. Don’t let me bother the people who are around me. Just take me.”

The Anambra-born actor prayed for Armah’s speedy recovery and also offered financial assistance towards his treatment.

“Emma, I believe that you will recover someday. You will. By the grace of God, Emma, you will recover.”

Armah’s wife speaks

Responding to Edochie’s question about her husband’s prolonged illness, Stella said Armah had been battling the condition for almost 11 years.

She explained that the veteran actor’s health problems started when he was in the United States for work, while she was in Ghana.

According to her, Armah was unaware that he had high blood pressure, and his cholesterol levels had also increased, GhanaWeb reported on Thursday.

“He was working in the US when it happened. He had high blood pressure he did not know, and the cholesterol also went high. That was how the whole thing started. | wasn’t there by then; I was in Ghana, and this is what they told me.”

Stella also told Edochie that doctors were optimistic about the actor’s recovery, although he continues to experience pain across his body and has been reluctant to undergo physiotherapy.

She said she recently made arrangements for him to begin physiotherapy in Kasoa, where he is now receiving regular treatment.

“Doctors are saying he could get better, but you know him, he listens to himself. The whole body is aching, and he does not allow physiotherapy. But now | sent him to a physiotherapist at Kasoa, so they are working on him. They massage him every day,” she noted.

Stella added that despite her husband’s condition, he still remembers many people he worked closely with during his career and often asks about them.

“He remembers everything. He mentions their name. Sometimes he would call and ask if this person is around, and would say, ‘Have you been hearing from this person?’ Sometimes he will ask a lot of questions, and sometimes he asks me if I don’t hear from this particular person, he can take me to the person.”

World.title: How do I empathise with my Lebanese friend?, By Osmund Agbo
World.content:
Perhaps this is the most uncomfortable lesson of all: oppression does not automatically teach the oppressed empathy. Sometimes those who have experienced subjugation, once they acquire power themselves, become capable of inflicting upon others the very indignities from which they once suffered.

As Israeli bombs rained down on southern Lebanon in 2024, I found myself thinking about Rabih, a Lebanese man I had once met at his furniture store on Lagos Island. I wondered what had become of him and his family back in Beirut. By October, the escalating hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah had displaced more than 1.2 million people, while Lebanon’s already tenuous infrastructure lay in ruins and its beleaguered economy was once again teetering on the precipice of collapse.

My first impression of Rabih was that of an exceptionally pleasant man, which, of course, is hardly unusual for a business owner eager to make a sale. But Rabih seemed to possess something beyond the customary affability of a salesman. He was genuinely vivacious, the kind of man one might instinctively describe as the life of the party. He appeared particularly amused when I asked how good his dabke was, the exuberant Levantine folk dance performed in lines and circles at weddings and other celebrations.

I have always been fascinated by the Lebanese diaspora and the extraordinary economic footprint it has established across the world. In Nigeria, the Chagoury brothers, Gilbert and Ronald, have built a formidable business empire spanning construction, real estate, hospitality and manufacturing. In Mexico, Carlos Slim Helú, the son of Lebanese immigrants, built a telecommunications and industrial empire that, at one point, made him the richest man in the world.

Across West Africa, Latin America, North America and beyond, the story is the same. Lebanese communities have repeatedly demonstrated a remarkable capacity to transform displacement into enterprise, adversity into opportunity, and diaspora into enduring commercial networks.

But the Lebanese diaspora did not emerge because Lebanese people simply developed a preference for life abroad. Far from it. It was forged in the crucible of repeated violence, economic deprivation, political instability and war. Significant emigration began in the second half of the nineteenth century, particularly following the sectarian violence that engulfed Mount Lebanon in 1860 and amid the economic dislocation and eventual collapse of the traditional silk industry. Between approximately 1860 and 1914, more than 300,000 people left the region that would eventually become modern Lebanon, many of them bound for the Americas, Africa and Australia.

Then came the First World War and the catastrophic famine that devastated Mount Lebanon. The pattern continued thereafter. In other words, the Lebanese diaspora was not the product of a single catastrophe but of a recurring historical cycle: violence, insecurity, economic desperation, departure, and then the powerful pull of family and community networks drawing others through the same door.

Once Lebanese communities became firmly established in countries such as Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Sierra Leone, they developed commercial and social networks that made subsequent migration considerably easier. The Lebanese experience became, in many respects, a masterclass in the transformation of displacement into economic influence.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

One might, therefore, expect that a people whose history is so deeply marked by displacement would possess an instinctive understanding of the vulnerability of immigrants. Yet this is precisely where Lebanon’s treatment of migrant workers becomes so difficult to reconcile with its own history.

For decades, Lebanon has depended heavily upon migrant domestic workers, overwhelmingly women from countries including Ethiopia, the Philippines, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and several African nations. Before the economic crisis that began in 2019, more than 250,000 migrant domestic workers were estimated to be living in the country. By 2024, that number had fallen substantially.

These women perform work upon which countless Lebanese households depend. They clean homes, prepare meals, care for children, tend to the elderly and perform the innumerable tasks required to sustain domestic life. Yet their vulnerability has been extraordinary. Human rights organisations have documented allegations of unpaid wages, confinement, passport confiscation, physical abuse, sexual abuse, and other forms of exploitation. The numbers are deeply disturbing.

A study based on interviews with 913 migrant domestic workers in Lebanon found that 68 per cent reported experiencing at least one incident of sexual harassment. The reported behaviour ranged from sexual comments and unwanted touching to exposure, sexual propositions and attempted or actual sexual assault.

There is also the haunting 2016 documentary “A Maid for Each,” by Lebanese filmmaker, Maher Abi Samra. The film takes viewers into the world of a Beirut domestic worker agency, where African and Asian women are recruited and matched with Lebanese households in a manner disturbingly reminiscent of a commodities market. Its portrayal of the industry is devastating.

In December 2020, Lebanon enacted Law No. 205, criminalising sexual harassment and establishing protections for victims and witnesses. The legislation was rightly regarded as an important legal development. The problem is, migrant domestic workers remained largely outside the protection afforded by Lebanon’s ordinary labour law framework. Their vulnerability is further compounded by what is known as kafala, the sponsorship system under which a migrant worker’s legal status is closely tied to an individual employer.

This is where the language of modern slavery becomes difficult to avoid. Kafala was not conceived as a system of slavery. Its stated purpose was to regulate migrant labor. But when an employer exercises extraordinary control over a worker’s employment, residency and ability to leave an abusive relationship, the conceptual distance between employment and coercion can become frighteningly narrow.

A worker may arrive in Lebanon carrying a passport, a contract, and the hope of earning enough money to improve the lives of her family back home. But if her passport is confiscated, her wages withheld, her movements restricted, and her legal status made dependent upon the very person abusing her, the absence of physical chains does not necessarily signify the presence of freedom. Tragically, that has been the reality experienced by many migrant workers in Lebanon.

Modern slavery does not always require an auction block, iron shackles or an overseer standing over a field with a whip. Sometimes, all that is required is a passport locked inside a drawer, a telephone taken away, an unpaid salary, a locked door and an immigration system that grants the person holding the key extraordinary power over the person trapped behind the door.

In 2020, a Lebanese man posted a Facebook  offering a Nigerian domestic worker for $1,000. He displayed her passport and described her as a 30 year old domestic worker who was “active and clean.”

There is also the haunting 2016 documentary A Maid for Each, by Lebanese filmmaker, Maher Abi Samra. The film takes viewers into the world of a Beirut domestic worker agency, where African and Asian women are recruited and matched with Lebanese households in a manner disturbingly reminiscent of a commodities market. Its portrayal of the industry is devastating. Domestic labour becomes a marketplace in which the employer assumes the role of master and the worker is reduced to something approaching property.

Then came the war of 2024. As Israeli strikes intensified across Lebanon, thousands of Lebanese families fled their homes in search of safety. But some migrant domestic workers discovered that they had nowhere to flee to.

Reuters documented the case of Fajima Kamara, a Sierra Leonean domestic worker whose employers fled to Dubai, leaving her without her passport, telephone or belongings. She eventually made her way towards Beirut, where she became homeless before finding temporary refuge in a volunteer run shelter. Similar stories unfolded among thousands of predominantly female live-in domestic workers, many of whom lacked the documentation required to move safely.

That is the deeper pathology of kafala. The problem is not simply that some individuals are cruel. It is that a system can confer upon cruelty an extraordinary degree of leverage. The failure, therefore, is not merely one of individual compassion. It is a failure of equality before the law.

Lebanon, however, is not alone. In Saudi Arabia, the 2022 census counted 13.4 million non-Saudis, representing more than 40 per cent of the country’s population. Migrant workers are indispensable to the Saudi economy, working in construction, transportation, hospitality, health care, domestic service, and countless other sectors.

The Gulf, however, is not a monolith, and it would be both inaccurate and intellectually dishonest to portray every Arab country, or every Arab employer, as participating in an identical system. Meaningful reforms have taken place.

I still feel empathy for him… But I also think about Fajima Kamara, abandoned in a country where she had worked to provide another family with comfort. I think about my country woman whose passport was displayed beside a $1,000 price tag on Facebook. I think about the hundreds of thousands of African and Asian women who have crossed oceans in pursuit of a better life, only to discover that the door through which they entered can, under the wrong circumstances, become the very door that imprisons them.

Qatar introduced a minimum wage and reforms allowing many migrant workers to change jobs without their employer’s permission. Saudi Arabia introduced labour reforms intended to reduce employer control over migrant workers. Other Gulf states have enacted legislation addressing workplace abuse, discrimination and harassment. Yet these reforms also illuminate the larger problem: legislation on paper does not automatically translate into freedom in practice.

There is responsibility on the other side of the migration equation as well. The strongest chain is sometimes not forged by an employer. It is forged by desperation. When home becomes the mouth of a shark, even a perilous journey can begin to resemble salvation.

African governments therefore cannot simply watch their citizens board airplanes and disappear into foreign labour markets. Countries that send large numbers of migrant workers abroad require robust systems of licensed recruitment, enforceable employment contracts, pre-departure education, consular support, monitoring, emergency intervention and repatriation. A woman should not have to depend upon the benevolence of strangers on another continent to discover that the job she was promised has quietly transformed into a prison.

There is something profoundly unsettling about the human species. We have spent centuries abolishing slavery in law. Britain passed the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833, and slavery was subsequently abolished throughout most of the British Empire. Yet nearly two centuries later, we have demonstrated an extraordinary ingenuity for constructing systems capable of reproducing some of slavery’s essential characteristics without ever having to call anyone a slave.

No chains. No auction block. No shackles. Just poverty on one side, privilege on the other, and a legal system that can sometimes make escape almost impossible.

Perhaps this is the most uncomfortable lesson of all: oppression does not automatically teach the oppressed empathy. Sometimes those who have experienced subjugation, once they acquire power themselves, become capable of inflicting upon others the very indignities from which they once suffered.

History is replete with such ironies, and this realisation has complicated my feelings about Rabih and his people. When I think of him now, I still see the cheerful Lebanese man in Lagos, the man who laughed when I asked about his dabke, the man whose family may have been terrified and displaced when Israeli bombs descended upon his country.

I still feel empathy for him. I still feel empathy for innocent Lebanese families who have repeatedly found themselves caught in wars they neither initiated nor chose. But I also think about Fajima Kamara, abandoned in a country where she had worked to provide another family with comfort. I think about my country woman whose passport was displayed beside a $1,000 price tag on Facebook. I think about the hundreds of thousands of African and Asian women who have crossed oceans in pursuit of a better life, only to discover that the door through which they entered can, under the wrong circumstances, become the very door that imprisons them.

And that is where my empathy becomes conflicted and it should not have to be.

A people’s suffering should never require another people’s suffering in order to become visible.

If anything, the long and painful history of Lebanon should have taught us a simpler and more universal lesson: there is no dignity in escaping one cage only to construct another for someone else.

Osmund Agbo is a medical doctor, author, and the 2026 recipient of the Thabo Mbeki Prize for Scholarship and Public Service

World.title: We got funds for constituency projects during emergency rule – Rivers lawmaker
World.content:
Deputy Chief Whip, Rivers State House of Assembly, Justina Emeji.

By Davies Iheamnachor, PORT HARCOURT

The lawmaker representing Emohua State Constituency at the Rivers State House of Assembly, Hon. (Mrs) Justina Emeji, has revealed that the lawmakers got funding to execute projects during the period of emergency rule declared in the state by President Bola Tinubu.

Emeji, who is the deputy chief whip of the 10th Assembly, made this disclosure during the inauguration of one of her constituency projects, Echonwere Royal Hall in Okporowo Ogbakiri Clan in the Emohua Local Government Area of the state.

Emeji in her address commended President Bola Tinubu and the Minister of Federal Capital Territory, Chief Nyesom Wike, for their efforts in ensuring the development of the state.

Emeji said, “I want to thank President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. It was during the emergency rule this money was released to us.

“When we got the money, our speaker (Martin Amaewhule) asked me to go and put something on the ground so that my people would remember me. That was how I came home to do this.”

She disclosed that aside from the commissioned town hall, she had seven other people-orientated constituency projects going on across the 14 wards of the LGA.

She said the projects, which included a lodge for corps members at Oduoha Ogbakiri, a market at Isiodu Emohua, six classroom blocks at Ibaa Community, teachers’ quarters at Akpabu, six classroom blocks at Egbeda and another six classroom blocks at Ovogo Community, would impact positively on the people.

Emeji further empowered 150 persons from the 14 wards of the LGA with N30m as an empowerment fund.

However, the Speaker of the State House of Assembly, Hon. Martin Amaewhule, hailed Emeji for being a dependable member of the 10th Assembly, adding that she has not failed her people.

He said, “We are here to commission one of the projects nominated by Hon. Justina Emeji for her constituency, which is this town hall right behind me. She nominated these projects after consulting with her people, and they said they want these projects.

“She ensured that the project is supervised and completed, and today this town hall is ready for use,” Amaewhule said.

Amaewhule stressed that representation is a core mandate of a legislator, involving identifying the needs and aspirations of constituents and working with government to actualise them.

He noted that before the 2027 general election, the state would witness a harvest of constituency projects across all constituencies.

He said, “Let me also re-emphasise that she has seven other projects that are ongoing. That shows that she is representing her people well. The 10th Rivers State House of Assembly has members that are representing our people effectively and delivering on their mandates.”

World.title: FCT Police arrest suspect for raping, impregnating 12-year-old
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

The FCT Police Command said on Saturday that its Anti-Kidnapping Unit, on 2nd October 2026, while on routine patrol around Airport Bridge Taxi Park, observed a fully tinted navy blue Volkswagen vehicle with registration number KMC567LQ parked with its windows wound up.

Spokesperson of the command, SP Josephine Adeh, said the vehicle was observed to be shaking.

“The officers, suspecting foul play, approached the vehicle and opened it, only to see one Zayyanu Halilu raping a twelve (12) year old minor.

“Following the discovery, the suspect was promptly arrested and the victim was rescued.

“Preliminary investigation revealed that the suspect had, on several occasions, lured and sexually abused the underaged victim in the said vehicle parked at the same location, with threats to “deal with her” if she reveals the abuse to anyone.

“Medical examination also revealed that the victim is about three months pregnant as a result of the abuse.

“The victim is currently receiving medical care and assessment, while the suspect remains in Police custody and will be charged to court upon conclusion of investigations.

“The Commissioner of Police, FCT Command, CP Ahmed Muhammed Sanusi urges parents and guardians to remain vigilant and pay close attention to the whereabouts, safety and welfare of their wards at all times.

“Members of the public are also enjoined to remain security conscious and promptly report suspicious activities or persons to the nearest police station or through the Command’s emergency lines: 08032003913, 08028940883.”

World.title: ‘Drone found NYSC abductors’ hideout, but camp is mined with IEDs’ — Imo CP
World.content:
The Imo State Police Command has located the hideout where suspected kidnappers are holding abducted National Youth Service Corps, NYSC, members and other victims, Commissioner of Police Audu Garba Bosso has disclosed.

Read Also: Bandits hijack two buses, kidnap corps members, others in Imo

Bosso said security operatives used drones to track the abductors and were able to identify their exact location in the bush, but said the rescue operation had been delayed by intelligence indicating that the area was heavily mined with improvised explosive devices.

Speaking to journalists on the ongoing operation, the Imo CP said security forces had already moved into the area and would continue efforts to safely reach the victims.

“Yesterday we were in the bush; we trailed them up to a particular location. But at that point in time, we couldn’t move in to where the coordinates showed us where they are,” he said.

According to him, the drones provided security operatives with the exact location of the abductors, but the presence of IEDs around the camp posed a major challenge to the operation.

“But our predicament is that with the intel we have, the camp is mined with IEDs,” Bosso said.

He added that security forces were preparing to deploy heavy equipment, including high-velocity vehicles, bulldozers and armoured personnel carriers, to gain access to the area and rescue the victims.

“We are moving in there with high-velocity vehicles. We are moving with bulldozers and APCs to see how we are going to rescue these victims,” he said.

The kidnap

The victims were among passengers abducted after suspected gunmen attacked two buses along the Owerri-Onitsha Expressway in Imo State on October 1.

The buses were reportedly carrying prospective corps members travelling from Ibadan to orientation camps in the South East and South South when they were attacked around the Umunoha axis of the road in Mbaitoli Local Government Area.

The Imo State Police Command had earlier said 10 victims were rescued at the scene, while the exact number of those still in captivity was being verified.

The Defence Headquarters subsequently said 20 passengers were abducted from the two buses, including several prospective corps members, while 10 passengers, among them eight identified prospective corps members, had been rescued.

It said a joint search and rescue operation involving troops of Operation Udoka, the Nigeria Police Force and the Department of State Services, with support from the Nigerian Air Force, was ongoing to locate and rescue the remaining victims.

World.title: Ndume hails Tinubu over military salary increase
World.content:
Ndume

By John Alechenu, Abuja

Former Senate Leader, Senator Ali Ndume, has commended President Bola Tinubu for fulfilling his pledge to increase the salaries of Armed Forces personnel.

Ndume, who represents Borno South, gave the commendation in a statement made available to newsmen in Abuja on Saturday.

Recall that the Presidency had in September announced its commitment to implement a new salary package for certain categories of military personnel.

According to a statement signed by Presidential Media Aide, Bayo Onanuga, officers above the rank of colonel, including brigadier generals, major generals, lieutenant generals and generals, would get 30 percent increase.

Those from colonel down to warrant officer 50 percent, while private to staff sergeant would get 80 percent.

Onanuga said the package would raise the annual salary bill from N660 billion to N924 billion and benefit over 250,000 personnel.

Director of Defence Information, Maj-Gen. Samaila Uba, confirmed implementation of the review to Defence Correspondents on Friday.

Ndume, a former Chairman of the Senate Committee on Army, said the President has shown commitment to boosting morale.

He said, “Making a pronouncement is one thing, redeeming your pledge is a different ball game entirely.

“President Tinubu has shown times without number that he keeps to his words. It is heartwarming to note that the salary increment he promised the Nigerian Army has been redeemed.”

The federal lawmaker further said, “I want to urge our officers to redouble their efforts to curtail insecurity since the present administration is doing everything to boost their morale.

“They should do more now that they also have more troops on the ground with the recent recruitment.

“The activation of the Army Aviation would also go a long way in complementing the efforts of the Air Force now that we also have attack helicopters in the six geo-political zones.”

He restated his call for better synergy between infantry and Air Force in the war against insurgency and banditry.

World.title: IEA members release 325m barrels of oil from strategic reserves
World.content:
Gasoline prices are seen at a Shell gas station in Houston, on October 2, 2026. Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP.

The International Energy Agency said Saturday that member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, from 400 million barrels promised in March.

The update came a day after G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the US-Iran war.

The G7 did not say whether the 100 million barrels included the outstanding 75 million barrels from the March IEA commitment, or came on top of that.

The US government of President Donald Trump has been pressuring allies to release diesel reserves to ease a spike in prices for the fuel, being felt in America and elsewhere.

Restricted diesel supplies is one of the consequences of the war in the Middle East, where Iran has been throttling ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for US and Israeli attacks.

Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, part of the fightback against Moscow’s strikes, have also affected the market.

The IEA said in a statement on Saturday that “around 325 million barrels of the IEA collective action announced on 11 March have so far been released, representing over 80 percent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged in the action”.

The March pledge was offered up by the IEA’s 32 member countries, a grouping that includes all the G7 nations: of Britain, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

The G7 countries on Friday agreed to release over the next four months 100 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products, “including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days”.

They also said there would be no ban on diesel exports between them — heading off a threat Washington had brandished, and which Trump later said would not be enacted.
