"And so, to be able to connect the dots, I think makes them feel pretty good about their dad and just about themselves and our family as a whole, just understanding that football is a part of our family."

Stewart sees football as a teacher of many of life’s important lessons.

"Football is family and you show up no matter what. It teaches you the selflessness of our lives. It teaches you responsibility; it teaches you prioritization. But most importantly, it teaches you more about yourself and what you can get out of yourself," Stewart said.

Watching kids grow and develop, both as players and as people, is incredibly rewarding for Stewart.

"Me and Luke have a favorite player, his name is Jack... and Jack is probably as big as this pencil or this pen. Not really, but like he's a smaller kid. But I would take Jack to a battlefield because I know Jack will have my back. I know that he's loyal to the game. I know he's loyal to the cause. I know that he believes in the cause and he'll do whatever it takes to make it right. He might get it wrong, but if you give him a shot, he's going to put in the effort every single time," Stewart said.

"And so last year we had him as a seventh grader, and now he’s an eighth grader, and he helps out the seventh graders. He’s more vocal this year and just seeing his confidence just kind of rise through the surface, it’s really cool. And yesterday we had a game and he’s making tackles now. He plays corner, and I’m not talking about like, just wrapping guys up, I’m talking going in for the kill."

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

"We put him in at running back yesterday, and we gave him a toss, first toss of the year. Stiff-arm a guy, scores a touchdown, right? And that’s what makes you feel good."

In today’s day and age, when it feels like we see parents brawling with each other, yelling at referees or even running onto the field during a play, remember that youth sports are for the kids.

And youth sports aren’t even about the game; it’s about the community that comes with it.

ORAL-B AND CREST PARTNER WITH THE NFL

Oral hygiene is incredibly important, and the NFL has partnered with Oral-B and Crest to make them the official toothbrush, toothpaste, floss and mouthwash of the league. Stewart has introduced a Panthers toothbrush into his routine.

"Oral hygiene and taking care of yourself is just as important as working out, right? Like, just as important as what you're eating on a daily basis as far as the health standard, right? Because we're talking about our gut health," Stewart said.

In addition to waking up and brushing his teeth, the former running back said he uses mouthwash about four times a day. Unfortunately for him, not all the coaches in his career cared as much about their breath as Stewart did.



"Some coaches I’ve had, I won’t name them, but they got some ranky breath. I can tell you that. It’s unfortunate when you meet people that have funky breath because they don’t even know," Stewart said.

Stewart spent 10 seasons with the Panthers and one with the New York Giants. In 134 career games, Stewart rushed for 7,335 yards and 51 touchdowns while catching 162 passes for 1,295 yards and seven touchdowns. He made the Pro Bowl in 2015.

World.title: ‘Activist judge’ rules Congress cannot bar noncitizens from voting in federal elections
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Biden-appointed judge is being labeled an "activist judge" by conservative critics after ruling that the federal government's application of a law barring noncitizens from voting in elections violates the Constitution in a federal criminal case.

In a 31-page ruling, U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz of the Southern District of Florida dismissed federal charges against Chelsea Cox, a woman originally from Jamaica who voted in the 2020 presidential election, despite not being a U.S. citizen. The ruling comes as the Trump administration has intensified efforts to prevent noncitizens from voting, including through federal prosecutions and attempts to verify citizenship on state voter rolls, sparking legal battles with Democratic-led states and voting-rights groups. President Donald Trump's election integrity efforts have been driven in large part by his and his allies' belief that the 2020 election was "stolen" — an unproven claim he continues to maintain.

Leibowitz ruled that the Constitution gives states — not Congress — the authority to determine who qualifies to vote in elections, effectively ruling that a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) criminalizing noncitizen voting in federal elections is unconstitutional as applied to Cox.

"The Constitution commits to the States, and the States alone, the general power to set voter qualifications in federal elections," Leibowitz wrote in his ruling. "This is clear from both the text of the document and the debates at the Constitutional Convention in 1787."

WATCH: MIKE LEE EXPLODES ON VOTING ERROR THAT 'KEEPS HAPPENING' AS HUGE NUMBER OF NONCITIZENS FOUND ON ROLLS

The ruling garnered sharp blowback from Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, who is co-author of the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which is currently being stalled in the Senate and unlikely to be passed before the midterm elections.

"This insane ruling will certainly be overturned," Lee wrote on X. "But it gives the game away: Democrats pretend we don’t need the SAVE Act because non-citizen voting is already illegal… while activist judges try to destroy laws banning non-citizens from voting!"

Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow with Advancing American Freedom, agreed that Leibowitz's ruling will most likely be "squashed" by the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals.

"Judge David Leibowitz’s opinion that the federal law barring aliens from voting is unconstitutional is patently wrong," Spakovsky told Fox News Digital. "It is true that states have the constitutional authority to set the qualifications of citizens who are eligible as voters in federal elections. But he ignores the fact that in Article I, Section 8, Congress is given 100% authority over naturalization."

Spakovsky said the Constitution gives Congress authority to decide how noncitizens enter the country and what activities they may engage in once here.

"That gives the federal government the authority to ban aliens from voting or otherwise in any way participating in the democratic process," Spakovsky said.

STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS

Spakovsky pointed to Bluman v. FEC , a 2011 decision written by then-Judge Brett Kavanaugh and later summarily affirmed by the Supreme Court, which upheld restrictions on foreign nationals' campaign spending. The opinion said the government may exclude noncitizens from activities tied to democratic self-government.

"The Supreme Court has long held that the government (federal, state, local) may exclude foreign citizens from activities that are part of the democratic self-regulation in the United States," Kavanaugh wrote. "For example, the Supreme Court has ruled that the government may bar aliens from voting, serving as jurors, working as police or probation officers, or teaching at public schools."

However, Bluman v. FEC involved campaign contributions and expenditures, not a federal criminal prosecution for voting.

Anhishek Kambil, a partner at Holtzman Vogel Law Firm, said he'd be "surprised" if the federal government did not prevail in its appeal.

Kambil pointed to Oregon v. Mitchell, in which the Supreme Court ruled the the government had the authority to set voting age in federal elections, which would be a voter qualifier.

"So the Supreme Court has held, in an instance, that there is federal government authority to regulate in certain instances some types of qualifications of voters, but the way that this judge read it kind of made everything a mess," Kambil told Fox News Digital.

Leibowitz rejected the federal government's argument that the Constitution grants Congress total authority over regulating immigration and noncitizens.

DHS APPROVES PLAN TO VERIFY VOTER CITIZENSHIP, MONITOR MAIL BALLOTS AS TRUMP PUSH INTENSIFIES

While he acknowledged that Congress has "broad, undoubted power" over immigration and noncitizens; he said those powers are not "a series of blank checks" and cannot override the Constitution’s "foundational constitutional constraints" assigning voter-qualification authority to the states.

The judge also rejected the federal government's reliance on the Elections Clause, which allows Congress to regulate how states conduct federal elections, including by passing laws to combat voter fraud. Leibowitz said the statute at issue was not designed to regulate election procedures or prevent fraud but instead created a federal voter qualification by determining who could vote.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

While Leibowitz ruled that the federal government cannot continue prosecuting Chelsea Cox, Florida would still have the authority to bring state charges.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

President Joe Biden nominated Leibowitz to the federal bench in 2024. The Senate confirmed him, 64-33, in a bipartisan vote, with then-Sen. Marco Rubio, R-Fla., voting in favor. Thursday's ruling is his most politically consequential decision from the bench to date.

World.title: Dining with someone you love may help the body in surprising ways, new research suggests
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Eating with a close partner may influence the body in a surprising way, new research suggests.

While researchers say the effect varies from person to person, a recent study suggests that eating with a loved one impacts how the body regulates blood sugar after a meal.

Participants in the study were given meals containing the same amount and type of carbohydrates, and researchers measured their blood glucose after eating.

THIS AMOUNT OF DELI MEAT ASSOCIATED WITH HIGHER DEMENTIA RISK IN COMPELLING NEW REVIEW

When participants ate together, researchers observed a smaller rise in glucose and a quicker return toward baseline compared with when they ate alone.

The findings, however, do not mean that everyone will experience the same effect.

Shir Atzil, Ph.D., the study's co-author and a professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel, told Fox News Digital that researchers observed substantial individual differences.

"While we observe the principle of social physiology at the population level, we have seen tremendous individual differences in how much individuals benefit or even actually lose from being together — so not everyone benefits the same amount," Atzil said.

"Some people gain a huge benefit from being with their partners," she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Some people gain a small benefit — and some people actually regulate themselves better when they're alone."

The research, published in the journal Science Advances in late September, was based on a concept known as social physiology, which examines how being near a close partner may affect physiological processes.

Atzil described the theory as suggesting that "our most basic physiological processes, [our] bodily homeostasis, the process of just keeping the body up and running, is actually working more efficiently when we're in proximity with a close partner."

More research is needed to understand why people respond differently, Atzil emphasized.

CLICK HERE TO 

She said she plans to continue testing the social physiology theory.

Social setting is also only one of many factors that can affect blood glucose.

Erin Palinski-Wade, a New York-area registered dietitian specializing in diabetes, told Fox News Digital that the amount and type of carbohydrates consumed are particularly important.

She noted that blood sugar can also be affected by factors including stress, sleep, physical activity and a person's surroundings.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Stress, whether you had [quality sleep] the night before, how active you were that day, even things like the temperature of the room, noise pollution — all of those things can impact blood sugar," Palinski-Wade said.

Persistently elevated glucose can contribute to serious health problems over time.

Regulating blood sugar after meals is important because persistently elevated glucose can contribute to serious health problems over time, including heart, kidney, eye and nerve damage, according to the National Institutes of Health.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) specifically recommends monitoring glucose two hours after a meal for many people with diabetes — and notes that keeping blood sugar within the target range helps prevent or delay serious health issues.

World.title: DA did not review statements and other evidence collected in alleged rape of Cornell student
World.content:
Cornell University police spoke to witnesses and received anonymous tips about an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house in the first weeks of its investigation two years ago, but the local prosecutor did not review the additional information before deciding not to bring charges.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said he based his decision not to pursue charges on the accuser’s initial six-page statement given to police.

Investigators from the campus police department documented those witness interviews and other steps taken to determine whether Jane Doe, a 20-year-old woman who reported the incident, was the victim of sexual assault during a party at the Chi Phi house from Oct. 19 to 20, 2024, according police records obtained by NBC News.

Documents reviewed by NBC News offer the most thorough look to date at how police handled the allegations from Jane Doe, who last month filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and seven Chi Phi brothers who she alleges sexually assaulted her over the course of hours while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana.

Van Houten, along with police and university officials, has come under intense fire for their handling of the matter. Jane Doe’s attorney has argued that she was failed by authorities who did not conduct a thorough investigation and who prejudged the events based on her earlier statement that she consented to parts of the night.

Gov. Kathy Hochul on Thursday announced the appointment of Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to consider whether charges are appropriate.

“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript” of the victim’s interview, Hochul asked Friday at a news conference announcing James’s appointment.

On Nov. 25, 2024, a police investigator approached Van Houten’s office to tell them about interviews they’d done.

An investigator in Van Houten’s office, according to the documents, replied that “he and several [attorneys] at the District Attorney’s Office had read [Jane Doe’s] statement … [and] stated that they all agreed that, based on [Jane Doe’s] statement, criminal charges would not be pursued in this case.”

Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Friday. Heather Ainsworth for NBC News

Van Houten defended his decision Monday and said that Jane Doe’s statement did not allege criminality. He also agreed to reopen his inquiry before that role was assigned to the attorney general.

When reached for comment by email Friday, Van Houten argued “there was nothing to review” in that discussion with police because the interviews flagged “were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney.”

Van Houten did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers.

The records also show that police were receiving portions of a larger Snapchat thread where one member of the group announced there was “free p----” in the alumni room of the house, where Jane Doe engaged in what she said was initially a consensual threesome.

“Similarly there was no material obtained by CUPD from Snapchat (what was provided came from a witness),” Van Houten added. “So again nothing to review.”

It was unclear whether Van Houten was aware that on Nov. 26, 2024, police made a request to Snapchat for a more complete data history.

That request was answered on Dec. 23, when police said they obtained 1,665 pieces of data from five Snapchat accounts.

“After reviewing all of the data returned from Snapchat, there appeared to be only 3 snapchats that included [Jane Doe] or mentioned this incident,” a CUPD investigator wrote. “None of these 3 snapchats show anything that can be construed as being criminal in nature. No further action taken.”

Jane Doe was only notified by Cornell police about the district attorney’s Nov. 25 determination not to pursue charges nearly two months later on, Jan. 21, 2025.

Van Houten added that his office had “no part in the timing” of conveying his decision to Jane Doe, who was never interviewed by his office.

Thomas Giuffra, the attorney representing Jane Doe, learned about that delay from NBC News’ request for comment Friday. He said that his client — during that two-month window — believed “they were still investigating.”

“I was unaware that they had made the decision to not prosecute in November,” Giuffra said. “If so, that is worse than I thought.”

On Nov. 7, 2024, two weeks after the incident at Chi Phi, Jane Doe submitted to a sexual assault examination and evidence collection process, according to the police records. She had gone to the university health center shortly after the alleged assault to get treatment for a urinary tract infection, but was not offered a rape kit at the time, Giuffra said. He called it “the first failure post assault when she was trying to get help.” Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The attorney called it “a code or cry for help to say something bad happened” when Jane Doe told them that she “has a UTI of a traumatic origin.” Giuffra said the medical staff should have asked her: “What kind of trauma do you think caused this UTI?”

He noted that had the health center referred Jane Doe to an outside facility for an examination, there might have been recoverable DNA because she was there within 48 hours.

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

World.title: Democrats regain ground on voter registration in key states after steep post-2024 drops
World.content:
After having suffered massive voter registration losses in the wake of the last presidential election, Democrats have stemmed the bleeding in several key states heading into this year’s midterms, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis.

NBC News’ Decision Desk analyzed voter file data from TargetSmart, a progressive data firm, for seven of the states that were the closest in the 2024 election and that registered voters by party: Arizona, Maine, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina and Pennsylvania. From late 2024 through late 2025, Republicans significantly improved their voter registration margin over Democrats in all seven states, including by a net of roughly 100,000 in Pennsylvania and North Carolina.

But from late 2025 through the middle of this year, Democrats managed to reverse, though not completely erase, those losses in five of them, adding more registrants on net than Republicans in Arizona, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. And in New Hampshire and North Carolina, Democrats have slowed the decline.

While party registration is not 100% predictive of vote choice, the recent movement toward Democrats on this front provides another reason for optimism for the party this fall. Arizona, Maine, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina and Pennsylvania are all holding critical races for the Senate or governor (if not both), while New Jersey, which has become more competitive in recent years, is hosting a battleground House contest.

The trend comes not only amid a backlash to President Donald Trump that has grown over the course of the year, but also as Democrats campaigned in consequential primaries that often centered on what direction the party would take after its 2024 defeat.

Meanwhile, the pool of unaffiliated voters continued to expand in many of those states, reflecting a growing distrust of both major parties.

There are three primary ways the party registration margin can change: new voters signing up; registrants switching parties; or registrants being removed from the rolls after having moved out of state, routine maintenance or dying. A total of 30 states and Washington, D.C., register voters by party, while the rest — including battlegrounds like Georgia, Michigan and Wisconsin — do not.

To track recent voter registration trends, NBC News analyzed TargetSmart data after the 2024 election, at the end of 2025 and in mid-2026, with the most recently available data in each state ranging from late June to September.

Democrats’ biggest post-2024 issue on this front largely came from voters leaving the rolls. But the analysis of the voter registration data reveals that the problem was not as severe for Democrats as it might appear, as many of those people were infrequent voters to begin with.

In all seven states, turnout in the 2024 election was significantly lower among the people who subsequently left the rolls than among those who stayed. For example, in Pennsylvania, the 2024 turnout among people who subsequently left the rolls was 37%, compared with 81% for those who stayed.

In battleground Pennsylvania, Republicans had their biggest net gain in voter registration (more than 110,000) from late 2024 to late 2025 of the seven states analyzed. But from the end of last year to this summer, Democrats gained a net of around 46,000.

Despite those big 2025 losses, Democrats actually gained around 22,000 registrants from new voters over that period. But that was offset by net losses from party registration switches (about 43,000) and registrants leaving the rolls (about 90,000). It all adds up in a state Trump won by 120,000 votes in 2024.

The data through this fall tells a different story, though. New registrants and party switchers gave Democrats net gains of around 45,000 and 11,000, respectively. That was more than enough to make up for more modest losses among registrants leaving the voter rolls.

Pennsylvania Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale said he aggressively prioritized voter registration efforts when he took over in September 2025.

About 150 staffers are now “having conversations with people in every single corner of our commonwealth, listening to their concerns, listening to their issues and making a case of why they should register as Democrats,” he said, while also crediting Trump’s growing unpopularity.

North Carolina, however, has remained a bright spot for the GOP: For the first time in the state’s history, the party holds a lead in party registration. From late 2024 to late 2025, Republicans’ net voter registration gain was just shy of 100,000. Democrats managed to keep the net loss to around 16,000 from late 2025 to last month.

“Traditionally, the Democrats have always just been better at this than Republicans,” said Felice Pete, a Republican National Committee member from North Carolina.

But in recent years, she said, conservative groups like Turning Point USA and Americans for Prosperity helped Republicans in the state boost their registration numbers through door-knocking and events.

“It’s almost like evangelizing, if you will,” she said.

Below the surface, there is a promising trend for Democrats in North Carolina. While new registrants gave Republicans a net gain of around 11,000 last year, they gave Democrats a net gain of around 6,000 this year.

In North Carolina and four of the other states analyzed — Arizona, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania — the number of people who either did not register with a party or registered with a party that was not the Democrats or the Republicans steadily grew from late 2024 to mid-2026. In Maine and New Jersey, that percentage slightly declined.

A significantly larger number of new voters in all seven states are registering as unaffiliated compared than are those currently on the rolls. And much of the movement away from the Democratic Party is from Democrats choosing to become unaffiliated, rather than registering as Republicans.

World.title: Global tech policymakers agree to embrace AI in science
World.content:
The United States on Sunday will release a joint statement with 15 other countries describing a shared vision for a “golden age of science” that embraces the potential of artificial intelligence.

The announcement is expected in Kyoto, Japan, at this year’s Science and Technology in Society Forum, an annual gathering of experts and policymakers that began in 2004.

The statement, titled the “Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science,” begins by recognizing science and technology’s benefits to society then goes on to encourage research that integrates artificial intelligence. (The statement calls it “super intelligence,” given President Donald Trump’s recent executive order renaming the technology.)

“Super Intelligence and new ways of organizing research are opening entirely new frontiers of discovery,” reads the statement, which was seen by NBC News. “We recognize the opportunity to take advantage of these changes.”

Michael Kratsios, head of the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy, spearheaded the vision statement, which also says the participating countries welcome the “growing field of metascience,” a term that describes the study of the scientific process itself.

Tech ministers from Japan, Korea, the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates were among the representatives from other countries that endorsed the statement.

In remarks Kratsios plans to deliver at the forum, shared in advance with NBC News, he will outline a vision for an era of scientific progress in which laboratories run by robots and AI systems can design scientific experiments, iterate and analyze results at superhuman speeds.

“Super intelligence applied to science will be an incredible force for democratization of research and breakthrough developments,” he plans to say.

Leading AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI have recently launched initiatives to connect biomedical laboratories to powerful AI systems, while other companies have attempted to automate laboratories for years.

“The landscape has changed everywhere, the ground is moving beneath our feet, and we must all reinvigorate our research enterprise and lay new foundations for knowledge, innovation and prosperity,” Kratsios is expected to say in his remarks.

The vision statement also says that public trust is the bedrock of scientific innovation and progress and that there’s value in “a deliberate portfolio of funding mechanisms” for science.

The Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to make drastic cuts to federal funding for scientific research. Its proposed budget for the 2027 fiscal year would, for example, cut funding for the National Science Foundation by about half.

Gretchen Goldman, CEO of the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the administration had undermined many scientific research efforts. “They’ve shattered the trust of the American people in the way they’ve treated the U.S. science and technology enterprise,” she said, pointing in particular to cuts to the National Institutes of Health.

“It’s hard to take seriously any promises of increased trust and transparency when you look at the actions they’ve taken,” Goldman said.

The statement comes as part of a wider push by Kratsios to reform how the U.S. incentivizes scientific innovation. In July, he submitted a report to Trump recommending changes to the ways the federal government funds research. He plans to host a summit about it in Washington, D.C., on Thursday with scientific and business leaders.

Kratsios is also leading the Genesis Mission, a national effort Trump launched last year to “unleash a new age of AI‑accelerated innovation and discovery.”

The forthcoming vision statement puts a particular emphasis on metascience, an area of study that has received wider government attention in recent years.

Its prominence in the statement signals increased international adoption, according to Jenn Gustetic, director of metascience and research and development policy at the nonpartisan think tank Institute for Progress.

“Metascience efforts have built momentum in the U.K. and the U.S. and it’s encouraging to see other nations embrace this mindset of experimentation and evidence building,” Gustetic said.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced that it would establish an Office of Metascience (OMS), charged with evaluating new approaches to funding and identifying which award mechanisms lead to the best scientific outcomes.

“Through the OMS, NSF will become a learning, self-improving institution that tries new approaches, measures their effects, admits candidly when they do not work, and scales them when they succeed,” the agency’s acting director Brian Stone wrote in a letter.

The Science and Technology in Society Forum is intended as a venue for leaders to discuss how to maximize the benefits of science and address ethical and safety issues.

During the three-day gathering, scientists and policymakers from around the world are expected to discuss how AI is impacting education, how experts can foster trust in scientific research, recent breakthroughs in personalized medicine and more.

The vision statement is set to be released just days after Trump gathered the country’s leading tech executives at the White House to forge consensus on how to regulate and minimize risks from AI. The meeting culminated in the ‘White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” which laid out a four-part voluntary approach for companies to independently oversee their own safety protocols.

Kratsios participated in the AI meeting.

“If you take the risks and benefits of superintelligence seriously, the most important thing you can do is to develop your country’s ability to understand and use it,” he said at a United Nations Security Council meeting on AI last month.

World.title: Mike Tomlin gives fans a glimpse inside the Minecraft city he spent 12 years building
World.content:
As the coach of one of the NFL’s most successful franchises, the Pittsburgh Steelers, for nearly two decades, Mike Tomlin was charged with building championship-caliber teams.

In his free time, Tomlin was building something different: an elaborate cityscape in the video game “Minecraft.”

On his YouTube channel on Wednesday, Tomlin revealed part of that map, which he said he had been working on for more than 12 years. Within four hours, the episode had been viewed more than 334,000 times. By the next morning, that total had doubled.

“I’ve always had an interest in architecture and so forth,” Tomlin said in the video, which has amassed over 900,000 views. “And so I started building this creative city.”

Tomlin may have been perfecting the map for more than a decade, but his hobby had only become public three weeks earlier.

The 54-year-old stepped down as the Steelers’ coach in January after 19 consecutive winning seasons, which included a Super Bowl victory. As his debut season as a broadcaster for NBC’s “Sunday Night Football” began last month, Tomlin revealed in an interview with Craig Melvin that his passions, in fact, ranged beyond football.

Watching his then-young children spend hours playing “Minecraft” had inspired him to see what all the fuss was about. As they became teenagers and went off to college, their interest waned.

Not Tomlin’s, though.

“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me,” Tomlin said. “So, mindless entertainment. I’m not a big TV watcher. It allowed me to detach from the realities and the pressures of life.”

With the Steelers, Tomlin was known for unique sayings referred to as “Tomlinisms.” In 2020, he famously wouldn’t allow Covid restrictions to be used as a hardship, saying, “We do not care.” So it stunned some football fans last month to hear that what Tomlin privately did care so much for was a video game that is immensely popular with elementary-age kids.

Since its creation in 2009, “Minecraft” has become the bestselling game of all time, with more than 300 million copies sold, Microsoft said in 2024, and has since spawned a popular movie.

An open-world “sandbox” game, “Minecraft” allows users to build whatever their creativity desires using a variety of materials, from different types of stone and wood to beyond. Some players build fantasy worlds where building physics don’t apply.

Players often build in multiple maps. Tomlin stuck to just one, however, preferring to build what appears to be a midsize city centered on bodies of water and with a dense urban core that includes sports stadiums, high-rises and a PNC Bank. The map showed hills and wooded suburbs.

In other words, not all that dissimilar to … Pittsburgh.

Narrating his tour with a matter-of-fact delivery not out of place from his past weekly news conferences, Tomlin used verbiage a real estate developer would approve of while saying that his map all began by creating a bay. Then he built a boutique hotel, complete with an executive spa, therapy rooms and an “appropriate number of public restrooms.” Showing off a glass ceiling over the hotel’s conference room, Tomlin called his design philosophy “lighting-conscious.”

00:23 Mike Tomlin says he's been working on a city in 'Minecraft' 00:00 00:00

Some commenters online questioned how much time Tomlin had spent building while also working in the NFL, an industry known for its workaholic culture. Former Steelers running back Le’Veon Bell wrote, “we were tryna win super bowls and coach T was on minecraft building cities 😭.”

More so, the reaction tended to center on Tomlin’s dedication to realism.

“Never thought I’d watch Mike Tomlin discuss lighting and basement speakeasies,” one YouTube commenter said. On a Reddit thread devoted to Tomlin’s build, one person wrote, “When Mike Tomlin first mentioned this whole thing, I was NOT expecting such an impressive city!”

Tomlin built buildings by themes, intentionally placing them next to rivers, bays and lakes he carved out of the map. His designs are intricate; residential buildings included different floor plans for the penthouse than the lower floors. Kitchens featured islands. Bathrooms featured plants. Bedrooms included paintings. The living spaces in one high-rise, which was down the street from buildings named “CVS” and “7-Eleven,” wrapped around a central aquarium. Nearby were stadiums for professional soccer and baseball.

At some point, Tomlin acknowledged becoming “obsessed with rooftop penthouses” with great views. That focus then spilled over into designing spaces for indoor and outdoor entertainment, balconies, home offices and his-and-hers bathroom concepts.

“Find someone who loves you like Coach Tomlin loves a Jack & Jill bathroom,” another YouTube commenter said.

It was one of many jokes sparked by Tomlin’s “Minecraft” devotion. Yet, perhaps it shouldn’t have been all that surprising. In “Minecraft,” Tomlin seems to have found similarities to the mixture of creativity and discipline required in the world of the NFL. Coaches’ lives abide by a rigid structure of practices, games and the offseason calendar. They conceive exotic play designs and defensive coverages, then put them into practice by obsessing over details and precision.

“Football is an emotional game played by high-energy men who are really emotional,” Tomlin said in 2022. “They need to hear a steady voice. They need to hear consistency in messaging in belief, and so it’s my job to exemplify that.”

Former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin. Getty; Minecraft

Tomlin was praised as a coach for his never-too-high, never-too-low personality. The kind of person whose idea of winding down after a long day in the spotlight might include ensuring his “Minecraft” map had a “certain density,” as he said. When Tomlin dropped his son Dino off at college, he said he was inspired to re-create the look of off-campus housing into his own city.

“Bro I used to come home sometimes and my PlayStation would just be gone,” one of Tomlin’s sons, Mason, posted on X. “And I wasn’t in trouble.”

At one point during Tomlin’s tour, he focused on a tall, beige building labeled “Trump Tower.”

“Not an endorsement,” a chyron said on the video. “This build is (circa) 2015… We didn’t think he would win. Twice.”

Its penthouse had an “unbelievable open floor plan,” Tomlin said approvingly.

He promised his roughly 76,000 YouTube subscribers more episodes.

“I’ll give you a tour of this aquarium at some point,” he said. “It’s crazy.”

World.title: Affording America: How a single mother in Chicago turned to gig work to survive
World.content: Jade Crossfrench is a single mother supporting three children with a day job selling insurance. But that isn't enough to provide for her family. For over a year she's been making extra money as a gig worker, doing DoorDash food deliveries around Chicago, often with her kids sitting in the back seat of the car.Sept. 30, 2026

World.title: Coast Guard searching off Nantucket for missing Boston-bound jet
World.content:
The United States Coast Guard is searching for a Gulfstream jet carrying six people that lost contact with flight controllers Saturday morning on its way to Boston from the island of Bermuda.

The Coast Guard says air and surface crews have launched in search of the aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 jet.

The plane was carrying out a medical evacuation in Bermuda, said Clarence Togeretz, Director of Flight Operations at Latitude Air Ambulance, which operates the plane.

“We always get rather concerned when our crew doesn’t report to us in a timely manner,” he told NBC News. “But I will say that again, optimistically and positively, that doesn’t mean that the worst has happened.”

Togeretz added that Latitude Air Ambulance had an emergency response plan in place “absolutely for anything that might occur to any of our missions.”

The current search area is “off the coast of Nantucket,” the Coast Guard Northeast District said in an update on X. Data from FlightRadar24 showed a number of aircraft searching south of the island.

The Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement that it issued a search and rescue notice for the jet at 1.20 a.m. ET on Saturday, and is coordinating with the USCG and Rescue Coordination Center to locate the aircraft.

Bermuda is a British overseas territory in the north Atlantic Ocean, about 650 miles from North Carolina.

World.title: More details emerge about FlyDubai co-pilot who tried to crash plane
World.content:
Days after a FlyDubai co-pilot made a violent attempt to crash the passenger aircraft and was subdued by passengers and other crew members, questions about his motive continued to swirl. He is currently being questioned in the United Arab Emirates.

The flight Wednesday from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

The co-pilot is currently being questioned in the United Arab Emirates.

There were 174 people on board the plane. No passengers were seriously injured in the incident. The pilot sustained stab wounds in the attack. Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries, and the co-pilot remained in custody on Thursday.

Who was the FlyDubai co-pilot?

The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified, although multiple sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News on Friday that his name is Hamam al Hamami.

Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.

One of the sources said the pilot resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty. He left the airline around 2024.

At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of El Al Israeli Airlines planes in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, a well-known al Qaeda leader who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.

Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.

Al Hamami is an Omani citizen but was not born in Oman, the sources said. He lived most of his life outside Oman, according to the sources, who disclosed that his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani.

The Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.

The sources said it is possible he had dual citizenship because that could explain how he was allowed to fly to Israel.

A FlyDubai flight bound for Dubai is seen before taking off from Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv on Sept. 30, 2026. Jack GUEZ /AFP via Getty Images

Co-pilot's motive unknown

The co-pilot's motive in the alleged attack remains unknown. The UAE's attorney general said Saturday he attacked his fellow pilot with the cockpit's emergency ax.

"As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer; the attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane with its passengers," Netanyahu said in a statement Friday. "We are investigating whether he was dispatched, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price."

Netanyahu speculated to CBS News on Wednesday that the incident looked "like a suicide attempt," referring to witnesses who said the co-pilot had tried to jam the plane's equipment instead of stabilizing the aircraft. After passengers subdued the co-pilot, he shouted for someone to kill him, Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday.

In the same interview with Fox, Netanyahu said "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning had led Israel to the conclusion that the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination." He did not offer more information.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Wednesday called the incident "an attempted jihadist terror attack," and referred to the co-pilot as a "terrorist."

President Trump suggested Thursday that the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."

"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."

His comments went further than Netanyahu's, who told Fox it was "too early to say" if Iran was involved.

An Israeli security official told CBS News that authorities were investigating the possibility the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and were also probing whether the attacker was working alone. Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

Co-pilot to be questioned in UAE

The co-pilot was placed under arrest immediately.

He was transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the UAE for questioning by Israeli, UAE and Saudi officials, an Israeli official confirmed to CBS News on Friday.

On Wednesday, Netanyahu said the man was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities" and confirmed that Israeli authorities would "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly."

Netanyahu has not said what information has led investigators to conclude the co-pilot underwent radicalization.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect that the pilot resigned from Oman Air and wasn't fired.

World.title: Iowa approves pricy foreign-owned steel plant project in swing district
World.content:
"Stop the Steal" — or rather, steel — has an entirely new meaning for some Iowa voters in 2026.

Protesters at the Iowa statehouse Friday carried signs reading "No Steel Steal!" as lawmakers raced through a one-day special session to award Mesabi Metallics $1.36 billion over ten years in tax incentives for a new steel plant in Lee County. Mesabi Metallics is owned by the Indian conglomorate Essar Group.

The Iowa House passed it 75-17, the Senate 28-19. Gov. Kim Reynolds signed it into law Friday night.

It comes after President Trump's Monday announcement that the largest steel plant in U.S. history will be built in Iowa. Mr. Trump promised the $15 billion steel plant would create 1,750 permanent jobs and roughly 6,000 construction jobs.

The announcement caught many in the state, including lawmakers who would be counted on to approve the tax incentives, by surprise. When Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters at the White House "the deal is done" on Monday, lawmakers in Iowa still hadn't received details to review or timing for the special session held Friday.

Opponents of the $1.36 billion in incentives are largely supporters of the project, but they wanted more safeguards and guarantees of public benefits. The incentives roughly amount to about $777,000 in credits per permanent job over 10 years, a hefty price tag by any standards. Proponents argue that math leaves out roughly 6,000 construction jobs — which opponents point out are all temporary.

And a time when many of Iowa's farmers are struggling, more than a billion-dollars in tax credit for an India-based conglomerate is a hard sell for some.

(L-R) Mesabi Metallics President and CEO Joe Broking, Chairman Rewant Ruia, board member and Essar Capital director Ravi Ruia, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright listen as President Trump speaks in the Oval Office on September 28, 2026. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

Why Iowa?

There are places in the U.S. synonymous with steel, but Iowa has never been one of them. The state has a couple scrap-fed steel mills — a small fraction of the size Mesabi is promising — and no commercial iron ore. Mesabi Metallics is based in Minnesota, and its argument is that Iowa is conveniently downriver on the Mississippi.

But Iowa has something that Minnesota doesn't: one of the most tightly contested congressional races in the nation. The state also has tight Senate and governor's races.

The plant is proposed for Iowa's first congressional district, where Republican Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending one of the GOP's most at-risk seats. In 2024, the recount had her ahead of Democrat Christina Bohannan by just 798 votes. Sabato's Crystal Ball just moved the race from "toss up" to "leans Democratic" before the steel announcement.

Bankruptcy and broken promises

Mesabi and Essar Group have a long history of missed deadlines and unfulfilled job promises. In 2008, Essar announced a $1.6 billion iron ore mine and steel plant in Nashwauk, Minnesota, home to some of the country's richest iron ore deposits. It promised more than 700 permanent jobs. But the steel mill plans were dropped in 2015. Essar Steel Minnesota filed for bankruptcy in 2016, was renamed Mesabi Metallics under new owners, and later came back under Essar's control.

The India-based Essar has recevied billions of dollars in loans from the Russian state-owned bank VTB, according to local media. CBS News has not independently verified these reports.

Signage for Essar Steel Ltd. is displayed as workers load items onto a truck at the company's Pune Facility near Pune, Maharashtra, India, on Friday, Oct. 26, 2018. Dhiraj Singh / Bloomberg via Getty Images

There are also echoes of other regional mega-projects gone awry. No one in the Hawkeye state wants the steel plant to be the 2026 version of Foxconn. In 2017, President Trump and Foxconn promised a $10 billion plant and create 13,000 jobs in the battleground state of Wisconsin. By 2021, the plan was scaled back to $672 million and 1,454 jobs. Republican Gov. Scott Walker championed the deal — and lost his 2018 reelection bid as public support for it soured.

Tricky politics

On Friday, Republican State Senator Kevin Alons told the Des Moines Register that lawmakers needed more time ahead of Friday's vote.

"The political extortion is breathtaking," he said.

But in the end, he voted for it.

State Senator Dave Sires, also a Republican, voted no to the project, complaining the process was rushed. State Senator Dan Dawson, another Republican, called it the "largest corporate giveaway in the state of Iowa's history." And Republican State Senator Jeff Taylor raised concerns that the state was already in a real budget crunch.

Taylor was swapped off the Senate Ways and Means Committee at the last minute to ensure the bill would pass committee. It passed 10-8, with 6 Republican State Senators voting against the bill.

It's a careful political calculus for Republicans in the Iowa Senate. They're trying to thread a fine needle: follow their leaders and bring home jobs, without being seen as rushing more than a billion dollars in taxpayer money to a foreign-owned company with no time for review.

Photo taken on May 14, 2026 shows the building of Iowa State Capitol with a gold-leafed dome in Des Moines, Iowa, the United States. Zhang Fengguo/Xinhua via Getty Images

Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who has campaigned against corporate handouts, made a case for supporting the bill. He called the idea of an Iowa steel plant a "once in a lifetime" exception.

Democrats have been navigating tricky political territory as well, trying not to oppose job creation while pushing back on the rush to issue nearly $1.4 billion in tax breaks before early voting starts on Oct. 14. Democratic nominee Rob Sand, currently the state auditor, called the steel plant "a promising idea for Lee County" but wanted to see more details first.

"You look at these data center deals that this administration has done over the last few years and we gave away the farm," Sand said. "I want to make sure this is a real opportunity, but also at the end of the day Iowa is getting served by it and not getting fleeced."

Iowa Senate Democratic Leader Janice Weiner said she wants good-paying jobs and investments in the state but balked at the rapid timeline that left taxpayers out of the conversation.

"If we were doing this the right way, we would be waiting until after the election," she told CBS News on Saturday. "We have a responsibility to our taxpayers to make sure our hard-earned dollars are well spent. If it's a good deal now, it will be a good deal in January when due diligence has been done."

Meanwhile, State Representative Dave Jacoby, a Democrat, voted yes, "with the hope that this plan is real," while still cautioning, "today is not a ribbon cutting."

The ribbon cutting, if it comes, is years away. The tax credits don't kick in until the plant is running, and Mesabi says that won't be before 2030. Iowans begin to cast their votes in just a few days. So the question on the ballot isn't whether Iowa gets a steel mill. It's whether voters believe it will — and if $1.36 billion was the right price to pay for it.

World.title: Clinical trial helps treat woman's "insufferable pain" from sunlight
World.content:
Emily Pearson was 8 years old when the attacks started. Just minutes in the sun would leave her hands and feet hurting. Her extremities "felt like they were in a hot oven" while being poked "with pins and needles." A short while outdoors could leave her in pain for days. Worst of all, no one knew why.

Over the next decade, Pearson's parents tried to identify the cause of her reactions. Sunblock didn't help. She started wearing protective clothing and staying indoors as much as possible. Vacations at her family's Minnesota cabin became an endurance test. If she slipped up and found herself in the sun for too long, her hands, feet and face paid the price.

"It was just insufferable pain. I would never wish that pain upon anyone, because it's so horrible," said Pearson, who lives in Minneapolis.

When she was 17, a doctor at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, made the diagnosis of erythropoietic protoporphyria, a rare skin disorder that means a person is essentially allergic to the sun. Having an answer was a relief, Pearson said — but it also meant she had to grapple with not being able to do much about her condition.

One form of comfort was running. Pearson had been a competitive swimmer for 12 years, then transitioned into running half-marathons out of high school. She had to either layer up or run in the dark, at sunrise or at sunset, to avoid having a reaction. But the difficulties were worth the joy it brought her, she said.

Pearson dreamed of running a marathon, but believed her condition made that impossible. Throughout college, braving the sun for a few hours of fun without protective gear would leave her "in severe pain" later.

Emily Pearson runs in layers. Emily Pearson

"Going to the grocery store, going to get gas, going for any kind of car ride or working outside, you constantly have to think about what you're doing and how it's going to affect your health, and dealing with those consequences after," Pearson, now 25, said. "It was really hard, and it was really, really stressful. It was a big mental load, and it was never-ending."

In 2025, Pearson volunteered at Sun Escape, a weekend camp for kids with EPP and similar conditions. There, she learned about a clinical trial for a drug called bitopertin. She was intrigued and searched for more information.

"I was very wary of it, like, 'Does it really work? I know it works for other people, but will it work for me?'" Pearson remembered. "There was that anxiety of the unknown."

"I can't believe I'm hearing this"

Bitopertin works by targeting protoporphyrin IX, a naturally occurring molecule in the skin that is activated when people are exposed to sunlight, said Dr. Sioban Keel, a porphyria expert at the University of Washington who is involved in the clinical trial.

In patients with EPP and similar conditions, mutations mean the body creates too much protoporphyrin IX, resulting in painful reactions. Bitopertin, taken as a once-daily pill, lowers the amount of protoporphyrin IX in those patients, Keel explained.

Emily Pearson in protective gear. Emily Pearson

Pearson was part of the trial's second phase. Clinical trials in the U.S. have four phases, as defined by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The first stage involves a small group of participants and determines if a drug is safe and sets its dosage. In the second phase, up to several hundred people are studied for months or years. This is the stage that determines how effective a drug is, as well as what side effects it may have. The third and fourth stages expand that to an even larger population for longer periods. After the process is complete, the FDA reviews the data and decides whether or not to approve the medication for use in the general public.

As a participant in the trial's second stage, Pearson began taking bitopertin regularly in July 2025. She had regular appointments with physicians in Boston to follow her progress. Within weeks, she began to do "really, really well," and her tolerance to the sun started to increase. Keel, who did not treat Pearson, said she's heard similar stories from other patients involved in the trial.

"The impact I've seen it have on my patients has been a game changer. Patients that previously could never go out in the sun are able to go out in the sun ... You're like, 'I can't believe I'm hearing this,'" Keel said.

Clinical trial data published by Disc Medicine in April said the use of the medication "significantly reduced protoporphyrin-IX levels" and led to "improved measures of sunlight tolerance" for EPP patients, with "no notable safety concerns."

EXTERNAL EXPERT QUOTE

"My life has literally changed so much"

Bitopertin is now in Phase 3 clinical trials, with 183 patients enrolled and data expected in the final quarter of 2026. The FDA has declined to review bitopertin for expedited approval, citing a desire to see more data proving its impact on patients, according to a written statement from Disc Medicine. The company said it believes the Phase 3 data will show the information the FDA has requested.

EXTERNAL EXPERT QUOTE

Pearson remains on the medication through an open-label extension, an optional phase of clinical trials where enrolled patients are given the choice to stay on the drug. Her tolerance to the sun has increased. In October 2025, she was able to realize a long-held dream and run her first marathon.

Emily Pearson runs her first marathon. Emily Pearson

"I was outside the whole day, running and having fun," Pearson said. "I just got to wear shorts and a T-shirt. And everyone running around you doesn't know what you're going through, but I was really proud of myself."

The race encouraged Pearson to keep pushing her limits. She trained for another marathon this spring, then ran the race in June. In July, she spent a week at her family's cabin. Unlike past years, she spent the whole trip "outside every day, sunup to sundown, no reactions." She noted that sometimes she experiences minor reactions after spending lots of time outdoors, but said the pain is far less and her tolerance is much higher.

"It's unimaginable. I cannot explain how big of a difference it makes, because the cabin and going outside used to be such a source of anxiety for me. Now, I had the best week ever," Pearson said.

She plans on taking it easy for the next few months, but plans to run another marathon in June 2027. She also wants to expand her horizons and try a triathlon, combining her love of running with her history as a competitive swimmer. Now that she no longer has to "pick and choose how to" spend time outdoors, the future feels full of possibility.

"I'm able to feel free and live without all the worry and anxiety that I was before," Pearson said. "I'm 20 times happier. I'm more energetic. My life has literally changed so much."

World.title: G7 nations will release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel to combat high prices
World.content: G7 nations' oil and diesel release G7 countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products, starting with diesel. Joe Brettell, founder and principal of Forward Energy, joins CBS News to discuss.

World.title: Makers of "Atonement" discuss their new film about a Marine and the first Iraq War
World.content: Makers of "Atonement" discuss new film A new film, "Atonement," is based on the true story of a U.S. Marine who served in the first Iraq War. In the early days of the war he mistakenly fired on a family driving through a chaotic Baghdad intersection. Shots were being fired in many directions, but the Marine gunfire killed three civilians. The movie chronicles the Marine's long-simmering guilt and trauma and an elongated effort to reach out to the surviving family members in an attempt to find some manner of reconciliation. Reed Van Dyk, the film's producer and director, Dexter Filkins, who wrote the New Yorker story the film's script is based off of, and Boyd Holbrook, who stars in the movie, join "The Takeout" to discuss.

World.title: CBS News poll finds voters split on state v. national focus in Maine Senate race
World.content:
Anyone who's walked its rugged coast or skied in its mountains knows Maine can get windy.

But right now Maine's Senate race seems a bit insulated from the national political winds — which otherwise seem to favor the Democrats — at least enough to keep incumbent Republican Susan Collins in a tied race with Democrat Troy Jackson in a state that otherwise has a Democratic-leaning electorate.

Collins is drawing enough voters and enough of Maine's Democrats, while she is bolstered by those who say they're voting more on state matters than national ones, to keep the race at a tie.

And she has an edge on who would bring back more federal funds to Maine.

Jackson's challenge is that Collins peels off one in five voters who disapprove of Trump — a rate higher than what Republican congressional candidates get nationally.

Jackson's backing, in turn, is driven by those who think Collins is too much in agreement with President Trump, as well as by voters specifically opposed to tariffs, by those trying to give national Democrats control of the Senate and by those prioritizing change over experience.

A sizable 10% of voters say they could still change their minds — another dynamic that underscores that this could still break either way.

Even when voters think Jackson's policies would make them financially better off, Collins gets almost one in five of those voters, too.

Overall, Maine's voters do feel Trump's policies have hurt the Maine economy. Jackson wins most of those who do.

But long-time service isn't entirely working against Collins, even if it's an "anti-incumbent" year: Collins does especially well among voters who say they've voted for her multiple times in the past.

Jackson may be feeling the effects of the primary season: four in 10 Democrats and most independents wish someone else were the Democratic nominee.

Jackson also runs behind the Democrats' gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree, as Pingree's lead in the governor's race hews much more closely to the state's overall partisan lean. (Kamala Harris won the state.) Pingree gets some of the voters who are splitting their tickets to back Collins.

This CBS News/YouGov survey was conducted with a representative sample of 1,144 registered voters in Maine interviewed between September 23rd -October 1, 2026. The sample was weighted according to gender, age, race and education based on U.S. Census data, as well as to 2024 presidential vote. The margin of error is ± 4.7 points for registered voters.
