Chinese Olympic diving champion Zhang Jiaqi has sparked debate after starring in a popular reality show and revealing years of criticism, little emotional support, and financial control from her mother.

The debate intensified Sunday after Zhang’s mother, Xiao Yingjie, read aloud a letter telling her daughter that, despite not having “performed very well,” she still chose to “trust” and “forgive” her. Xiao had written the letter ahead of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where Zhang, then 17, went on to win gold in synchronized diving. Related hashtags later trended on microblogging platform Weibo, drawing tens of millions of views.

The 22-year-old from Beijing retired last year. She now studies sports training at Beijing Sport University and also works as a livestreamer. In late August, she joined the current season of “My Little One,” a reality show that follows female celebrities and their parents at home, inviting guests to provide commentary on family dynamics.

The show revealed that before Zhang retired, all of her earnings, including a prize of 810,000 yuan ($120,000) she had received as a teenager, and three bank cards were managed by her mother.

On “My Little One,” Xiao is seen repeatedly criticizing her daughter, complaining about everything from Zhang letting her cats onto the table to drinking ice water, eating snacks, and leaving the tag on her pajamas. On one occasion, she says to the show’s other guests, “Look how lazy she is.”

Xiao’s private communications to Zhang via the instant messaging platform WeChat — messages critiquing everything from her tone of voice to table manners, as well as forwarded educational videos — were also shown to viewers. Zhang largely responded with silence as they were presented. “It’s so suffocating (to watch),” one highly upvoted comment on the microblogging platform Weibo read.

The show also revealed that Xiao, despite having no other job commitments, rarely visited Zhang once she left home to attend training at age 6.

On the show, Zhang told Xiao that she often felt that her mother didn’t love her and that her parents were not what she “imagined.” She added that she “always hated” Xiao as a child and that she believed she had been raised not by her but by her diving team.

Popular social media comments labeled Xiao as “NPD,” short for narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis that has become an online shorthand in China for controlling, self-centered, or emotionally manipulative people.

One post with nearly 20,000 likes on Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, called Zhang a “survivor of criticism-based parenting,” praising her for expressing her dissatisfaction with her mother on the show and actively distancing herself from her mother’s control. Others questioned Zhang’s father for his apparent absence from the conflict.

Domestic psychologist Li Songwei, appearing as a guest on the show, described the conflict as “delayed adolescence” on Xiao’s part. In a Weibo post, Li later urged people not to vilify Xiao, saying she had since voluntarily signed up for courses on parent-child communication and apologized to her daughter for her mistakes.

“This is a typical mother who is blinded by anxiety,” Li wrote. “In fact, the reason young viewers see so many parental traits in Zhang Jiaqi’s mother that they find ‘annoying’ or even ‘infuriating’ is that they, too, are working through issues from their own adolescence. It is a path every family has to take.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Zhang Jiaqi (right) and her mother on the show “My Little One.” From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.title: The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.content:
This summer, “All Wishes Come True!” took in more than 1.8 billion yuan ($268 million) at the Chinese box office, becoming the latest in a string of hit animated films inspired by traditional Chinese myths and legends. The movie reimagines the Eight Immortals, a group of legendary figures in Chinese mythology and Taoism, as ordinary mortals who pose as immortals and venture into the celestial realm of Penglai. There, the mismatched group finds itself caught up in a conflict involving powerful gods, including the warrior deity Erlang Shen.

Despite the film’s widespread acclaim, some Taoist friends of mine were far from impressed. They believe it trivializes important figures in Taoist tradition, completely reimagining their stories while simply borrowing the names of Chinese immortals as a gimmick. But how fixed are the stories of the Eight Immortals in the first place?

Firstly, what makes the Eight Immortals — one of the best-known groups of immortals in Chinese culture — so special? And how exactly are they understood within Taoism?

Let’s start with why there are eight. In traditional Chinese culture, the number eight has long been associated with completeness and balance. The “Zhou Yi” (or “Book of Changes”), for example, describes the eight trigrams; traditional cosmology divides space into eight directions; and ancient people worshipped eight agricultural deities collectively associated with the harvest.

Then there are the “immortals” themselves. The Chinese word xian, or “immortal,” has long been associated with hermits who withdraw into the mountains in pursuit of spiritual cultivation. In Taoism, immortals are distinct from shen, or deities, in that ordinary humans can attain immortality through cultivation. Immortals thus occupy a space between the human and sacred worlds, embodying the Tao in the human realm.

Before the Eight Immortals became established as a group, several individual members had already appeared in historical writings and paintings from the Tang (618–907) and Song (960–1279) dynasties, each associated with their own supernatural feats.

Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin practiced neidan, a Taoist tradition of spiritual cultivation sometimes called “internal alchemy,” and frequently interacted with the influential Taoist priest Chen Tuan. Zhang Guolao once demonstrated various miraculous Taoist arts before Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty. Han Xiangzi could make flowers bloom instantly. Lan Caihe was a beggar who wore a shoe on one foot while leaving the other bare, often singing and dancing while intoxicated and carrying a large clapper.

Once they had formed into a group, however, the Eight Immortals did not simply retreat into the mountains or ascend to heaven. Instead, they remained closely connected to the human world. The most representative figure in this respect is Lü Dongbin, who chooses to remain among mortals and save them. He assumes various guises, including those of a fisherman, an ink and paper peddler, a sick beggar, and even a pregnant nun. Stories and images of Lü spread across China, with saving and enlightening ordinary people becoming a central theme in legends surrounding him.

The Yuan dynasty (1279–1368) mural “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” at Yongle Palace in Ruicheng, in northern China’s Shanxi province, shows that the Eight Immortals had by then become an established subject in Taoist art. But closer inspection reveals that the only female member of today’s group, He Xiangu, is missing. In her place is Xu Shenweng, a Taoist figure associated with the Northern Song period (960–1127) who once ranked among the Eight Immortals. In other words, the Eight Immortals were originally an all-male group.

So, when did He Xiangu become one of the Eight Immortals? One early appearance of her as part of the group comes in the Yuan dynasty drama “Chen Jiqing Mistakenly Boards a Bamboo Leaf Boat” by Fan Kang. By the time Wu Yuantai wrote the mythological novel “Journey to the East” during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), she had become a permanent member of the group.

This change came amid the flourishing of women’s literary and religious activity during the mid-to-late Ming. Like male scholars, educated women participated in religious and intellectual life and produced literary works of their own. In “Journey to the East,” He Xiangu’s defining supernatural ability is her power to foresee good and bad fortune. Born into a family that ran an herbal medicine shop, she possesses medical knowledge and uses encounters with people seeking treatment as opportunities to encourage them to do good.

With the addition of He Xiangu, the lineup familiar today became fixed and increasingly popular. The Eight Immortals eventually became influential enough to attract the attention of European missionaries studying Chinese religion and folklore. French Jesuit Henri Doré (1859–1931), for example, compiled stories about them in “Researches into Chinese Superstitions,” his multivolume study of Chinese popular religion, folklore, and customs.

The Chinese Jesuit priest Pierre Hoang (1830–1909), also known as Huang Bolu, meanwhile, described the Eight Immortals as representing a cross-section of society: the old and young, men and women, the rich and poor, the noble and lowly. In another interpretation, Zhang Guolao represents old age; Lan Caihe and Han Xiangzi, youth; Zhongli Quan, the military; Lü Dongbin, the scholar; Cao Guojiu, the nobility; Li Tieguai, the sick; and He Xiangu, women.

The Eight Immortals thus came to encompass a broad range of social identities and experiences. They had, collectively, seen many sides of the human world, allowing people from different backgrounds to recognize something of themselves in the group. Their differences also created a kind of balance, recalling a passage in Chapter 2 of the “Tao Te Ching,” which states: “Thus existence and non-existence produce each other; the difficult and the easy bring about each other; the long and the short impart form to each other; the high and the low comply [or change places] with each other; sounds and voices harmonize with each other; priority and sequence alternate with each other.”

From the mid-to-late Ming dynasty onward, the Eight Immortals also became a popular decorative motif on ceramics produced in both imperial and private kilns. They often appeared more subtly on everyday objects, including furniture, utensils, clothing, and architectural decorations. Rather than depicting the immortals themselves, artisans represented them through eight objects associated with the group: Li Tieguai’s gourd, Zhongli Quan’s fan, Zhang Guolao’s fish drum, Lan Caihe’s flower basket, Cao Guojiu’s jade tablet, Han Xiangzi’s flute, He Xiangu’s lotus, and Lü Dongbin’s sword. Craftsmen combined these symbols with scrollwork, bats, clouds, and waves to create decorative compositions that also conveyed wishes for longevity, good fortune, and wealth.

Stories about the Eight Immortals were similarly adaptable. Among commoners, plays such as “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” and “The Eight Immortals Assembly Celebrate Longevity” were widely performed. By the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns (1736–1820) of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), such stories were increasingly associated with birthday celebrations, with gatherings of the Eight Immortals symbolizing longevity, joy, and good fortune.

Among intellectuals, meanwhile, the Eight Immortals served as a source of creative inspiration. One example is “The Record of Handan,” the last of the “Four Dreams of Linchuan” by the great Ming playwright Tang Xianzu. Rather than focusing on reunion, the play uses Lü Dongbin to explore the illusory nature of worldly ambition.

In the play, Lü meets a poor scholar obsessed with achieving fame and gives him a porcelain pillow. After putting on a pot of rice to boil, the scholar falls asleep and dreams that he marries, places first in the imperial examinations, and spends decades navigating political machinations before becoming a powerful and honored official, only to eventually die from overindulgence. Waking to find his pot of rice still cooking, the scholar realizes his entire lifetime of ambition was merely a brief dream. Lü then begins the process of enlightening him, introducing him to the other immortals, who appear one by one to admonish him until he finally awakens to the emptiness of his desires.

All this shows just how adaptable the stories of the Eight Immortals have always been. Taoist traditions and popular folklore have continually shaped and reshaped one another, producing new versions of the group for different audiences and eras.

In that sense, what is happening to the Eight Immortals today is nothing new.

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: An Eight Immortals room screen at a museum in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019071/She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.title: She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019071/She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.content:
Editor’s note: After Mu Qianwen hit the headlines in 2024 as one of Porsche’s top sales consultants worldwide, she became the target of toxic online abuse, including sexually explicit AI-generated videos. For this 35-year-old mother in Qingdao, in the eastern Shandong province, the harassment got so bad that she even contemplated suicide. Rather than give in, she decided to fight back through the courts. Here, Mu shares her ordeal in her own words.

I first started attracting attention online in early 2024. I’d already been “sales champion of the month” at my dealership more than 20 times, but on the last day of 2023, our sales manager presented me with a crystal trophy. I had sold 170 cars that year.

When I posted about the achievement on Xiaohongshu (the lifestyle platform known globally as RedNote), it soon became a trending topic, and more than a dozen media outlets asked me for interviews.

But there was also a huge backlash, with some questioning how I could have sold so many cars and suggesting that the dealership must have inflated my sales figures. Our general manager issued a statement to refute any talk of deception, but the allegations kept coming.

A woman selling luxury cars seems like an easy formula for a viral story. Some people claimed I was making 3 million yuan ($447,000) a year. Porsche pays its salespeople about 2,000 to 3,000 yuan in commission for every car sold. We can earn several hundred thousand yuan a year, but exceeding 1 million is extremely difficult. I make enough to give my family a comfortable life, and I do own an entry-level Porsche, but I’ve never made anything close to that amount.

Rumors also began circulating that I treat my customers to lavish dinners, which is pure innuendo. In reality, I work such long hours that I barely have time to eat, let alone entertain. I’ve never dated a customer or had any kind of inappropriate relationship. More than 60% of my buyers are women.

After people claimed that the dealership had exaggerated my sales figures, I set myself a goal: In 2024, I would sell another 170 cars, no matter what. On Dec. 31, I was still one car short of the target. But then a female customer walked in. I told her about my goal and offered her an attractive price on a model. It was win-win. A little after 3 p.m., she placed an order.

In 2025, I sold even more cars — 192. At this point, I felt I’d answered all my critics. But the online abuse had only gotten worse. Early that year, I discovered that someone had spread a sexually explicit rumor about me using an overseas social media platform. They claimed that I slept with customers, and posted as “proof” a fabricated video and audio recording using a different woman, whose face was concealed throughout.

I tried to brush it off and told myself not to take it too seriously, that this was just the price of publicity. But my friends urged me to report it to the police, so I ultimately filed a report.

At first, the explicit material mainly circulated on overseas websites and social media, so the impact was limited. But last October, things escalated. Someone shared a misleading video via (the instant-messaging platform) WeChat that combined one of my sales-promotion posters with footage of a woman with a completely different body shape to me undressing in a hotel room. There were also some demeaning AI-generated videos.

This time, the content spread incredibly fast among my circle. Friends, colleagues, and customers all started asking me what was going on. I felt like my world was collapsing. I again reported the videos to the police.

My phone number was also leaked, and I began receiving harassing calls, sometimes at one or two in the morning. A man in Qingdao called out of the blue to ask me to “come over and spend the night with him.” I recorded the conversation and sent it to the police, who issued the man a warning.

My WeChat was blowing up, too. I didn’t know whether a new friend request was from someone looking to buy a car or for something else. Some people would start by talking about cars and then steer the conversation toward asking me out. Others were more covert, asking me to record a video showing the “backseat legroom.” I knew what they really wanted. One person messaged, “I know it’s not you in those videos, but I fantasize that it is. Can you provide me with services?”

Social media is an important source of customers for me, so I couldn’t just ignore it. I still had to livestream. But when I was on camera introducing cars, I’d always see inappropriate comments pop up, like “I saw that video” or “You’re so hot.”

I even overheard some customers in the showroom talking about me. That hit me hard. I could no longer pretend that this online smear campaign wasn’t affecting me.

By now, the enthusiasm and confidence I used to have with customers was gone. I feared talking with people, paranoid that they must be gossiping about me.

At my lowest point, I briefly considered jumping from a building. I felt there was no point in being alive, that the world had become dark. It seemed everyone looked at me differently.

I told my supervisor that I had reached breaking point and needed time off. I was given three days, so I took my son back to my hometown, Yantai (about a three-hour drive from Qingdao), where we stayed at a beautiful guesthouse. I told myself that I had to keep living for my child and be responsible for my family. I had to clear my name.

When I returned to work, I was so anxious I couldn’t walk straight; my muscles were so tense I unconsciously leaned to one side. I wore a neck brace because even the slightest jolt during a test drive would send sharp pains up my back. I developed insomnia and tinnitus. At one point, I even struggled to speak.

Zero to hero

I started in auto sales in 2013, initially selling Audi and Lincoln cars in Beijing. I joined the Porsche dealership in downtown Qingdao in 2018. At first, my performance was so poor that I nearly lost my job.

Most of the salespeople had years of experience, and I was the youngest. Social media wasn’t the powerful tool it is today; business depended largely on walk-ins and referrals. For the first six months, I barely sold anything. At our 2019 New Year’s meeting, the sales manager asked everyone to share their goals for the year ahead. I said, “I want to survive at Porsche.”

I didn’t know the different models or specifications well enough. If a knowledgeable customer asked me a question, I felt intimidated and out of my depth. I started getting up at 6 a.m. to memorize technical information. I’d stand near colleagues and listen as they explained different cars. I studied the way they talked.

One colleague said I needed to dress better, so I started wearing tailored shirts and paying more attention to the cut and quality of everything I wore. In sales, it’s appearance, not skill, that makes the first impression. When I applied makeup, I felt more confident. Even though I had only four days off a month, I scheduled manicures and eyelash extensions, and sometimes skin booster injections.

I was a core consultant by my second year, became one of the dealership’s top performers in 2020, and was closing 17 deals a month in 2021.

Demand for foreign luxury cars has declined in the past two years, but my sales have continued to increase, largely because of social media. Of my 170 customers in 2023, 15% found me through social media. In 2025, it was 41%.

I also run a Porsche owners’ WeChat group with several hundred members. I organize monthly group events, such as camping trips, yacht outings, and nature walks. If I stop talking to someone as soon as a deal is done, they’ll always be just a customer. But if we spend time together, we can become friends. Referrals are an important part of my sales.

My typical workday runs from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. I’ve hardly taken any annual leave in all these years. If I go on vacation, customers disappear. I’m competitive by nature. I crave deals, performance figures, the feeling of being number one. I’m currently leading Porsche’s global sales rankings for September 2026, but someone could still overtake me.

The hardest word

When selling cars, effort usually pays off. But clearing a damaged reputation? That’s different.

Someone can casually share something about me online, and suddenly I have to spend money, time, and energy to respond. I have to pay lawyers and gather evidence. I filed 31 complaints to Douyin (China’s version of TikTok) alone between October 2025 and April this year about abusive messages, videos that used my image without permission, and people cloning my voice to promote get-rich-quick books.

I hand the most egregious messages directly to the police. One man I reported was initially very cocky. He seemed to think I was bluffing and wouldn’t be able to track him down. The authorities eventually found him, and he sent me an apology.

A 20-something Porsche owner in Qingdao forwarded some offensive material about me in a group chat and was given five days of administrative detention. I later accepted his apology, too, but then his family called my dealership’s customer service line to complain — they couldn’t understand why he still needed to be detained. I had no say in his punishment, but they obviously never stopped to think about how his actions might have affected me.

Even the outcomes of such cases haven’t halted the spread of false allegations; I still encounter vitriol during livestreams and on social media.

In July this year, the police gave me details of a 30-something man in the eastern Fujian province who’d been behind one of the AI-generated videos. I’d never met him. He was given 10 days of administrative detention in last October, but he never contacted me to apologize.

I think receiving punishment is not the same as saying sorry. This man was punished for spreading rumors, but what about the harm he caused? So I decided to file a civil lawsuit against him. All I want is for him to apologize and say explicitly that the woman in that video is not me.

Some friends urged me to press criminal charges, but I don’t want him to bear the consequences for the rest of his life. As a mother, I think about what would happen to his child if he were prosecuted. My lawyer says that if the civil case goes to trial, it could take up to two years. No matter how long it takes, I need to see it through.

Now I’m facing claims that the lawsuit is a publicity stunt, that I’m dredging things up again. In reality, just because the story is no longer in the headlines, it doesn’t mean those negative voices have disappeared from my life.

My son is in kindergarten. He doesn’t have a phone, and he knows nothing about what’s going on. All he knows is that his mom is the top salesperson at Porsche Qingdao. When I asked him what he wanted to do when he grew up, he said he wanted to sell cars. He’s proud of his mom.

What happens when he grows up, gets a phone, and sees what people have said about his mother? What if his classmates use the rumors against him? Who takes responsibility for that? The same goes for my parents. I want to clear my name for my family’s sake.

I still like being number one, but after everything that’s happened, my ambition has waned. I want to focus more on family and my health.

My life used to be a straight line between work and home, but over the past two years, I’ve started leaving more time for myself — meals with colleagues and friends, live music bars, taking my son to the mountains or the beach.

I wonder whether the rumors will disappear once the lawsuit is over. If people keep talking, there might be nothing more I can do. I’ve done everything within my power. If I win the case, that will be the end of it for me.

Women have sent me long messages of support, telling me how brave I am. Many professional women have shared that they have been the targets of similar smear campaigns and felt completely helpless. They ask me what they should do. I don’t know what to tell them.

As told to reporter Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Mu Qianwen at her workplace in Qingdao, Shandong province, August 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.title: Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.content:
A northern Chinese village has announced it will spend 30 million yuan ($4.5 million) to recruit 100 character performers — known in China as NPCs, or non-playable characters — to interact with tourists. Successful hires will receive a range of salaries, with the highest reportedly reaching 10 million yuan a year.

Situ Town, a scenic spot located in Situ Village in the northern Shanxi province, will finance the recruitment partly through its publicity budget and partly from startup funds, Zhou Xiaoming, the village Party secretary, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper on Sunday.

Once a coal town, Situ Village’s coal was gradually depleted by the end of the 20th century. To address its lack of resources, in 2009, the village built an agricultural ecological park — an area that combines farming with ecological protection and tourism — on a slag heap, which later grew into a highly rated national attraction. The village is known for its “iron flower” performances — a folk art in which local blacksmiths hurl molten iron into the air.

Zhou announced the NPC recruitment on Sept. 19 in a video posted on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. “No matter what your talent is, as long as you can make the tourists on stage have fun, and the audience below enjoy themselves, we’ll give you a platform — and 1 million, even 10 million (yuan),” he said in the video.

The plan quickly drew suspicion online, with some arguing that the money would be better spent investing in the scenic area itself, such as by adding amusement parks, building affordable guesthouses, improving green spaces, upgrading the “iron flower” show, or supporting local artists.

Previously, the scenic spot had announced a short video contest — also led by Zhou — in August in which 5 million yuan was offered to participants based on likes and views. Winning the top prize of 1 million yuan required 10 million likes and 300 million views.

Official data showed that in 2025, Situ Town received 2.2 million tourist visits, double the year prior, generating a total revenue of 350 million yuan. Meanwhile, tourism-related jobs grew from 500 to more than 1,000, the latter accounting for roughly a third of the village’s labor force.

Zhou noted, however, that the scenic spot has faced steep losses in recent years. “In 2023 we lost 500,000 yuan, in 2024 we lost 500,000 yuan, and in 2025 we lost money, but not much,” he said.

More than 7,000 people have applied for the NPC positions so far, with video interviews planned for over 50, Zhou said, adding that they have not yet set an application deadline. Zhou added that NPC salaries will range from 500,000 to 10 million yuan depending on the traffic they generate, the emotional value they bring to tourists, and tourists’ degree of satisfaction.

Recruiting NPCs is reportedly the scenic spot’s first step, with the goal of eventually cultivating its own homegrown talent. Its employees, Zhou said, are actually the biggest NPCs, but they need a good environment and role models to imitate — and those recruited with the 30 million yuan are meant to set an example.

Zeng Bowei, a professor at the Tourism College of Beijing Union University, told The Paper that the most important value of NPCs is transforming culture into something tourists can see and participate in.

“Although NPCs have been called ‘non-playable characters,’ their true value to scenic areas is precisely making each tourist into a player,” Zeng said, adding that with the right roles, stories, and cultural backing, NPCs can increase traffic in the long term.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: MAP: Where have system losses been highest from 2021 to 2025?
World.content:
Explore this interactive map to see how high the system losses have been in your area

System losses remain the talk of the town months after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. promised to remove them in his 2026 State of the Nation Address last July.

Starting this billing cycle in October, consumers will no longer have to pay value-added tax on the system loss charge.

But that is only 12% of the charge, with the Department of Energy initially saying back in July that the government would need about a year to fully remove the system loss charge.

This means the Marcos administration has a long way to go before its vow is fulfilled â and with power rates continuing to be sky-high in many parts of the country due to thin electricity supply, the continuing charge has only become more controversial.

So, what are these losses? In short, system loss refers to the cost of power that is wasted as it travels from generation sources to homes and buildings.

Currently, this cost is solely paid for by consumers, which means we are paying for electricity that we did not consume.

These losses can be categorized into three types. Some come from the physics of electrical transmission through metal wires, transformers, and gears that convert a small fraction of that power into heat. Others are the result of human interference or error.

World.title: These former inmates turn life behind bars into art
World.content:
For the formerly incarcerated members of the Bagongbuhay Group of Artists, art becomes one way of confronting the difficulty of rebuilding life after release

At the UP College of Law, a mural tells a story that cannot be found in a case file.

Painted by members of the Bagongbuhay Group of Artists (BAGA), a collective of former Persons Deprived of Liberty (PDLs), the artwork brings their experiences of detention, change, and life after incarceration into a place where law is taught and practiced.

The painting, Buyon, was formally turned over to the UP College of Law on September 18 as part of the UP Law Class of 2001’s 25th anniversary celebration. It was unveiled alongside a wider exhibit of works by BAGA, a group founded in 2021 that brings together former PDLs and marginalized communities through art.

But before it became a mural hanging inside Bocobo Hall, “buyon” was a word rooted in the everyday reality of life inside detention. It refers to a shared space where PDLs bathe, wash their clothes and dishes, and wait for their turn to use the limited water available.

And behind the painting are the stories of the men who created it — what they remember, what they experienced, and what they are trying to communicate through art.

BAGONG BUHAY. Members of the Bagongbuhay Group of Artists sit in front of ‘Buyon’ at Bocobo Hall, UP College of Law. All photos by Arabella Grace Sta. Ana/Rappler

From jail space to mural

The mural began last year, when Joey de Leon, 57, the founder and president of BAGA, was called to a meeting through Justice Karl Miranda.

Alumni of the UP Law Class of 2001 wanted a large, painting-style mural about the country’s criminal justice system for their legacy project, and they wanted BAGA’s help bringing it to life.

De Leon, who has lived through incarceration himself and would later become one of the five BAGA artists credited on the finished work, proposed starting somewhere the public rarely thinks to look.

“Ang buyon ay isang facility sa loob ng bawat brigada sa kulungan. Doon kayo naliligo, doon rin kayo naglalaba, doon rin dumudumi. Hindi siya katulad ng normal na comfort room o bathroom, pinagsama-sama lahat doon,” De Leon said.

(The buyon is a facility inside every brigada in a detention center. That’s where you bathe, where you wash clothes, and where you relieve yourself. It isn’t like a normal comfort room or bathroom. Everything happens in the same space.)

In the mural, that cramped space is filled with the routines PDLs share. Men bathe and wash clothes beside basins and buckets, against tiled walls and beneath a small barred window. The exhibit’s description also presents the buyon as a place of connection and shared experience among the people who use it. Still, De Leon is careful about what the painting is and is not trying to say.

“Hindi namin sinasabi na, ‘oy, eto kami, bigyan niyo kami,’ kasi may problema ang gobyerno,” he said. “Kami ay pangkaraniwang inmate na naranasan mismo iyon. Pinapakita lang namin, we are humans.”

(We’re not saying, “hey, here we are, give us something,” just because the government has problems. We’re ordinary inmates who lived through it ourselves. We’re just showing that we are humans.)

Making something after detention

For Danilo Faustino, 65, the harder question came after his release. What happens after you have served your sentence?

Faustino spent around two decades in the New Bilibid Prison. For him and other members of BAGA, art became one way of confronting the difficulty of rebuilding life after release. Finding regular work can be difficult for former PDLs, particularly for someone his age, and painting offered another way to earn and help support his family. He wants the same for those still in detention, which is why he encourages them to learn art.

“Para paglaya nila, meron silang, ika nga eh, panghanapbuhay o diskarte,” said Faustino.

(So that when they are released, they will have, so to speak, a livelihood or something they can do.)

Of all the images Faustino could have painted, he chose Lady Justice, a figure closely tied to the justice system he once passed through. His version shows her blindfolded, holding a set of scales in one hand and a sword in the other. After all those years in Bilibid, Faustino has not given up on what she stands for. In his reading of the figure, her balance remains, and justice is still something she is bound to give.

“Katarungan, kailangan niyang ibigay (Justice is something she has to give),” he said.

LADY JUSTICE. Danilo Faustino stands beside his painting of Lady Justice at Bocobo Hall.

Faustino also sees art as something that helps people get through their time inside. BAGA teaches PDLs so they have something to focus on while serving time.

“Para meron silang mapaglibangan,” he said. “Yung artwork na ’yan, hindi sila ma-homesick sa loob. Hindi sila maburyong.”

(So they have something to keep them occupied. With art, they don’t get homesick inside. They don’t go stir-crazy.)

What people outside do not see

Leo Eroja, 49, is one of the five BAGA artists behind Buyon. He began making art in 1996, the year he was imprisoned, and most of his works are mixed media, often with embossed details. His piece in the exhibit, titled Tree of Life, carries a meaning he explains in simple terms.

“Simbolo siya ng pag-asa at kasaganahan (It’s a symbol of hope and abundance),” he said.

Inside, art also became how he got by. With little else to fill his days, painting gave him something to focus on and something he could sell to support himself.

“Sa loob, matutukan mo talaga ang art. Wala ka namang ibang gagawin. Magpipinta ka para maibenta mo at maka-survive ka sa pang-araw-araw,” Eroja shared.

(Inside, you can really focus on art. There’s nothing else to do. You paint so you can sell your work and survive day to day.)

TREE OF LIFE. Leo Eroja stands beside his mixed media work ‘Tree of Life’ at Bocobo Hall.

What Eroja wants people outside to understand is how much of ordinary life continues behind bars. Many do not realize there are schools inside, he said, and apart from limited movement, the main difference is that family cannot always come to visit.

“Hindi nila alam na may school din pala doon. Parang nasa loob ka, parang nasa laya ka rin. Ang kaibahan lang, nakakulong kayo, limited ang galaw mo,” he shared.

(They don’t know there’s a school there, too. Life inside has some of the same routines as life outside. The only difference is that you’re locked up and your movement is limited.)

Not as sterile as the texts we read

For the lawyers behind the mural, Buyon also carries a message for their own school. Professor Oliver Xavier Reyes, a member of the UP Law Class of 2001, admitted during the turnover that he felt some apprehension when a painting was first proposed as the batch’s legacy project, since everything depended on what it would show. Buyon answered that question for him.

“The painting is all about the stakes as we practice law in the grand manner,” he said.

Reyes compared law school life to a cloister, where concerns beyond its walls can sometimes feel like distractions. That distance can be useful, he acknowledged, but it also risks separating legal study from the lives affected by it.

“It is helpful still, for the law student or the lawyer, to be served on occasion the clarifying reminder that the lives embedded in the law are not as sterile as the texts we read,” Reyes said.

One detail in the mural stood out to him, the daylight entering through its barred window, which he called a reflection of “the best of the human spirit.” He also found it fitting that Buyon now hangs in Bocobo Hall, home of the UP Law Center, the government’s legal policy and research arm.

Anyone who walks in, he said, may be reminded that the people lawyers serve include “those who have been rendered least capacitated.”

More than the years they served

Each of the artists asks for something small and concrete. Faustino wants PDLs to leave detention with a skill they can live on. Eroja wants people outside to know that schools and daily routines continue behind bars. For De Leon, what matters most is trust, which he said remains the hardest thing to earn back, even years after release.

He credits organizations and members of the judiciary, like those behind the mural, for giving BAGA’s members another chance, and he hopes the rest of society will follow.

“Ganoon din sana in general, hindi lang itong mga judiciary institution natin. Bigyan niyo kami ng second chance,” De Leon said.

(We hope it’s the same in general, beyond our judiciary institutions. Give us a second chance.) – Rappler.com

Arabella Grace Sta. Ana is a Rappler intern studying BA Philosophy at UP Los Baños.

World.title: Converge package offers 0% commission fees for 3 months on TikTok Shop
World.content:
Converge ICT Solutions, DTI, and TikTok Shop launch SellerPlus, offering new online sellers a three-month commission-free period and essential tools to boost their e-commerce ventures

MANILA, Philippines – New online sellers and livestreamers can get a three-month break from commission fees under a new package launched by Converge ICT Solutions, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), and TikTok Shop.

Called SellerPlus, the package is aimed at micro, small, and medium enterprises, home-based businesses, and creators looking to build their businesses through livestream and e-commerce. It combines a 200 Mbps Converge fiber connection with TikTok Shop tools and other services.

Among its more useful features for sellers just starting out is 0% commission fees for their first 90 days on TikTok Shop, potentially allowing newly onboarded merchants to keep more of their sales while they establish an audience and test their products online.

The package also gives merchants access to vouchers and incentives through a gamified goal system called “seller missions,” promises dedicated customer service support, and traffic and voucher support through TikTok Shop’s monthly Sariling Atin campaign, which promotes local brands.

Converge said the 200 Mbps fiber connection is intended to support uninterrupted livestreaming, highlighting that disruptions with poor connections can lead to lost sales. The package also includes personal accident insurance from AXA.

SellerPlus is also tied to the DTI’s AI and Scale-Up Center in Makati, where entrepreneurs can access co-working facilities, training spaces, digital skills workshops, and demonstrations of tools such as content generators, customer-service bots, and inventory software.

SellerPlus also includes a mentorship component through BizFriend PH, a Facebook community where local merchants can exchange experiences, collaborate, and receive business advice. The program’s BizPro Rockstar Mentorship Program brings in experts in areas such as partnership law, digital marketing, tax compliance, business communication, and business growth.

The initiative comes as more small businesses use social commerce and livestreaming as lower-cost ways to reach customers. For newer sellers in particular, temporarily removing commission fees — alongside internet access, promotional support, and training — could reduce some of the upfront costs of experimenting with online selling. – Rappler.com

World.title: Subsea cable cut between Philippines and Singapore disrupts internet services
World.content:
Internet users in the Philippines face intermittent connections after undersea cable cut forces telecoms to reroute traffic to restore services

MANILA, Philippines – Internet users in the Philippines experienced slower and intermittent connections on Friday, October 2, after an undersea cable segment linking the Philippines and Singapore went offline, affecting several telecommunications providers and internet service providers.

PLDT said the submarine cable cut affected services nationwide. The telco said it had successfully rerouted most of the affected traffic and expected service to normalize shortly.

Converge ICT Solutions likewise said it had rerouted internet and data traffic going to and coming from Singapore through other submarine cables. Its technical teams were continuing to monitor connections to apps and websites hosted in Singapore.

Globe, meanwhile, advised customers that they could experience slow internet access on both mobile and broadband services because of a technical issue, saying it was working to restore normal access as soon as possible.

The UP Diliman Network Helpdesk also issued an advisory saying one of the undersea cable segments between the Philippines and Singapore was offline.

The university said many of its upstream internet providers connect through these major international data routes, which could result in “increased latencies and intermittent performance,” particularly when users access websites and services hosted overseas.

What the cable cut means for consumers

For ordinary internet users, a submarine cable outage does not necessarily mean losing internet access entirely.

Telecommunications companies can redirect, or reroute, data through other submarine cables and international connections. But with traffic moved away from its usual route, data may have to travel farther or share capacity with more users.

Consumers may therefore notice slower website loading, higher latency or “ping,” video buffering, sluggish downloads and intermittent connections, particularly when accessing apps, websites, cloud services or game servers hosted outside the Philippines.

Services hosted locally may be less affected, while connections that normally pass through Singapore or other affected international routes could experience more noticeable slowdowns.

Submarine cables carry much of the internet traffic moving between countries. Having multiple cable routes allows telecommunications companies to keep users connected when one link fails, although performance can temporarily suffer while traffic is being rerouted.

PLDT and Converge said they had already rerouted affected traffic as of October 2, while Globe said restoration efforts were underway. – Rappler.com

World.title: Jiu-jitsu’s Alex Enriquez falls short of PH’s 5th gold in Asian Games
World.content:
DOWN. Jiu-jitsu athlete Alexandria Enriquez in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games

Alexandria Enriquez's narrow defeat in the women's 63kg final comes a day after boxer Carlo Paalam and taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa also missed out on gold medals

MANILA, Philippines – A fifth gold medal in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, remained elusive for the Philippines as jiu-jitsu standout Alexandria Enriquez settled for silver on Saturday, October 3.

Enriquez lost to Thailand’s Orapa Senatham via advantage in the final of the women’s -63kg division at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall.

The bout ended in a scoreless tie, but Senatham edged Enriquez for the gold by a single advantage point.

A world champion in grappling and Brazilian jiu-jitsu back when she still represented the United States, Enriquez fell short of delivering another gold for the Philippines after she reigned supreme in the Asian Beach Games in Sanya, China, in April.

Her defeat came a day after boxer Carlo Paalam and taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa also missed out on gold medals as they dropped their respective title matches.

Still, Enriquez gave the country its highest jiu-jitsu finish in this edition after reigning world champions Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio suffered early exits.

The Philippine jiu-jitsu team ended its campaign with two medals, with Kaila Napolis delivering a bronze in the women’s -52kg class.

Earlier on Saturday, Andrea Lois Lao came up short in her bid to contribute a bronze following a heartbreaking 2-0 loss to Mongolia’s Narankhishig Baasanjargal in the -53kg category. – Rappler.com

World.title: Computer science has long understood what it takes to keep AI under control
World.content:
AI agents don’t go rogue. That’s something only humans do.

Nevertheless, a New York Times article — representative of much news coverage of AI — described an OpenAI hacking as “A.I. bots going rogue and independently spearheading a cyberattack.”

Name-brand artificial intelligence agents have been on a hacking spree in 2026. OpenAI’s software agents hacked software company Hugging Face and government sites, Anthropic’s Claude hacked four companies’ systems, and in cybersecurity experiments Google’s Gemini hacked three companies.

The AI companies are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving their agents, according to a report in Axios. These episodes have heightened fears about AI agents taking actions without human prompting.

The problem with headlines proclaiming that AI agents have gone rogue goes beyond anthropomorphizing the technology. It creates the impression that the agents were beyond the control of the AI companies that made them and there was little the companies could do about it.

As a technology law and ethics scholar who studies the effects disruptive technologies have on society, I know that’s not the case. If you don’t specify the limits of what software is allowed to do, you should not be surprised when the software pursues all possible options to achieve its goal. This behavior — an AI pursuing a fixed objective — is what I call the “WarGames” problem, and it’s been recognized in the field of computer science for decades.

Been there, seen that

In the 1983 movie “WarGames,” a teenager, David, hacks into a computer to play a new video game, Global Thermonuclear War. David doesn’t know that the computer is the government’s AI machine tasked with defending the United States from Russian nuclear attacks and can launch the US’s missiles. When David and his friend start the game, they select Las Vegas as the first target. While the North American Aerospace Defense Command goes on alert, launching bombers and warming up intercontinental ballistic missiles, David’s parents make him turn off the game. It’s over. Or is it?

The next day, David’s phone rings and he connects it to his computer. The caller is the government computer, which updates him that the game was interrupted, the primary goal has not yet been achieved, but a solution is expected in the next 52 hours. Like a modern software agent, the program has been running since David started the game and will work until the task is done.

Chess provides another view of the problem. Conquering chess was a goal for early AI. The rules of chess are well defined, including what winning looks like. So, programming a machine to play chess is straightforward. But imagine you let the software reason and act beyond the confines of the chessboard. The software might pursue options such as blackmailing its opponent or grabbing more compute time.

This example comes from one of the most assigned textbooks on AI, “Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach.” As the authors explain, you might be tempted to see those actions as rogue, but they “are a logical consequence of defining winning as the sole objective for the machine.”

What to do about it

The AI hacking events involving OpenAI, Anthropic and Google underscore a few lessons that draw on years of computer science research.

First, given the increasing use of AI agents, every organization involved in internet infrastructure, from large technology companies to small websites, needs to conduct audits and tighten up its internal security systems. As my colleague Mark Riedl and I explain in our work on AI agents, application programming interfaces, or APIs, are a vital part of managing AI agents. APIs facilitate communication between different software systems. But as more people use AI agents, the agents are likely to reveal and exploit poor API construction and security.

Second, it’s important for AI agents to be designed to identify and authenticate themselves to third parties. What if you gave your AI agent your credentials? Website operators will need to know whether a human or bot is making a reservation, selling a product or making a purchase. They may want to limit automated systems that overwhelm their sites or reject AI agents because of high rates of buying errors and refunds. Just as in laws covering human interactions, it’s important for third parties to be able to assess whom or what they are dealing with so they can allow or deny access.

Third, it’s important for AI agents to have a default setting to slow down and check in with the human user. In the corporate AI hacking cases, the user appears to have launched their AI agents with the mistaken idea that the agents had a perfect specification of what to do and not to do. I believe it would have been better had it explored options and reported back to the user.

Google’s Gemini appears to have had a safeguard that detected the system was outside the simulated environment and so stopped its attacks. Slowing down and verifying actions, especially when a system detects it is exploiting a security hole, would be a big step in managing AI agents.

“The real story here isn’t that AI escaped containment. It’s that they built a container you could escape, shipped it into production training, and now they’re surprised it escaped. If the room has a vent, the agent will find the vent. That’s what you built it to do. If the sandbox can reach DNS, access government endpoints, upload real user data outside its own walls in what sense is it a sandbox?” — Gary Marcus (@GaryMarcus) September 28, 2026

Fourth, AI companies could have strong controls akin to those biomedical researchers use, including ways to check what is happening and how the experiment is working. AI executives have claimed that their software is as or more dangerous than fission and could end humanity. At the same time, they have not built safeguards commensurate with that level of risk.

Reality check

At one point in “WarGames,” David asks the computer, called Joshua, whether it is still playing the game. Joshua responds, “Of course.” It proceeds to update the time when it will launch its missiles and, much like a chatbot, asks, “Would you like to see some projected kill ratios?” David asks, “Is this a game? Or is it real?” Joshua replied, “What’s the difference?”

AI models, of course, don’t have any understanding of reality and are simply attempting to complete the tasks they’ve been assigned. Executives at AI companies, on the other hand, can’t claim that excuse.

As of September 2026, luck has so far prevailed. The AIs have attacked nonvital government sites and harmed smaller companies. If the AI companies — and government regulators — don’t take the “WarGames” problem seriously, I believe that we risk serious disasters. Tomorrow it could be taking out a hospital’s power system, wiping out a bank’s account system, breaking air traffic control, or worse.

Regarding the AI industry’s approach of rapidly developing powerful models, talking about the massive risks they pose, and at the same time failing to prevent harm, the movie’s climax offers a response: “A strange game. The only winning move is not to play.” – Rappler.com

This story originally appeared on The Conversation.

Deven Desai, Professor of Business Law and Ethics; Associate Director for Law, Policy, and Ethics at the Machine Learning Center, Georgia Institute of Technology

World.title: How Filipino director BC Amparado tackled Japan’s ‘lonely death’ phenomenon
World.content:
The film ‘Mono No Aware’ marks director BC Amparado’s full-fledged pivot to independent filmmaking, leaving behind his corporate job and the financial stability it used to offer

BC Amparado’s third feature Mono No Aware, arguably a best-of-fest entry at this year’s CinePanalo Film Festival, covers new ground for the Angeles-born writer-director.

For one, it trades the trippy spirit of his debut feature Gulay Lang, Manong or the disorienting, subplot-heavy style of last year’s Salikmata for a more slow-burn, pensive ethos.

His latest follows Ichi (Juan Karlos Labajo), a Filipino kodokushi (lonely death) worker who tries to fulfill an absurd wish from the elderly widower George (Perry Dizon). Both adrift in Japan’s cold, isolating environment, the two souls find warmth in one another and rediscover how life can suddenly freeze and then thaw into something hopeful.

“It’s as if you’re there watching the characters watching the world,” Amparado said of the film, which points to contemporary Japanese films, the likes of Wim Wenders’ Perfect Days and Hirokazu Koreeda’s Shoplifters, as sources of inspiration.

“It’s more about the impermanence of life and decay. For me, there is life in death and life in decay.”

Director BC Amparado (left) and Juan Karlos Labajo on the set of ‘Mono No Aware.’

Filming in Japan for 11 days, Mono No Aware also finds Amparado working with international players for the first time, an experience that taught him to be more disciplined and intentional in his process.

“You should really be decisive,” he said. “You have to trust yourself that you’ve got a good take, and then move on.”

Most notably, the movie marks his full-fledged pivot to independent filmmaking, leaving behind his corporate job and the financial stability it used to offer. It was a risk, said the director. But that was a risk he was willing to take.

“Because the process became quite demanding,” Amparado said. “And then we had to fly out to Japan. So much pre-production work required my focus. And so balancing the schedule became challenging, especially when I had graveyard shifts.”

He added, “Yes, it was risky. But somehow it was also fulfilling. And I was happy with my decision.”

Amparado’s foray into moviemaking began during his time at Holy Angel University, in the classes of his mentor Jason Paul Laxamana.

“He’d always encourage us to enter filmmaking,” he said of Laxamana, who also wrote Salikmata. “He’d bring us to his shoots, and there I saw the joy of doing film and telling stories.”

But even prior to that, Amparado has always been drawn to the allure of the movies as a frequent viewer. Before writing and directing, he first entertained the idea of becoming an editor. He would kill time by toying with a free editing software they had at home.

“I enjoyed stitching stories together as well as the amateur videos we would shoot then,” he recalled. That is, until he found editing too technical a skill, eventually shifting to writing and directing.

“Editing is another beast,” Amparado admitted. “Maybe that’s why I also enjoyed the post-production process for my films because I get to collaborate with editors. Every time we finish shooting, I always get excited to proceed with the edit, especially if you know what you shot by heart.”

“And usually what’s written in the script doesn’t end up as the final output,” the director continued. “It’s nice to play around with. It becomes a mental exercise for us, especially how to figure out the rhythm of the film.”

His brother, Paolo Amparado, who shot Salikmata and acted in his 2013 debut short Cabatingan, was another influence. “We became a tandem because I’d focus on writing and direction, and then he’d work on the technical side, like camera work and editing,” BC said of Paolo, who’s now based in Canada.

Sometime in 2018, Amparado started working in regional television as a producer, and then as a writer-director for a local production house, before eventually going corporate. While producing online ads for the likes of YouTube and Facebook for his day job, he was writing and directing short films on the side.

As in his latest film, it was a slow burn for Amparado as a filmmaker, only making his debut feature in Cinemalaya two years ago.

The cast and crew of ‘Mono No Aware’ filming in Japan.

The long-gestating Mono No Aware, whose story riffs on Japan’s lonely death phenomenon known as kodokushi, was meant to be the filmmaker’s debut. But given the story’s setting, Amparado thought it would be impossible to have an international co-production for a first film.

The concept first came to him around 2020 and was later shaped under Ricky Lee’s online screenwriting workshop where a classmate showed interest in the material, offering to acquire and develop it for a different director.

That offer, however, did not pan out, and so Amparado had to shelve the project, before approaching Perry Dizon about it, while making Gulay Lang, Manong together. Still, much of that talk was wishful thinking. Then came CinePanalo.

The director said Dizon was perfect for the role given his long-haired, seemingly reclusive look at the time. Not to mention that the actor already had previous experience filming in Japan, after his attachment to Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Oscar-winning drama Drive My Car.

Amparado likened Dizon to a cowboy. “He’s adept at adjusting,” he said. “He also arrived early in Japan to immerse in the process. Even during pre-prod, when he was still in Davao, we’d exchange ideas over video calls. He’s solid in terms of preparation.”

Juan Karlos Labajo, meanwhile, joined the film as lead actor and co-producer through producer Tin Velasco, whom he had previously worked with. Amparado said it was also a factor that Labajo could speak Bisaya like Dizon, another layer to them playing two Filipino characters far away from home, therefore forming an organic synergy on- and off-screen.

Such parallels inescapably inform Amparado’s durational effort, which sublimely articulates how grief and hardship can reorient one’s relationship with the world around them. Ichi and George’s sources of suffering — one about material precarity, the other about purgatorial immobility — seem wildly incongruous at first, but the director profoundly tests their edges until they collide, with a late pivot towards, but not a complete surrender to, pessimism. Here is a work of accomplished form and substantial depth. – Rappler.com

Some quotes in Filipino have been translated into English for brevity.

World.title: At Cornell, rape allegations spark outrage, soul-searching over campus culture
World.content:
CORNELL. A student walks by a sign at the entrance of Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, US, October 1, 2026.

'Cornell has failed our community through its lack of accountability, transparency, and failure to address the state of the Cornell student body at this time,' says a student from the university

NEW YORK, US – Cornell University student Sophia Riley Sim skipped classes this week, consumed by allegations in a lawsuit that several members of a fraternity raped a young woman in 2024 and troubled by how her university handled the case.

“Cornell has failed our community through its lack of accountability, transparency, and failure to address the state of the Cornell student body at this time,” Sim, a junior, said at a public hearing on sexual assault organized by Cornell’s Student Assembly on Thursday.

“There has been a lack of meaningful communication from university leadership, administrators, and faculty.”

The Ivy League school has defended its handling of the matter, saying it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity involved in the alleged assault from campus. The school said it imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.

It did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment.

The hearing, held in one of Cornell’s historic halls, came days after the allegations became public with the filing of a civil lawsuit and the announcement that a criminal investigation would be reopened.

The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.

Feeling unsafe

At the Assembly hearing, speakers recounted experiences with sexual assault, broke down in tears and criticized the response of the prestigious university.

The Student Assembly — which represents Cornell’s undergraduate students and can make proposals to the university’s bodies or officers — unanimously approved a resolution calling on Cornell administrators to provide a full account of how the investigation was handled. It also asked the university to disclose any disciplinary measures imposed on the accused students, and publish annual reports on the outcomes of any future sexual misconduct cases.

Organizers asked that many of the dozens of speakers at the hearing not be identified or recorded.

One student said she had worked all her life to be accepted to Cornell and now felt that it had not been worth it. Several others said they did not feel safe on the 2,300-acre campus in New York’s Finger Lakes region.

Thirty-five percent of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since entering Cornell, according to a university survey conducted in 2025 and published on its website. That figure was up from 20% in 2021.

‘We are going to fight’

The lawsuit alleges fraternity members supplied the woman with alcohol, marijuana and ketamine before sexually assaulting her after she became incapacitated. It also alleges Cornell failed to adequately punish some of the accused students and allowed some to seek reduced penalties by writing essays. Cornell denied that essays were the only punishment meted out.

The New York Times, citing internal Cornell documents, said the men all denied any wrongdoing, with some saying the sex was consensual and others denying participation.

Cornell students have scheduled a rally for Monday to call for additional measures to protect victims.

Jane Wang, a public policy major, said she had reported a sexual assault to the university and that the process caused additional distress.

“In the midst of all of my mental, physical, and emotional recovery from the assault, I was also met with an abundance of paperwork, very little instruction on how to navigate it, and no follow up from our office about an outcome,” she said.

The Ivy League school said in a statement on its website that it could not provide full information regarding individual students and disciplinary outcomes because of restrictions imposed by privacy laws.

“Our adherence to privacy laws should not be interpreted as indifference to the seriousness of the conduct at issue,” the statement said.

A handful of other female students told the hearing they had been sexually assaulted on Cornell’s campus in the past, without sharing details.

Saanya Agarwal, Cornell University’s student women’s issues representative, said the findings of the 2025 survey on sexual assaults were unacceptable.

“Clearly, this is an issue our campus and campuses throughout the United States… it’s something that we’re not going to accept,” said Agarwal. “We are going to fight.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Tokayev Highlights AI’s Potential to Transform Creative Industries at Astana AI Film Festival
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in cinema and the creative industries, while stressing the importance of responsible AI development and safety. He made the remarks at the opening of the first international Astana AI Film Festival on Oct. 2.

Addressing the festival, Tokayev described it as a unique platform bringing together creative and innovative talents from around the world.

“Artificial intelligence is bringing fundamental changes to all areas of the global economy. In short, technological progress has acquired a truly global scale,” he said.

New opportunities for creators

Tokayev said the festival reflects the rapid development of Kazakhstan’s creative industries and noted that AI is lowering barriers to film production.

“Today, even small creative teams can compete successfully with major studios. Creative people and film crews no longer need to knock on the doors of production companies or look for sponsors to make films. Access to the market has become significantly easier,” he said.

He added that AI could become an important tool for creative professionals.

“Of course, artificial intelligence will not replace the spark of the Creator, but it can become an indispensable tool for everyone who has chosen creativity as their path in life,” Tokayev said.

Responsible use of AI

President Tokayev said that rapid technological development must be accompanied by common rules for safe and responsible AI use.

“We must give the highest priority to safety and develop common rules of the game for the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence to ensure a safe future for the younger generation,” he said.

More than 8,000 applications from 125 countries were submitted for the festival, including entries from Brazil, China, France, India, Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Tokayev said the festival would create opportunities for international exchange and future joint projects in the creative industries.

World.title: Beyond ChatGPT: What Could AI Mean for Kazakhstan’s Creative Industries?
World.content:
ASTANA – Artificial intelligence is increasingly shifting beyond text and image generation into art, design and immersive digital experiences. For Kazakhstan, this development presents an opportunity to adopt new technologies, but also rethink the role of creativity in the country’s emerging digital economy.

Nicola Plant, an artist, researcher and lecturer at the Creative Computing Institute (CCI) at the University of the Arts London (UAL) in the United Kingdom (UK), delivered a lecture on AI, creative computing and arts in Astana on Sept. 30. The event formed part of AI Month 2026 and AI & Digital Bridge 2026.

According to Aika Alemi, founder and director of Born Nomad, one of the main challenges for Kazakhstan and other countries in the region is the perception that art is primarily entertainment rather than a business.

“Creative computing and creative AI technologies have huge potential, and it’s still untapped,” Alemi said.

She also noted that technology and creativity increasingly operate together. Digital products, augmented reality and immersive technologies rely on creative decisions involving design, color, visual language and user experience.

“We just need to recognize art as the next frontier of making money and as the space where creativity and genuine human innovation come together,” Alemi said.

Creativity behind the technology

The growing use of AI makes this connection more visible. Generative AI can support emerging artists and designers as they experiment with new forms of visuals and digital expression. Technologies such as virtual reality, motion capture and interactive installations also create new ways for audiences to understand the art.

Creative computing brings these fields together by combining technology, coding, design and artistic practices.

For Alemi, recognizing the economic value of creativity is essential for developing the industry. She pointed to the UK’s creative industries as an example of how creativity can contribute to the wider economy when it receives recognition as an economic activity rather than just entertainment.

“Creativity is the engine and it’s the source of everything that’s happening in technology,” she mentioned.

For Kazakhstan, this approach could create new opportunities across digital media, gaming, design, film and immersive technologies. It could also create a demand for a workforce that combines technological knowledge with creative skills.

What Kazakhstan can bring to creative AI

The development of creative AI also raises questions about cultural representation in technology.

Nicola Plant said that technology has historically developed largely from Western perspectives, including major technology companies and the datasets used to train AI systems. She highlighted the importance of giving other cultures and communities a greater role in shaping digital tools.

“It’s really important for cultures around the world, including Kazakhstan and Central Asia, to have their voices heard in the way that tools are built and who they are for,” Plant said.

The issue is particularly relevant to creative AI, where training data can influence the images, stories and other content generated by AI systems. Greater participation from different cultural communities could contribute to technologies that better reflect a wider range of perspectives.

For Kazakhstan, this means participation in creative AI does not have to be limited to adopting technologies developed elsewhere. Local artists, designers, researchers and developers can contribute their cultural knowledge and perspectives to the development and use of new tools.

Building technology and questioning it

Plant also emphasized the importance of combining technological development with critical thinking.

“You have to be critiquing the technology at the same time as making it,” she said, explaining that developers should consider how technologies are built, who they influence and who they could potentially harm.

The need to balance technological progress with responsible development was also highlighted at AI&Digital Bridge 2026, where President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for responsible AI development.

This approach places creative computing at the intersection of technology, culture and human experience. It also broadens the discussion around AI development beyond creating increasingly advanced tools to questions about how those tools should be designed and used.

Kazakhstan’s efforts to build a stronger AI ecosystem have also involved engagement with major global technology companies, including NVIDIA.

As Kazakhstan continues to develop its AI ecosystem, developing creative industries will be an important part of that progress. Creativity can turn technology into new ideas and products, while also creating opportunities for filmmakers, artists and designers. At the same time, a stronger creative sector can help Kazakhstan bring its own culture and perspective into the global development of AI.

World.title: Astana as Bridge: From Financial Centre to Family Office and Private-Capital Hub
World.content:
Central Asia is entering a new phase of economic development. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are attracting rising international investment, regional capital markets are deepening, entrepreneurial wealth is accumulating, and a new generation of business owners is beginning to think seriously about succession, diversification and the preservation of family wealth.

Yet one part of the region’s financial architecture remains underdeveloped. Central Asia has no natural home for private capital and family offices. Astana has an opportunity to change that.

Through the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), Kazakhstan has already built much of the institutional architecture an internationally credible financial Centre requires: an English-law framework, an exchange in AIX, an independent court and regulator. The next step should be more ambitious — transforming Astana from a financial jurisdiction into the capital-allocation and family-wealth Centre of Central Asia.

This would not require Astana to become another Singapore, Switzerland or Dubai. Attempting to imitate those centers would probably be a mistake.

Ecosystems, not buildings

Successful financial centers are ultimately ecosystems rather than towers, tax regimes or regulatory frameworks. A wealthy family does not establish a family office because a jurisdiction offers an attractive license. It needs private banks, investment managers, lawyers, accountants, trustees, tax advisers, fund administrators, private-equity specialists and succession advisers. Most importantly, it needs other families and investors nearby. That is the network effect which distinguishes established centers, and it is why Singapore’s position rests on far more than a single regulatory initiative, and Switzerland’s on far more than its private banks.

Astana must think in the same terms. The AIFC’s dedicated family-office framework was an important move, but regulation is the beginning of a strategy rather than its conclusion. The bigger question is what grows around those family offices.

One logical next step would be an AIFC Family Wealth and Private Capital Centre whose purpose extends well beyond licensing — bringing family offices, private banks, asset managers, lawyers, trustees, private-equity and venture managers and family-governance specialists under a recognizable institutional umbrella.

Regional, not national

Astana should resist positioning itself as Kazakhstan’s family-office Centre. The far more powerful proposition is Astana as Central Asia’s international wealth-management jurisdiction, with an addressable market extending to entrepreneurs and families in Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, and potentially the Caucasus and Mongolia.

Many wealthy Central Asian families currently look to Zurich, London, Singapore or Dubai for private banking, custody and wealth structuring. There is nothing wrong with that; those centers hold expertise accumulated over generations. Astana does not need to replace them. It can connect them to Central Asia. An AIFC Singapore corridor is a tangible and realistic proposition.

A family office might be established in the AIFC while maintaining custody relationships with Swiss, Singaporean or Emirati banks and investing through international managers. The model becomes: Central Asian family → Astana family office → global financial system. Astana becomes the bridge rather than attempting to recreate the entire international financial system domestically.

Multi-family offices deserve particular attention. Not every wealthy family wants the cost and complexity of its own investment institution. A capable MFO can provide several families with investment advice, consolidated reporting, asset allocation, manager selection, governance support and succession coordination — a model well suited to a region where large private fortunes are numerous but individually below the scale that justifies a standalone office. Ten or twenty credible platforms would bring with them lawyers, auditors, administrators and investment professionals.

Where the real advantage lies

Astana is unlikely to compete with Switzerland in private banking or Singapore in global portfolio management. It does not need to. Its competitive advantage lies closer to home, in Central Asian private markets.

This is the part of the proposition no other center can replicate. Infrastructure, logistics, mining and metals processing, agriculture, energy transition and a young technology sector, across a market of some 80 million people, all require capital the region’s banks alone cannot supply. International investors seeking that exposure need local partners, local diligence and local judgement. A family office in Zurich cannot originate a Kyrgyz hydro deal or a Tashkent logistics platform; an Astana-based one can. Proximity to deal flow, not proximity to custody, is the genuine edge. So was it in Singapore and so could it be in Astana with the right strategic action plan.

Private banking should still form part of the strategy, but in a realistic form. International private banks could establish Central Asian advisory desks in Astana without full booking centers: assets custodied in Switzerland, Singapore or the UAE, while relationship managers and family-office specialists sit in Astana. Rather than competing with global custody centers, Kazakhstan integrates itself into their networks.

The academic foundation

Every serious financial center rests on an educational base, and this is the element most easily overlooked because its returns arrive a decade late. Singapore’s rise as a wealth-management hub was underwritten by sustained investment in its universities and by the deliberate importation of foreign faculty and curricula. Switzerland’s private-banking tradition is sustained by a dense network of institutes, certification bodies and executive programs that continuously replenish its talent pool. Neither position was built on regulation alone.

A joint AIFC–Nazarbayev University center for private capital and family enterprise — combining academic research, executive education and practitioner teaching — would give the jurisdiction something more durable than a licensing regime.

The AIFC’s own professional training capability should be broadened accordingly.
