At the same time, the prime minister told Likhachev that the Armenian government was continuing to consider proposals from other international partners.

Pashinyan stressed that the final decision would depend solely on economic considerations. These would include price, quality, safety, construction timelines and guarantees.

The statement also said Alexey Likhachev described cooperation with Armenian partners as constructive. The Rosatom chief also provided detailed information about the construction of not only large VVER reactors, but also small and medium-sized reactors.

World.title: Olive Festival to be held on Baku Boulevard (VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 3. Azerbaijan is currently in the olive harvesting season. Against this backdrop, an Olive Festival will be held at the Seaside National Park.

The festival, scheduled for October 23–25, will offer visitors a selection of delicious products, live music, art displays and a memorable atmosphere for family leisure.

The main goal of the event is to promote Azerbaijan’s centuries-old olive-growing traditions, showcase and support local producers, and contribute to the development of a national brand in the sector.

The festival will be held with the support of the State Tourism Agency and the Seaside Boulevard Administration, with “Absheron Olive Gardens” and “Olivea” serving as sponsors of the olive products.

Olives, an integral part of Azerbaijani tables and a symbol of abundance and prosperity, will be the central theme of the event. Various producers will showcase olives and olive products in pavilions set up across the festival grounds. The event will provide an opportunity to highlight the work of olive growers, olive-growing traditions and locally produced goods.

Holding the festival at the Seaside National Park, one of the favorite walking destinations for both local and international visitors, will also give a wider audience an opportunity to discover olives and olive products.

An engaging cultural and entertainment program will also be held on the Boulevard during the festival. Admission to the three-day festival, as well as access to entertainment and concert programs, will be free of charge.

World.title: "Whatever we acquired, we purchased with money": What was Ilham Aliyev's real message at New Azerbaijan Party Congress
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 3. The 8th congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party was held in Baku, and, naturally, the main event was the major programmatic speech by party chairman and President Ilham Aliyev. Most of the issues addressed by the head of state at the congress were easy to classify as entirely predictable - the outcome of the Victory, the economy, energy, transit corridors, and the reconstruction of Karabakh. But in the section devoted to security, there was a passage that made many people go back and read the transcript again. Some did so more than once.

Ilham Aliyev spoke about how Azerbaijan armed itself, and about who helped it and how. The short answer was: no one, in no way. And, seemingly answering questions that might have been asked, he uttered a phrase that probably shut quite a few mouths in very different parts of the world: “Whatever we acquired, we purchased with money.”

The quote is important enough to be read again, in full. Here is what Ilham Aliyev said:

“We need no one's help or patronage. When we needed help, no one helped us. When we had one million refugees, no one reached out to us. Whatever we acquired, we purchased with money. That includes all weapons, which were bought with money at world prices—down to the last bullet. I tell you this with full responsibility as Supreme Commander-in-Chief and as the person overseeing all these matters. You know how much Azerbaijan has armed itself since 2003, establishing local production and purchasing from abroad. Not once were we granted a single manat or single dollar discount. In fact, sometimes they sold to us at prices several times higher than the world market rate, and we were forced to turn a blind eye to it.”

Ilham Aliyev’s short punchline contains several important points at once: everything Baku received, it paid for, and it paid full price. There were no discounts. At times, our partners were frankly hiking prices, even above world-market levels, knowing that Baku had no alternatives at the time. There really were no alternatives, and Baku was forced to pretend it saw nothing.

Yesterday, Ilham Aliyev explained quite clearly that he had seen and understood everything. And, by the way, not only that. The president also made it clear that Azerbaijan needs neither assistance nor patrons, while reminding everyone of the “big backers” who help one warring country or another today. Behind every side, there is such an backer; according to Aliyev, some have several. Azerbaijan did everything on its own, the president reminded all those who may suddenly have decided to join the queue for “patronage.”

The fact that weapons were purchased is hardly a secret. What is striking is something else: why did the president feel the need to put it so bluntly, and why now?

The answer appears to lie in the information space of recent weeks. In a number of foreign media outlets and among popular bloggers - and it is not necessarily the case that this has happened without the help of yet another set of big backers - a narrative has been gaining traction that Azerbaijan was able to regain Karabakh only because it was supplied with equipment and weapons. From there comes the argument about “ingratitude” and “insufficient loyalty.” The logic behind it is simple: if Baku received something, then it owes something in return, and that debt can be presented at any time.

Ilham Aliyev dismissed that self-appointed bill. If the weapons were bought at full price, or even above it, then this was an ordinary commercial transaction, not a gift, and it cannot carry any political strings attached. The argument over authorship is closed. No one owes anyone anything and no one ever did. And someone else’s expectations are someone else’s problem.

It is also noticeable that Ilham Aliyev did not name the addressee. This is entirely in keeping with the speech as a whole. Azerbaijan, the president stressed, does not join any camps, and its word “is worth as much as its signature.” Publicly picking a fight with a specific partner under such a position would have been strange. Ilham Aliyev took a much subtler approach: he put it in such a way that the people who needed to understand would understand it themselves, while leaving no grounds for a diplomatic scandal. Those circles building campaigns around the idea that Baku is “in debt” surely got the message: the account is closed, the bill has been paid, move along.

At the same time, reducing the whole matter to a single addressee would be wrong. Domestically, this is first and foremost a reinforcement of the main narrative: the Victory belongs to the people and the state, not to someone on the outside. Ilham Aliyev himself linked this to ideological security, saying that pride in the Victory is the best protection against “ideological provocations.”

For foreign partners, it is a reminder of how Baku sees its relations. Azerbaijan has built ties with all poles and signed strategic partnership documents with both superpowers - China and the United States. In such a system, there is simply no room for “senior” and “junior” partners. And to those conducting information pressure, the president made it clear that no one is going to justify themselves. For those with a short memory, Ilham Aliyev once again reminded them that Baku responds to every strike - and does so several times harder.

In Baku, the question of who owns the Victory has long, and quite rightly, been seen as a question of sovereignty. It is no longer just history, but also an instrument of present-day politics: the various backers claiming co-authorship of the Victory are not doing so for nothing. They are claiming a semi-official right to tell Azerbaijan, or even dictate to it, what to do next. Ilham Aliyev patiently but firmly pushes back: do not tell us how to live. Your “noble support” has a very measurable currency equivalent, and you got what you were owed.

Ilham Aliyev was talking about weapons, but in reality he was once again talking about sovereignty. And he was doing it in Baku’s characteristic manner, without asking anyone to understand and without trying to win anyone’s approval. Instead, everyone interested was given a free lesson in political accounting. In the “income” column: weapons and equipment. In the “expenses” column: Azerbaijani money. And there was no column saying, “Now you owe us for the rest of your life.”

Judging by how quickly various foreign journalists and bloggers who were still intensely interested yesterday in the origins of the weapons and equipment of the Azerbaijani Armed Forces suddenly lost interest, Ilham Aliyev’s intended audience got the message.

Good for them.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Belarus agree to boost exchange-based trade
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 3. On the sidelines of a meeting of the Belarusian-Kazakh Business Council in Minsk, Belarusian Universal Commodity Exchange (BUCE) and the Kazakhstan Foreign Trade Chamber have agreed to step up efforts to involve Kazakh businesses in exchange trading with Belarusian companies.

According to the BUCE press service, the agreement was reached during a meeting between BUCE Head of Foreign Economic Activity Yaroslav Kovalchuk and Chairman of the Board of the Kazakhstan Foreign Trade Chamber Murat Karimsakov.

The two organizations will focus on promoting exchange trading instruments among Kazakh exporters and importers, organizing business events and identifying new promising commodities that are in demand in the markets of both countries.

Particular attention will be paid to simplifying access to BUCE for small and medium-sized enterprises, for which exchange trading can provide an additional channel for selling locally produced goods abroad.

“Our task is not simply to increase trade turnover between Kazakhstan and Belarus, but to make trade more predictable and transparent. These are precisely the opportunities provided by the exchange platform, which has an objective pricing mechanism, common rules for all participants and a number of instruments designed to minimize risks. Therefore, we intend to systematically inform Kazakh businesses about the advantages of working through the Belarusian exchange, including by organizing online seminars and business missions,” Karimsakov said.

Kovalchuk, in turn, highlighted growing interest among Kazakh companies in exchange trading and outlined priorities for cooperation with the Kazakhstan Foreign Trade Chamber.

“Throughout 2026, we have seen sustained growth in the activity of Kazakh participants. In the first nine months, the value of transactions between Belarusian and Kazakh companies already exceeded $45 million, which is one and a half times higher than in the same period last year,” Kovalchuk said.

He added that cooperation with the Kazakhstan Foreign Trade Chamber would allow the sides to organize targeted presentations of exchange trading instruments for companies from specific sectors with confirmed interest in the Belarusian market.

“This will significantly increase the effectiveness of our work with the Kazakh business community,” Kovalchuk said.

According to BUCE, Kazakhstan ranks among the top 10 countries by the number of companies accredited to participate in exchange trading. There are currently 228 Kazakh business entities accredited on the exchange, 27 of which joined the platform this year.

World.title: Azerbaijan and Iran discuss development of bilateral relations
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 3. Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and his Iranian counterpart Seyyed Abbas Araghchi discussed development of bilateral relations during a phone call today.

According to Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry, during the call, Bayramov expressed his deep condolences to Araghchi over the death of his sister and wished patience to the bereaved family and relatives.

The ministers discussed the current state and prospects for the development of Azerbaijan-Iran relations.

They also exchanged views on the current situation in the region and security issues. The sides stressed the importance of ensuring regional peace, stability and security, strengthening mutual trust, and expanding opportunities for regional cooperation.

The ministers also exchanged views on other issues of mutual interest.

Azerbaijan and Iran established diplomatic relations on March 12, 1992. The two neighboring countries maintain cooperation in trade, economy, energy, transport and logistics, agriculture and humanitarian fields, underpinned by historical and cultural ties. A State Commission for economic, trade and humanitarian cooperation has operated since 1992, and more than 140 bilateral documents have been signed. Recent years have seen progress on joint infrastructure projects, including bridges and railway terminals along the shared border, as well as growing transit cooperation within the International North-South Transport Corridor.

World.title: Teen charged for alleged crashing into crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters
World.content:
The alleged driver of the car which ploughed into a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters has been charged.

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, has been charged with three instances of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, three instances of negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and three instances of cause bodily harm by misconduct, according to court documents viewed by the ABC.

NSW Police said in a statement he has had his P1 Provisional license suspended and the vehicle was seized prior to undergoing forensic examination.

Mr Samarasinghe will appear in Newcastle Bail Court tomorrow.

Emergency services at the scene of a car crash at a Newcastle Knights supporters gathering today. (Newcastle Herald/Andrew Clysdale)

He was arrested at the scene after a car, police allege he was driving, crashed into a crowd at a roundabout on Newcastle Link Road, at Wallsend in Newcastle's west at about 9.30am on October 3.

The crash injured ten people who were taken to John Hunter Hospital, including a 5-year-old girl who police say is in a critical but now stable condition..

A 67-year-old man was also injured and is in a serious but stable condition.

Police said four other people – a second 5-year-old girl, a 2-year-old girl, a 31-year-old woman and a 48-year-old man – remain hospitalised in stable conditions.

Three men – aged 24, 25 and 27 – along with a 63-year-old woman have been discharged from hospital.

Thousands gathered to send-off the Newcastle Knights ahead of their grand-final appearance at 7.30 October 4.

The Newcastle Knights team bus was due to pass through the area on its way to Sydney when police responded to reports of the crash.

Grand final send-off became 'absolute tragedy' Ten people have been injured — two of them critically — by a car that ploughed into a crowd gathered for the Newcastle Knights grand final procession. Here's what we know.

The Knights bus diverted to a different route away from the procession of fans.

At the scene of the crash, Police Minister Yasmin Catley said "what happened is an absolute tragedy — a tragedy that needn't have happened".

Following the incident crowds shouted at Samarasinghe as he was bundled into a police car and driven away from the scene.

Two other people were removed from the car by authorities after the "crowd turned on them".

Police said the two other passengers, both males aged 18 and 19, were not injured.

Helicopters landed on a nearby oval to help transport patients to hospital. (ABC News Piper Duffy)

Knights director of football Chris James made a brief statement when the team arrived in Sydney.

"The thoughts of everyone at our club are with those impacted by this event [including] their families and … those on scene," he said.

CEO Peter Parr praised the efforts of first responders and the staff of John Hunter Hospital.

"What was meant to be a special morning for our community, thousands of Novocastrians coming together to farewell our team and show their support ahead of the Grand Final, has understandably turned into a distressing morning," Mr Parr said.

Knights forward Phoenix Crossland also commented: "Thoughts are with you mate" on Clancy's post. (Supplied)

Crash victim Chris Clancy shared his condition from within the hospital, giving a thumbs up from his hospital bed despite suffering a broken collarbone and possibly broken foot.

"I will be JJH [John Hunter Hospital] for a couple of days but will let you all know," Mr Clancy said.

Newcastle Knights captain Kalyn Ponga saw Clancy's post and told him "the team and community are with yas [sic]".

"All the best with recovery mate," Mr Ponga said.

World.title: Verstappen claims pole at Grand Prix in Malaysia
World.content:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen claimed his first pole position of the season at the Formula One Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on Saturday, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton joining him on the front row.

It is the first time two great rivals have shared the front row of the grid since the Hungarian Grand Prix in 2023.

Verstappen's teammate, Isack Hadjar, was third fastest but will start eighth due to a grid penalty, with championship leader Kimi Antonelli in third alongside Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Oscar Piastri was pipped to sixth by his teammate Lando Norris, but will move up a position as a result of Hadjar's penalty to start sixth as McLaren locked out the third row of the grid.

George Russell, who so spectacularly won the last Grand Prix in Azerbaijan last week, will start seventh in what was an alarming performance for Mercedes, who came to Malaysia with a big upgrade package.

"It's very difficult to understand," Mercedes boss Toto Wolff told Sky Sports.

"We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we didn't see all year.

"But then you can say it's very hot, with the tarmac very different to all the tracks.

"[We] looked really good in the morning; we seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then in qualifying, it was a little bit back to what we saw before — just no performance."

Verstappen was the last driver to win a Grand Prix in Malaysia in 2017, in what was his second career victory, before the race was taken off the calendar after the government said it could not justify the costs.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start from the front row of the grid together for the first time in three years. (Getty Images: Formula 1/Mark Sutton)

Nine years and four championships later, the Dutchman showed he was still the man to beat in Sepang with a time of 1 minute 35.130 seconds.

"It's fantastic, we've been trying for many Grands Prix to get more, sometimes a bit closer to the others. But to finally get it from where we started the season [it's] pretty incredible," said Verstappen as he eyes his first win of the season.

Hamilton, who also has one victory in Sepang, struggled with tyre degradation in practice sessions but the veteran Briton snatched second from Hadjar in the dying stages of the final qualifying session.

"It's so hot here, I keep saying it. But that's made it a massive challenge for the tyres, for the car, for the mechanics in the garage," Hamilton said.

"We made so many changes through all these practice sessions because the cars are sliding, these tyres are overheating. It was really, really hard to find a good balance. We made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot."

Hadjar had exceeded his seasonal allowance for engines, which resulted in a five-place grid penalty.

"It's a bit unfortunate we take the penalty on a track that fast," Hadjar said.

"But you know, from P8, I'm confident we can go through the field and come back for a good result."

Reuters/ABC

World.title: De Minaur fights into quarterfinals in China
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has been pushed to the limit, before breaking the resistance of French qualifier Quentin Halys and advancing to his second consecutive China Open quarterfinal.

The Australian, who has had a seesawing second half of the year, lost the first set in Beijing on Saturday, before grinding his way back into the match.

After winning the first set 6-3, world number 50 Halys opened up a 5-3 lead in the second and was serving for the match, before de Minaur rallied to break back, then clinch a neck-and-neck tie break 7-5 to set up a decider.

The third set was another close affair, before de Minaur was able to break at 5-5 and secure a hard-fought 3-6 7-6 (5) 7-5 win in 2 hours 47 minutes.

Victory evened up their head-to-head record at 2-2 and put de Minaur into the quarters, where the world number 10 will play Andrey Rublev, currently ranked number 20 in the world, but a former top-10 player himself.

Rublev was also pushed to the limit before beating fellow Russian Roman Safiullin 6-2 3-6 6-4.

De Minaur will be looking to repeat or better last year's performance at the ATP 500 event, when he made the semifinals before losing to then world number 1 Jannik Sinner.

It has been an up-and-down year for de Minaur, who started 2026 off well by reaching the last eight at the Australian Open.

He continued that momentum into February, when he won the ATP 500 event in Rotterdam.

De Minaur followed that by reaching the French Open's third round and the fourth round at Wimbledon, before disappointingly bowing out in the second round of the US Open in September.

However, he bounced back impressively by steering Australia to victory over Poland in their Davis Cup clash in Brisbane, before beating in-from German Alexander Zverev at the Laver Cup in London.

Zverev, who has won two majors this year — at Roland Garros in June and Flushing Meadows in September — is top seed in Beijing and was scheduled to play China's Juncheng Shang later on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Crash axe used in flydubai attack on pilot
World.content:
The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 attempted to carry out a "terrorist" attack during the flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to the state news agency WAM.

The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft, the prosecutor general said.

A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies such as crashes.

Benjamin Netanyahu meets "heroes" who intervened on a flydubai flight bound for Israel. (Rueters via Amos Ben Gershon, Government Press Office)

The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.

While Emirati authorities have not publicly identified the co-pilot, Israeli officials have previously said he is an Omani national. Oman has not commented on the incident.

"Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack," WAM quoted UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying.

The aircraft plunged more than 5,000 metres in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the UAE to Israel. (ABC News)

The co-pilot was barred from flying in Oman but was hired by the United Arab Emirates-based airline, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation.

It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired in the Emirates.

Oman's move to bar the co-pilot from flying was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

UAE Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi's comments were the first by Emirati authorities to describe the incident as an attempted "terrorist" attack.

Disaster was averted on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had attacked the captain in what Israeli officials said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying more than 170 passengers and crew.

Israeli passenger Yaniv Hayoun has been hailed a hero after the mid-flight attack. (AP: Tomer Appelbaum)

A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

An Israeli government official told Reuters earlier that Israeli investigators would take part alongside Emirati authorities in the UAE-led investigation, which would examine what happened as well as the suspect's motives and background.

What happened on flydubai FZ1073 One pilot stabbed another and attempted to crash a flight, according to Israel's prime minister, with one passenger who intervened praised as a "hero".

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a "heavy price".

Earlier this week Mr Netanyahu said the co-pilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and appeared suicidal, though he said a motive had not yet been established.

Most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals.

The aircraft dropped more than 5,000 metres in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the UAE to Israel, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24.

The route is popular among Israeli travellers.

REUTERS/AP

World.title: Sharks could linger off Perth coast despite whale carcass removal
World.content:
Some of Perth's most seasoned swimmers are taking a break from the ocean after a whale carcass lured sharks close to shore, with an expert warning that the predators could be attracted to the area for weeks.

Several sharks have been spotted lurking off some of Perth's most popular beaches in recent days after a whale carcass washed up at City Beach on Monday, just over a week after a fatal shark attack at Sorrento Beach.

The City of Perth Surf Life Saving Club cancelled the Surf Life Saving WA (SLSWA) Enduro Championship at City Beach today, while placing all club-based training on hold until further notice.

City Beach remains closed after a beached whale attracted sharks to the area. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

City Beach, Floreat Beach and Swanbourne Beach have all been closed.

But the heightened shark activity in recent days has also discouraged swimmers and surfers further along the coastline.

Cottesloe's community ocean swimming group PodSquad is taking a break from its daily 2-kilometre morning swim.

"Even though the [Cottesloe] beaches are open at the moment, we're taking a break for a few more days," the group's founder Shane McGurk said.

PodSquad founder Shane McGurk wants to see the shark tagging program expanded. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"Our numbers will drop off now, understandably — it's a very emotive issue. [Some] people have a different relationship with these sort of events, about how they manage.

"Some want to get straight back in [and get] back on the horse, so to speak, and others want to take a break and come to terms with the tragedy at Sorrento, and also the whale at City Beach."

Calls for more tagging, AI drones

Ahead of each summer, around the end of October, the Town of Cottesloe installs a shark barrier at Cottesloe Beach.

Third person killed by sharks in WA this year The often-heated debate over how to protect beachgoers from sharks is likely to get hotter after the death of a third person this year.

But this year, it is due to be installed a couple of weeks early — on Wednesday, depending on weather conditions and seaweed movement.

Mr McGurk said PodSquad members would initially swim within the enclosure when members returned to their morning routine, and they would like to see the enclosure installed early again next year.

The group also called for an expansion of the shark tagging program and for investment in AI-powered drones that are capable of identifying shark species when the animals come in close to shore.

He said that could enhance the data available to swimmers when they were making decisions about whether to get into the water.

"We just want to know where the sharks are, and when we know where the sharks are we can keep safe," he said.

Cottesloe volunteer surf lifesavers did the first patrol of the season on Saturday morning. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Sharks could linger for weeks

Curt Jenner from the Centre for Whale Research in Western Australia said while the whale carcass had been removed from City Beach, sharks could still be attracted to the area for weeks.

"Whales are full of blubber and that blubber will break down into oil very quickly and that gets straight into the sand," he said.

"Sharks are cued in, on a molecular level, to detect small traces of oils or blood or anything like that and so they'll be tasting that for weeks to come."

Centre for Whale Research director Curt Jenner says traces of the whale will attract sharks to the area for some time. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Mr Jenner said sharks were also attracted to the south-west coastline between September and December because that time was the peak of the southern migration for humpback whales.

The predators also follow other prey, such as blue fin tuna, into the southern ocean.

"If you were going to be cautious about being in the water, this is the time," Mr Jenner said.

World.title: David Fifita leads Australia in wild mismatch against PNG
World.content:
A rag-tag Australian side has outclassed Papua New Guinea 60-10 in the annual Prime Minister's XIII clash in Port Moresby.

The Australians scored 11 tries and exposed the PNG side's defensive frailties almost at will in what was the 20th men's Prime Minister's XIII match.

It was hardly a conventional game at the National Football Stadium on Saturday, with Australia switching on and off as players became accustomed to their makeshift position.

Ezra Mam spent time at fullback. Jock Madden appeared to be playing on an edge. Jamal Fogarty stood in the centres, and Josh Curran kicked a goal.

At one stage they had three regular hookers on the field.

In one piece of consistency, captain David Fifita started and finished the match as a devastating left centre.

Commentator Cooper Cronk mused it was coach Ben Teo's way of keeping the Aussies engaged after a long, hard season.

It was at times chaotic and they dropped the ball a lot, but it was fun. Less so for the PNG side, who were not just outclassed but also ill-disciplined, missing 47 tackles — 28 in the first half alone.

With the PNG Chiefs' arrival in the NRL fast approaching, it is clear the next level of local players are still a long way from that standard.

On a positive note, earlier on Saturday the Junior Kumuls scored a historic first win over the Australian Schoolboys, 18-10.

If Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters hasn't settled on his squad for this month's Rugby League World Cup, several players put their hands up.

Regular back-rower Fifita, who showed his class and power in the centres on Saturday, first appeared in the PM's XIII game seven years ago and looked destined for higher honours that never arrived. Maybe that time is approaching again.

Mam and fellow half Lachlan Galvin showed more than one glimpse of their brilliance, while hulking front-rower Tom Hazelton was one of the best players on the field.

For former NRL and current London Broncos coach Jason Demetriou, who will guide the PNG Kumuls at the World Cup, there was not a lot to love.

Sylvester Namo should be there, while uncapped centre Stanford Talita and fullback Sanny Wabo were dangerous at times and could find their way into Demetriou's squad.

In the women's game, Australia was also successful, dishing out a 66-6 thumping of their hosts.

The PNG women's Prime Minister's XIII scored a point for the first time in three years, but the Aussies still came out on top in a big way. (AAP: NRL Photos/Anthony Kourembanas)

PNG might have scored for the first time in three years, but Australia was a class above, crossing for 12 tries to one to rack up the biggest winning margin in the fixture's history.

While the standard of PNG's second-tier players has improved alongside the growth of the national women's competition, the Santos Cup, so too has that of the Australians.

Several showed they would not be out of place if called up to coach Jess Skinner's Jillaroos for this month's 2026 Rugby League World Cup.

Jada Taylor scored three tries and was almost impossible to handle at times, showing her versatility by playing on the wing, despite playing her club football at fullback.

Half Kasey Reh, centre Tahlia O'Brien, hooker Taneka Todhunter and back-rower Tayla Preston were others who impressed in what was effectively an audition in front of Skinner for a grander stage.

PNG Orchids coach Craig Sandercock, who this year guided Wests Tigers to their first NRLW finals series, would also have enjoyed the opportunity to see the next generation of PNG players.

There was no doubt they were outclassed, and they struggled for time with the ball, having just 37 per cent possession.

However, they had an 85 per cent completion rate and tried hard in defence, before tiring late in each half.

AAP

World.title: Tornado rips through NSW south coast, causing damage around Ulladulla
World.content:
A tornado has torn through parts of the New South Wales south coast, causing significant damage around Ulladulla.

Just after 1pm today, the region was issued with a severe thunderstorm warning for damaging winds, large hailstones and heavy rainfall.

The Bureau of Meteorology has confirmed a tornado did move through the area, describing the event as "very unusual".

Vision shows the rotating column of air making its way across a residential area.

Images show a rotating column of air making its way across a residential area. (Supplied: Edwin Fletcher)

In other vision from outside a local cafe, staff can be seen scrambling to remove tables and chairs before heavy rain and strong winds sweep through violently, sending umbrellas flying into the harbour.

'Just a mess, big mess'

Cafe owner Julius Machado told the ABC that it had been a busy Saturday until about 1pm when the sky darkened and everything changed in "a blink of an eye".

"Just a big wind came through and it just swept away everything … the customers were sitting outside having coffee and lunch, and then they have to rush back in," he said.

"Some rushed into the kitchen area, some went to the front section and it was terrible."

Mr Machado has been running the cafe for close to seven years.

Loading...

He said while Ulladulla had weathered strong storms before, nothing compared, and likened the event to watching a diaster movie.

" Nobody got the chance to move or move the stuff. It just came through so quickly. In the 30 seconds, just swept over everything. "

Boats that had been chained to the harbour, Mr Machado added, were uplifted and thrown onto the car park.

And just as quickly as it had arrived, it disappeared.

"It [lasted] just for a couple of minutes. That's it. And yeah, back to normal after that, Mr Machado said.

"We had to close up early to clean up … all glasses were broken, plates, glasses everywhere; was just a mess, big mess."

Calls for help across NSW

The NSW State Emergency Service (SES) said they had received more than 90 calls for assistance across the state, including 29 around Ulladulla.

Crews are responding to roofs being ripped from homes, dislodged tiles and skylights, and fallen trees and powerlines.

Dozens of properties have also being hit with power outages.

An SES incident management team has been set up in Ulladulla, with crews from nearby Nowra — which has received close to 17 millimetres of rain since 9am— and surrounding areas responding.

The SES expects calls for assistance to increase, with severe thunderstorms expected to continue into the evening.

World.title: One Nation promises law-and-order boost in Victorian campaign launch
World.content:
One Nation has launched its campaign for the Victorian state election, promising to fund law-and-order measures by scrapping the Suburban Rail Loop and Treaty.

One Nation Victoria leader Warren Pickering was joined at the launch by the party's national leader Pauline Hanson and its candidates for the upcoming election, as the party unveiled its policies.

The ABC was not invited to the campaign launch at Melbourne's Crown Casino, and was barred from entering the event.

Pauline Hanson's entrance was met with applause and cheers as attendees rushed to film on their phones. (ABC News)

The event heard speeches from the two leaders, MP Rickie-Lee Tyrrell and candidates Colleen Harkin and Mark Nicholson.

Mr Nicholson led the attendees in a rendition of Advance Australia Fair before making an impassioned speech, saying "if I have it my way, Dan Andrews and Jacinta Allan, they'll be in prison by Christmas".

Ms Hanson received a hero's welcome at the event, making an impassioned plea for the roughly 750 supporters in attendance to back the party's Victorian candidates.

Pauline Hanson invoked Ned Kelly and the Eureka Stockade during her speech in Melbourne. (ABC News)

"What I've provided is a vehicle; now you are the engine, now you drive it," Ms Hanson said.

The Queensland senator spent much of her speech attacking the incumbent Labor government's record on crime, corruption and Victoria's growing debt, saying Victorians had been "treated like mugs".

Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most.

She also addressed comments made by Premier Ben Carroll, who last month said that the rise of One Nation in Victoria terrified him.

"If you're listening, Ben, don't be scared of me. I tell you what mate, he should be scared of you," Ms Hanson said, pointing to the gathered crowd.

Support for One Nation has surged in Victoria, with polling suggesting the party will seriously challenge both Labor and the Coalition in the upcoming election.

One Nation pledges boosts to law and order

Law-and-order measures featured as the centrepiece of One Nation's policy launch on Saturday, taking up the first several pages of a 63-page policy booklet.

One Nation has promised heavy investment into law and order including bolstering police numbers by recruiting ADF veterans through an accelerated program.

"The policy that I'm most proud of, and probably the most important to Victoria, is our crime policy," Mr Pickering said.

"We're proposing to utilise some of the estimated 10,000 suitably qualified contemporary veterans in this state to lean into the police force."

Warren Pickering says he is most proud of One Nation's crime policy. (ABC News)

One Nation said it would target youth crime in the state by imposing harsher penalties on violent young offenders.

The party plans to reduce the age of criminal responsibility for children to 10 years old, charge young offenders of serious violent crimes as adults, and hold parents liable for fines and property damage caused by their children.

The party said it would introduce "carefully governed AI" to cut down on administrative burdens and free up frontline officers, while providing sign-on bonuses and accommodation allowances.

One Nation revealed its 2026 election policies at an event on Saturday. (ABC News)

The judicial system has also been targeted for major investment under One Nation with pledges to increase the number of magistrates, fund a 24-hour bail court and build three new magistrates' courts in Melbourne's outer suburbs in a bid to speed up the judicial process.

It also promised to introduce UK-style self-defence in the home laws, and explore a "tightly controlled trial" of giving Victorians legal access to capsicum spray.

Suburban Rail Loop, net zero and Treaty on the chopping block

One Nation said it would fund its investments with a range of cuts to government projects, agencies and services.

The party announced it would scrap the Suburban Rail Loop (SRL) project, diverting the funds to infrastructure such as the Airport Rail line and the electrification of the Melton line.

One Nation says the SRL project will be scrapped if it is elected. (Supplied)

Government agencies and public sector jobs would also be targeted for cuts under One Nation, with the party pledging to review the state's public entities and agencies, and introduce expiry dates for the bodies.

It also said First Peoples' representative body Gellung Warl would be abolished and the statewide Treaty scrapped.

Climate policies were also earmarked as targets for One Nation cuts.

The party pledged to scrap all net-zero targets and subsidies, cancel transmission projects such as the VNI West and Western Renewables Link and reverse the ban on gas connections in new homes.

One Nation supporters were displaying their allegiances proudly at the campaign launch. (ABC News)

One Nation said it would also repeal the statewide ban on nuclear energy.

But the party stopped short of committing to scrapping taxes, saying it would instead wind back land tax increases and increase the threshold for payroll tax.

Rival parties dismiss One Nation launch

Ms Hanson took aim at rival political parties during her speech on Saturday, saying Victorians now had trust issues with the Liberal Party and that the opposition had not done its job.

The ABC guide to the 2026 Victorian election To learn more about the key electorates, candidates and swing seats in the coming election, head to this guide from the ABC's Chief Elections and Data Analyst Casey Briggs.

When asked about those comments, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson refused to mention Ms Hanson's party by name.

"I know that Victorians are looking for a change of government this year, and the only way to do that is to elect a Liberal and Nationals government," Ms Wilson said.

Government minister Nick Staikos dismissed the campaign launch by One Nation on Saturday entirely, saying it was "not a serious political party".

"We don't share anything in common with that party, we will not be making deals with that party," Mr Staikos said.

"They are importing the worst of American politics to our state."

About two dozen protesters rallied outside Crown in Melbourne in opposition to One Nation. (ABC News)

A small group of protesters was seen outside the One Nation event on Saturday, with about two dozen people holding signs and banners claiming that the party was racist.

"We've seen Hanson calling for an end to immigration, she says mass immigration is a problem and we think that's absolutely scapegoating the problems," protester Julie Monteiro said.

World.title: I visited one of the world’s great cities for eight hours and loved every minute
World.content:
Reviews & adviceEurope Opinion I visited one of the world’s great cities for eight hours and loved every minute Ben Groundwater Travel writer October 4, 2026 — 12:00am

October 4, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The clock is ticking. Barcelona, in eight hours. It’s a laughable challenge in many ways, clearly impossible. How could anyone feel they’ve adequately “done” an entire city, one of the world’s greats, in the time it takes to get through a single workday? But sometimes this is all you have. Your cruise ship arrives, it deposits everyone onto the dock, and at some point in the evening you will all pile back on again and depart. The Church of La Sagrada Familia, designed by Catalan architect Antoni Gaudi, is undoubtedly a Barcelona highlight. iStock So how can you feel you’ve experienced a place in such a short time? How can you enjoy yourself, while also coming to know a city and its culture and its heart, and maybe even checking off a few big-ticket items, in the space of eight hours? First piece of advice: do not, under any circumstances, attempt to do it all. You just can’t. Even attempting to do a lot of things will be a nightmare, an unenjoyable rush from one place to the next, with no time to take any of it in.



You could look at Barcelona and think: OK, I have to do all the Gaudi stuff. La Sagrada Familia, up to Park Guell, call past Casa Batllo. Whip through the Picasso Museum, walk around the Gothic Quarter, eat tapas for lunch, stroll Las Ramblas, have a dip at the beach in Barceloneta, ride the cable car across to Montjuic, take the Teleferico (another, more modern cable car) to the top of the mountain at sunset, jump in a taxi and be back at the port in time for the ship’s departure. 



The way to do that is to decide on your priorities, and this will be entirely personal. What brings you joy? Is it art, food, architecture, people, the opportunity to learn, the chance to wander aimlessly and see what you stumble upon? All of these will determine your final itinerary. You’ve only got eight hours, this is no time to be doing things just because you believe you should. Do it because you love it. So here’s how I would spend eight hours in Barcelona. Straight off the ship and over to La Sagrada Familia, Antoni Gaudí’s masterpiece. Book tickets well in advance, get there early before the bulk of the crowds arrive, take some photos from outside and then have a good hour or two inside to look around. From there I would take the metro to Passeig de Gracia, a point at which Barcelona splits into some of its most interesting and enjoyable neighbourhoods: the Gothic Quarter, El Born, Raval and L’Eixample. This is the ideal area to explore on foot, to just wander and see where it takes you, to call in for coffee somewhere that looks nice, check out a few shops, stroll with no agenda.



And then have lunch. This is a key area of interest of mine, and it’s also a lovingly observed ritual in Spain, so I’m reserving, frankly, a silly amount of time for lunch. We’re talking three hours here: sit down, relax, take it slow. Related Article Cruises Twelve of the most incredible experiences you can do from a cruise ship This is the key, I think, to exploration of this limited style. It’s far better to do a few things well than to do many things poorly. Part of the joy of a city, for me, is having the space to just sit or wander and take it all in. The chef and travel-show host Rick Stein calls it “mooching around”, the act of forgoing famous attractions and formal tourist behaviour in favour of doing very little for a while, just sitting in the sun with a beer or drinking a coffee and reading a book. The clock might be ticking but the idea of this sort of travel is to ignore that clock, to just forget about it for a while, pretend it doesn’t exist and enjoy yourself.



And so I’m off to El Xampanyet, an old-school tapas bar in El Born, with tiled walls and old wine bottles lining the shelves. I’ll drink vermouth and eat anchovies and watch as the crowd ebbs and flows and the day creeps by. Hours and hours well spent. The Picasso Museum is close, so that could be worth a wander later. Or maybe I’ll have a drink somewhere else, or walk narrow streets, or check out Santa Caterina Market before it’s time to head back to the ship. Barcelona, experienced and understood. I couldn’t be happier.

World.title: Jim in Japan: Treasurer to sell Australia as a safe bet in two-day Tokyo blitz
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalForeign investment Jim in Japan: Treasurer to sell Australia as a safe bet in two-day Tokyo blitz Nick Newling October 3, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers will hold a series of high-level meetings with Japanese investors and business leaders in Tokyo this week, as the government attempts to sell Australia as a safe harbour for middle-power investment amid an increasingly uncertain global economy. The Labor minister will market Australia as a renewable energy powerhouse and artificial intelligence leader, and highlight the $4.8 trillion superannuation system as a “deep pool” of capital, while also chairing a housing roundtable with leaders in Japanese residential development. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will make Tokyo his first stop in a three-country tour of Asia this month. Dominic Lorrimer “If investors want to make the most of the defining decade ahead, nowhere offers more opportunities than Australia. We’re making Australia an indispensable part of the transformation underway in the global economy, and we’re telling the world’s investors why they need a piece of the action,” Chalmers told this masthead. The trip comes after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last month used an address to the United Nations to declare the post-1945 international order “no longer fit for purpose”, forcing middle powers such as Australia to build new partnerships while defending the international rules-based order.



Albanese’s comments echoed those of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who in a historic rallying cry to the Australian parliament in March called for middle powers to unite or face subordination to bigger nations. During the two-day blitz, Chalmers is set to meet more than 30 CEOs, business leaders and investors from Japan’s largest firms, offering a five-pillared pitch of Australia’s “unique” investment advantages. The Treasurer will meet with Kenichi Hori, head of Mitsui & Co., one of Japan’s largest conglomerates and Juro Baba, executive vice president of Mitsubishi Corporation. Chalmers will pitch Australia as a resource leader for green energy and critical minerals, arguing that domestic renewable electricity production will be able to compete with traditional hubs such as the Middle East and Russia by 2050. The focus on Australia’s reliability and resources comes amid a time of tumult for the two nations, after the unveiling of a domestic gas reservation policy that rattled Japan as the primary importer of Australian gas. Australia provides around 40 per cent of Japan’s LNG, which supports a significant portion of the country’s energy generation.



Following the policy’s announcement, officials from Japan, South Korea and Malaysia – major consumers of Australian LNG – lodged appeals through the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade seeking certainty over contract protections. A modified version of the reservation plan to take effect from January 2028 will require liquefied natural gas shippers face a requirement to reserve up to 20 per cent of their export volumes for local customers. The policy is designed to force a 10 per cent domestic oversupply each year to push down the cost of the fuel. The policy has since been softened to ensure the oversupply is “modest”, quelling concerns from Asian trading partners. Albanese was also caught in a faux pas after his appearance on a podcast in which he joked about melons gifted to him by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The Japanese embassy in Australia later downplayed the incident, and the leaders posed for a picture together last month at the United Nations.



Part of Chalmers’ pitch in Japan will highlight the stable investment capacity of the nation’s superannuation pool, and Australia’s embrace of artificial intelligence and data centres. Related Article Opinion

Federal budget The world is changing rapidly. Albanese needs to follow suit Peter Hartcher Political and international editor “This is all about boosting investment in Australia, bolstering supply chains and economic resilience, and strengthening our relationships in Asia. As a reliable, responsible middle power with strong economic foundations and huge advantages in areas like energy, AI and critical minerals, Australia is an attractive investment destination,” Chalmers said. “Whether it’s our resources or renewable energy, our skills or our stability, Australia has exactly what the world needs when the world needs it.” Alongside meetings with counterparts and business leaders, Chalmers will host two roundtables on Monday. The first will take in investors and asset managers from Japan and Australia, while the second will focus on residential development including novel construction methods that could support increased supply in Australia.



The trip to Japan will be the first of three stops the Treasurer will make this month in Asia, ahead of a trip to Bangkok to meet with G20 finance ministers on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings. Chalmers will also meet with Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation counterparts in Hong Kong. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Ten people injured, P-plater charged after car crashes into Newcastle Knights fans
World.content:
A five-year-old girl was left fighting for her life and nine others were injured when a teenage P-plate driver allegedly lost control of his car and careered into jubilant crowds lining a Newcastle street to wave the Knights off to the NRL grand final. One of the injured, Chris Clancy, said the car appeared to speed up as it went through a roundabout, and then lost control on the wet road. “No-one had time to move,” he said. “I thought I was going to die, it happened so fast.” Fans at the crash site rushed to provide first aid as emergency crews rushed to the scene and word of the collision spread through the tens of thousands of excited fans waiting for a glimpse of their team. The team’s bus, which had not yet departed when the crash occurred, was rerouted, and players were informed. Loading “They were shocked, it was a very sombre bus ride,” said one of those aboard. “Our fans mean everything to us. For that to happen; horrible.”



The five-year-old girl was in a critical but stable condition in John Hunter Hospital on Saturday evening. A 67-year-old patient was in a serious but stable condition, and four others, including a 2-year-old and a 5-year-old girl, were stable. Four had been discharged, including three men in their 20s and a 63-year-old woman. Police arrested the 18-year-old driver, Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, at the crash site and took him for mandatory drug and alcohol testing. He was later released from hospital and taken to a police station where he was charged with three counts each of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and causing bodily harm by misconduct in charge of a motor vehicle. He was refused police bail to face a court on Sunday. Samarasinghe’s licence has also been suspended, and the vehicle he was allegedly driving has been seized to undergo forensic examination. The two male passengers in the vehicle at the time of the crash, aged 18 and 19, were both uninjured. NSW Police Assistant Commissioner David Waddell said officers were investigating reports the P-plater had been “driving erratically” before he lost control of the vehicle. Footage posted to social media depicted the BMW careering around the roundabout moments before the crash, as shocked onlookers were heard screaming.



The crash scene. TNV Scenes at Wallsend, Newcastle, after a car crashed into a crowd of Knights supporters. Onlookers expressed anger towards the occupants of the car after the crash, police said. “We had to get the three of them out of there because the crowd did turn on them,” Waddell said. Witness Dean Liddell said he could hear the vehicle coming towards the crowd and then “all hell broke loose”. “I watched the little girl get dragged underneath the car. Seeing the whole scene unfold, it took me 10 minutes until I could say anything to anyone,” Liddell said.



He said the crowd grabbed the driver from the wreck and a scuffle began before police intervened. “If the copper wasn’t there, the driver would have had massive injuries as well,” he said. The accident came after a joyous week in Newcastle, where the city threw its support behind a team that has not won a premiership for 25 years. The Knights had been expected to be inspired by the joy of their supporters during the grand final, but will now also feel the weight of the tragedy when they take the field. Newcastle Knights captain Kalyn Ponga said on social media that players’ “hearts are with everyone affected” by the crash. “We’re thinking of you, your families and everyone in our Newcastle community.” Longtime league watchers say no other grand final has been played under such a shadow.



“It’s heartbreaking for the whole rugby league community, not just in Newcastle,” said Brad Fittler, a former Roosters captain and a member of the league hall of fame. “We’ve never seen anything like this ahead of a grand final and it puts everything in perspective.” Australian Rugby League Commission executive chairman Peter V’Landys said he was deeply saddened by the crash. When asked whether it would affect plans for Sunday night’s game, he said “we’re just concerned about the victims at the moment.” Paramedics prepare to transport the injured by helicopter. Sitthixay Ditthavong NSW Premier Chris Minns said it was heartbreaking to see fans who were sending off their grand final team involved in such a terrible incident. “My thoughts are with the families and friends of loved ones who have been involved or injured in the crash. I also want to thank emergency services, including police and ambulance, who are responding to this tragedy”, the premier said.



“We’ve seen how this grand final has brought the Newcastle together, and I hope the whole community remains united as we continue to respond.” Newcastle Lord Mayor Gavin Morris said that, before Saturday’s crash, the lead-up to the grand final had been one of the “most incredibly joyous weeks in our city”. “It’s a tragedy. It’s something that we can’t take back,” Morris said. Morris said that passing vehicles were “revving up the crowd” as they drove past thousands of Knights fans lining the roadside before the crash.



“That just should not have been occurring, but it has,” he said. Asked whether bollards or fencing should have been installed at the roadside to protect fans, Morris said securing the 20-kilometre stretch of road between the Knights’ home ground and the crash site was “almost an impossible task”. The injured Clancy said a police vehicle was stationed near the crash site and responded quickly. He said the car came at the group of supporters too fast for them to jump out of the way. He was hit by the front of the vehicle. Knights fan Jed Partridge, 29, who arrived at 8.20am to join thousands of others in waving off the team bus, was among fans who watched the celebration turn to shock. “We were on the side of the road, just waiting. Everyone was happy, and then there was a real flurry of cop cars, ambos and rescue cars shooting past.” He said word soon filtered out that there had been a serious crash. “It was eerie … such a positive thing could quickly turn to this. It’s hard to wrap your head around.”



Fans urged the Knights to press forward and do their best on Sunday night. “It will be tough for them, but do what they’ve always done and do it for the town,” said Clancy. “I believe they can win. Regardless of whether they win or lose, they’ve done the town proud.” Loading Newcastle Knights fans gathered to send off their team. Nine Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Misguided misogyny musings miss the mark
World.content:
NationalNSWLetters Misguided misogyny musings miss the mark October 3, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I am a fully paid-up member of the sisterhood but we are witness to a couple of very long bows being drawn by Parnell Palme McGuinness (“Albanese got the gong but the real global citizen is misogyny”, September 27). Journalist Latika Bourke asked a graceless question of the PM as he accepted a Global Citizen Award in New York, for which she has received some criticism. Enter Palme McGuinness, who has tortuously conflated apparent misogyny aimed at Bourke with the Bondi murders in a misguided diatribe about treatment of female journalists. While misogyny is common in journalistic circles, Palme McGuinness goes on a spurious and rambling stream of consciousness trying to link antisemitism, sexism and gracious world leaders, ending up in a confusing soup of misguided accusations. Judy Hungerford, Narraweena Anthony Albanese receives his Global Citizen Award from New Guinea PM James Marape. Dominic Lorrimer I have no particular argument with Stephen Koukoulas being called a hypocrite, which is something he may excel in, but the rest of us, including even Parnell Palme McGuinness herself, can hardly claim to be entirely innocent of this. But here she goes once again, shaping anything she can into an argument against anyone to her philosophical left. Under the guise of supporting a fellow female journalist and railing against misogyny, instead of engaging with the fact that Latika Bourke’s question to the PM was composed of unnecessary and mostly unsubstantiated accusations, she pokes the stick at the PM. That actually appears to be the whole point of her article. McGuinness can carry on about hypocrisy and misogyny as much as she likes, and good on her, but she’d be more convincing if she chose her targets less self-servingly. Prue Nelson, Cremorne Point Words of wisdom Peter FitzSimons has done well to highlight the excellent speech by headmaster Michael Blake. (“Before his speech went viral, this boys’ school headmaster ran it past his daughter”, September 27). I thought Blake’s reference to St Francis of Assisi was poignant: “preach the gospel daily and occasionally use words”. Positive role models; the right choices; doing the right thing, even though it comes with a cost; what a true friendship entails – these are all important in life. Our young generations are lucky to have educators of the calibre of Blake. We have all met them, in many schools, education systems and life in general. As we see in our courts, our ICAC, in life situations, despite having the information, it comes down to individual choices. Life wasn’t meant to be easy – doing the right thing is not always easier. Geoff Nilon, Mascot



According to Peter FitzSimons, the headmaster of a boys’ private school should be praised for attempting to instil a sense of respect for females in his young charges. Good luck. This is one of the problems in single-sex schools. It is far better in most public high schools, where the mixture of boys and girls enables children, because that is what they are, to have a realistic view of each other. Respect follows when both sexes realise there is no inherent superiority in being one or the other. There is no mystique, no false outlook, just an acceptance of fellow human beings. Nola Tucker, Kiama Eco fail It looks like patient safety is a handy cover-up for a misguided move by the NSW Clinical Excellence Commission (CEC) to ban using “eco-friendly medical supplies in favour of single-use products that end up in landfill and cost taxpayers millions of dollars each year” (“Healthcare staff oppose ban on eco-friendly medical supplies”, September 27). Could this be the result of big corporate lobbying? There’s plenty of precedent to use eco products. Remanufacturing medical devices is commonplace in Britain, the US and Europe. Meanwhile, single-use devices that end up in landfill cost less to manufacture and throw away, saving money with safety being used to rationalise such practices. But get this: “about 8 per cent of all waste in NSW is generated from the healthcare sector”, according to the co-chair of Doctors for the Environment Australia. That amounts to 52,400 tonnes of waste – the weight of the Harbour Bridge. To cap things off, by reducing the resultant landfill in allowing remanufacturing, the $16 million saved can be reinvested in overstretched public healthcare. Let’s hope the CEC can be convinced to reverse this disastrous ban of eco-friendly medical supplies. Larry Woldenberg, Forest Lodge Problems with pride Your correspondent Adras Hidas exhorts Australians to take pride in their history and their flag (Letters, September 27). While such pride can be a positive and unifying factor, it also has its problems, especially for some Australians. The flag gives prominence to the colonising nation that seized control of a territory, by force, more than two centuries ago, with no recognition of the traditional custodians of this land. The land then was not a sovereign nation called Australia but an offshore detention centre run by the UK military and called New South Wales. Aspects of this have not been addressed sufficiently since then. I first voted in 1967 as an Australian (European immigrant) citizen at the age of 21, as was the rule at the time, in a federal election accompanied by a referendum to allow Indigenous Australians to be counted in the census, i.e. recognised as human residents of the land. Even that did not settle the formal recognition of these people. Indigenous Australians only acquired full voting rights throughout the nation in the 1960s Queensland state elections. Apart from First Australians, the treatment of some types of immigrants was grossly unequal. The White Australia Policy was only abolished in the 1970s. More needs to be done to make many of us feel genuine pride in this nation. Al Svirskis, Mount Druitt



You can call me Albo In the words of Paul Simon: “I need a photo opportunity, I want a shot at redemption/Don’t want to end up a cartoon in a cartoon graveyard” (“PM must convince voters UN trip was more than selfies with leaders”, September 27). Allan Gibson, Cherrybrook To submit a letter to the Sydney Morning Herald, email letters@smh.com.au. Click here for tips on how to submit letters.

World.title: ‘It was crazy’: Tornado sweeps through Ulladulla as severe storms hit Sydney
World.content:
Updated EnvironmentWeatherExtreme weather ‘It was crazy’: Tornado sweeps through Ulladulla as severe storms hit Sydney Emily Kowal Updated October 3, 2026 — 8:05pm ,first published 4:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A tornado swept through Ulladulla on the NSW South Coast on Saturday, shocking residents, knocking down trees and damaging buildings, as intense rain, flash floods and winds lashed Sydney. Greater Sydney and the CBD were struck by severe thunderstorms about 5pm on Saturday, with wind gusts reaching up to 72km/h in Sydney Harbour and up to 30 millimetres of rain falling in less than half an hour, triggering flash flooding in parts of the city. Houses were damaged by the tornado in Ulladulla. Brad Collins The State Emergency Service rescued two people from cars in floodwaters in Moore Park and Darlinghurst. In Edgecliff, vehicles were stuck in water as flash floods covered the street, while in Merrylands a tree was struck by lightning.



The tornado that ripped through Ulladulla tore roofs off homes and knocked down trees. The Bureau of Meteorology said the region recorded wind gusts of up to 98km/h. Ulladulla mother Wishaya La Spina was in her car with her baby when she saw the tornado hit about 1pm. A tornado swept through Ulladulla on Saturday Wishaya La Spina “It was already storming, but nothing too severe. Then the wind just started to pick up and the next minute we spotted that little tornado,” she said. She whipped her phone out to film, feeling helpless and unsure if she should stay in the car or flee.



“It was pretty scary,” said La Spina, whose baby was crying. “I was trying to protect him because you never know when a tree could come falling,” she said. The Bureau of Meteorology issued a severe thunderstorm and damaging wind gusts warning for central and south-eastern parts of the state, including Sydney, Wollongong, Katoomba, Penrith, Parramatta and Bowral. The SES recorded more than 230 calls for assistance across the state, most of which were located in Ulladulla. Double rainbows are seen at Sydney Olympic Park. George Chan
