World.title: Path to ruin: How Victoria’s mental health watchdog was stripped of its power
World.content:
Months later, in December 2025, an act of parliament was introduced to remove the four independent commissioners, sold as a cost-saving measure.

The MHWC’s former commissioners and senior executives drafted a scathing opinion piece, in June 2025, as part of a plan to go public about their diminishing independence and fears the government was turning its back on the royal commission recommendations, but did not follow through.

The commission was also blocked from accessing vital data by the Department of Health and did not act on concerns of excessive emergency department wait times for the mentally ill, or that health service administrators may be siphoning off mental health funds to prop up other areas of their struggling hospitals.

The hundreds of pages reveal the watchdog’s roles and powers have been so extensively undermined, it cannot investigate systemic issues such as whether there are enough new mental health beds for young people, whether restraints are being illegally used, patients being discharged into homelessness, or whether poor pay is contributing to a mental health workforce crisis.

Internal Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission documents, seen by The Age , detail how it was weakened to the extent it can no longer effectively monitor the sector or track the state government’s promised reforms – the two roles it was mandated to perform.

As Victoria’s new mental health commissioner starts in her job, the records show she will be inheriting a watchdog demanded by the royal commission that has been progressively diluted over the past 18 months.

A trove of leaked documents reveal how the state’s mental health watchdog was put on a path to ruin by the state government, with its powers, budget, staff and independence slashed to such an extent it could barely perform its safeguarding and oversight roles.

Official notes from that meeting detail discussions that would be typical for the organisation. A planning day for its lived experience team, a meeting with the Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service, and Victoria Police raising concerns that it did not have funding to train recruits in how to cope with mental health callouts.

When MHWC executives gathered for a commissioners’ governance meeting on February 20, 2025, there was no hint of the carnage that would soon befall the watchdog, the mental health system and, most importantly, the Victorians who need it.

The Department of Health said the MHWC remained independent and a critical part of Victoria’s mental health oversight framework.

When contacted by The Age about the reduction of its powers, budget and staff as detailed in its confidential documents, the commission stated it had upheld its independence and was focused on its role as it “navigated a period of significant organisational and governance change”.

Victoria’s new mental health commissioner Jennifer Black started her role on September 29, after being the NSW mental health commissioner for the past two years.

Health Minister Ingrid Stitt appointed a single commissioner in their place. Former NSW mental health commissioner Jennifer Black took up the role from September 29 – but with only half the staff and budget that the watchdog had a year earlier, and with a greatly reduced mandate to hold the government to account.

“The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission has been advised by the Department of Health that it will receive drastically reduced funding in the next financial year and that plans are afoot to change the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act which will reduce and reshape the role of the commission,” the MHWC executives heard.

But when the commissioners met on June 12, 2025, everything had changed, and recruitment was now the last thing being discussed.

There were no obvious alarm bells. The executives were so confident about the budget that the meeting moved on to a discussion about salary modelling in light of a mid-year recruitment drive.

The commission was told “the process was cabinet in confidence and was not given an indication of what was to come”.

An Instagram post from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission on April 28, 2026 – the day an act of parliament eliminated the role of the commissioners.

There was also a short update to let everyone know the mental health commission had submitted its 2025-26 budget bid, and that it was seeking a copy of the government’s final budget to see what it would receive.

The department told McKenzie that, despite the cuts, they still expected the commission to hold the government to account on progress with the royal commission.

To stem the bleeding, chief executive Simon McKenzie suggested to the Department of Health that senior leaders could work below full-time to provide savings.

By the middle of July, the commission learned its operating budget had been cut in half – from $9.93 million in 2024-25 to $4,761,000.

The MHWC had been so blindsided that it noted that the government “did not outline why it was making the changes” and planned to clarify to the public, via the media, that they were not engaged or included in any of these decisions.

“The government appears to have scrapped two elements of this central reform agenda – regional boards and the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission operating as outlined in the royal commission,” the June meeting heard.

Although details were limited, the MHWC already believed their role as a watchdog was being limited just 18 months after they had been established. They aired views that, through its mottled changes, the government was shifting power back to the department, which represented “a significant change from the intent of the royal commission”.

As part of this, the organisation’s four commissioners would be pared back to just one.

But month after month, the watchdog’s concerns grew that the department was refusing to hand over the data it needed to see what was happening inside mental health services, or whether the promised reforms were being implemented.

By law, the MHWC is required to monitor and report on the quality, safety and performance of Victoria’s mental health system.

By this time, the MHWC’s total staff had fallen from 43.9 full-time roles to 27.19. Those who remained had been relocated to share an office with the Health Complaints Commission, prompting privacy concerns over the discussion of highly sensitive information.

As of January 2, 2026, there were no staff in the System, Performance and Monitoring Team whose main role entailed tracking big-picture problems and assessing how Victoria was performing against its royal commission targets.

If the chief executive believed them in July, briefing documents show that by the end of 2025, the watchdog’s senior leadership was deeply worried that its key purpose was being wound back.

It labelled the department’s obstruction as “hurdles”, though they had huge consequences.

Information the watchdog struggled to access included basic details on the number of mental health patients admitted to beds or attending emergency departments, right up to safety data detailing how many patients were being subjected to bodily restraints, compulsory treatment orders or violent attacks.

While trying to prepare its annual report in June 2025, the MHWC’s governance committee raised the issue of the department withholding vital information.

“We note that the Draft Information Sharing Agreement as provided by the Department omitted critical information that the commission requested within the data-sharing schedule, and which is required to fulfil our functions. The commission is therefore seeking these data outside of the information-sharing agreement to facilitate timely extraction and provision of this information.”

The June meeting resolved to remind the department of its obligation to hand over the data, including spelling out the relevant sections of the law demanding it “provide reasonable assistance to the Commission” and that “the Commission may collect data and information from the Department in order to perform its functions”.

It also reminded the department it was a signatory to the Victorian Public Sector Data Sharing Heads of Agreement, and requested information about mental health patients be provided within 14 days, and details of the royal commission recommendation implementation to be handed over within five days of the end of the financial year.

By August, the governance committee reported its “assertive approach” of referencing the legal obligations had seen an improved turnaround by the department, though there were concerns the resulting data would not present an accurate picture, nor would it allow it to cover the entire 2024-2025 year in its annual report.

In December, the MHWC was denied access to data on the promised mental health system reforms while trying to complete its report into the government’s implementation of the royal commission recommendations.

But there was one massive hurdle the commission refused to jump.

In exchange for access to the data, the department asked the commission to sign a secret data-sharing agreement that included terms that would effectively remove the watchdog’s ability to independently hold the government to account.

The terms, seen by The Age, would have handed the department a right to review the way the mental health commission used its data, as well as the right to review any of its reports before publication.

It also demanded the right to seek advice on any “analytical risks” associated with use of its data.

The commission refused to sign up to the agreement, citing concerns for its independence, prompting the department in December to block its access to the data needed to perform its legislated oversight role.

“Have also been advised that despite words of assurance to protect data, it will not be shared unless there is a data-sharing agreement in place,” the MHWC heard in December.

“The department cited that the decision from the MHWC to pause progression of the data-sharing agreement without acknowledging the various hurdles/difficulties presented by the department, which influenced the decision to put it on hold,” the MHWC’s December meeting heard.

Rather than cede its independence, the MHWC decided to “do the best we can” with whatever information was already publicly available, while calling out the department’s obstruction in its report.

“Agreement that, based on the previous year, if expectations and timelines have not been met, to not let the department off the hook and communicate to the public that the MHWC will endeavour to report on anything that doesn’t meet the annual report submission requirements.”

However, the withholding of information may not even be the most concerning aspect of the department’s handling of mental health data to emerge from the documents.

Confidential information provided by the department’s executive director of governance and accountability reveals it does not even record data on the number of violent incidents occurring in its mental health units, nor the number of patients dying of suicide while being treated.

Warnings not delivered

Commissioners, executives and MHWC staff uncovered a host of serious failings and issues directly harming mental health patients while conducting a series of visits inside the state’s mental health units.

A report outlining those “pressing issues”, detected in 14 visits to mental health services across the state during 2024 and 2025, was presented to the MHWC’s leaders on August 5, 2025.

A clinical en suite door from the Swanston Centre in Geelong, which cannot be locked but is all that separates patients in the acute psychiatric ward.

It detailed critical staff shortages in mental health units that were up to five times higher than in other departments at the same hospitals, inconsistent documentation on patients being restrained, discrimination faced by lived experience workers, and challenges for mental health patients in emergency departments.

The report also raised concerns that features, including shared bedrooms and bathrooms, continued to be an issue at some “outdated facilities”, where infrastructure improvements had not been undertaken.

Seven months later, on February 22, 2026 – while the report and the concerns it raised had still not been made public – Michael McKeown was found dead inside his acute room in Geelong’s Swanston Centre, which was joined to the room of Joel Steinbock, who has since been charged with his murder.

The MHWC’s service visit report was eventually published, but not until July 7, 2026 – 11 months after being presented to the executive meeting, and more than four months after McKeown’s death.

While the published report continued to flag concerns over the transparency of funding and the sustainability of the royal commission reforms, additional allegations that mental health dollars were being misappropriated, which were contained in the August version, had been removed.

“Some services reported that mental health funding was being diverted to support sub-acute care, undermining the original intent of the reforms,” the August report had stated.

Later, the watchdog also privately flagged its need to investigate systemic issues harming mental health patients in emergency departments, though there is no evidence it followed through.

The MHWC’s January 29, 2026, governance meeting raised systemic issues stemming from prolonged emergency department stays. The meeting heard its investigators had two reports available, and the attendees detailed the legal provisions that gave the watchdog jurisdiction to launch an own-motion investigation into the issue.

At that time, 20 of the state’s 21 adult mental health units were failing to meet their target for admitting acutely mentally unwell Victorians to a bed within eight hours, and a host of leading medical groups were pushing for action amid grave fears for their patients.

While discussing their need to investigate, members of the MHWC executive suggested they meet with the deputy president of Australian College of Emergency Medicine to gain background and data on the issue.

However, there has since been no evidence of any investigation having been undertaken by the MHWC despite its January discussion. When asked by The Age, the College of Emergency Medicine said it had never been contacted by the mental health commission, and that it did not even have a position of deputy president.

Backed by more than five leading medical groups and unions, The Age this month revealed the extent of issues for mental health patients in emergency departments. When asked this month whether it was investigating the emergency department issues, the MHWC initially stated it did not have relevant information to discuss, and later confirmed it had received complaints – but pointed to an ongoing examination by the Victorian Auditor General’s Office, rather than any work it was undertaking.

Blowing the whistle

After learning it was set to lose its budget and remit, the MHWC in June 2025 developed a communications plan to blow the whistle on the government “walking away” from its royal commission commitments.

It planned a stinging rebuke that would inform the public of the government’s intent to centralise power back with the Department of Health in contravention of the royal commission’s findings.

Former Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission chair Treasure Jennings. Paul Jeffers

Presented at the commission’s June 12, 2025, governance meeting, a communication plan was hatched outlining the importance of getting on the front foot with public and stakeholder messaging before the changes were imposed.

One of the main objectives was the need to make it clear the MHWC was not involved in, or even consulted about, the decisions that would water down its functions and composition.

Its proposed key messages were blunt:

“These changes represent a significant change from the intent of the royal commission – to shift power away from a central government department to involve lived experience voices in decision-making.

“As the oversight authority – highlight the government is walking away from the RC [royal commission] to decentralise control of the system and operate a new system of governance.”

The commissioners and executives discussed plans to let the public know the MHWC’s funding had been “drastically reduced”, but that the government had not outlined why.

Its resolve even saw the MHWC draft an opinion piece, penned in the name of then-chief commissioner Treasure Jennings, which informed Victorians the government was stripping the watchdog of the powers it needed to hold them to account.

“Now it appears the government has decided to refocus the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission away from system oversight and more toward service oversight and complaint-handling,” Jennings’ unpublished op-ed said.

“If government is stepping away from the central mechanisms for enabling reform, however, there needs to be openness and transparency regarding the Mental Health levy and how it is used. We encourage the government to provide details.”

Two days after discussing its plan to speak out, a June 14 front page article in The Age revealed the watchdog’s “drastic” budget cuts and Jennings’ warning that the MHWC may be rendered unable to hold the government to account for the performance of the health system.

Jennings’ comments, however, did not extend to warning the public that the government was walking away from the wider mental health reforms it had promised.

The state government provided The Age information for that article stating the commission would get $5.97 million in funding for 2025-26 – a 40 per cent cut.

But when the MHWC met again for a “Budget Reprioritisation Meeting” on June 24, it had received confidential news that was even worse than the government had led it, and the public, to believe.

“DH shared that a letter (‘the Letter’) from the minister is expected to be shared shortly [with] the commissioners which will provide the MHWC’s Budget and Ministerial Directions. The budget reported in The Age is not the figure that will be communicated in ‘the Letter’. It is less than the reported figure,” the June 24 meeting was told.

After digesting the full scale of the cuts, the MHWC’s governance team in August debated another communications strategy. Its goal was how “best to illustrate the lack of support received from the department to perform our role/functions”.

Victoria’s new mental health commissioner Jennifer Black. Kate Geraghty

As well as highlighting that its modest funding would not meet the expectations of the royal commission, the MHWC wanted to highlight the government’s retreat from the lived-experience commitments at the heart of the reforms.

“It is likely that if we ask ‘why’ the department will provide a standard response. The philosophy should be ‘what is next?’ If the government is stepping away from the RC recommendations, there should be transparency about this and ‘what is next’.”

It’s a question the new commissioner, Jennifer Black, will now have to turn her mind to alone.

World.title: I visited one of the world’s great cities for eight hours and loved every minute
World.content:
Reviews & adviceEurope Opinion I visited one of the world’s great cities for eight hours and loved every minute Ben Groundwater Travel writer October 4, 2026 — 12:00am

October 4, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The clock is ticking. Barcelona, in eight hours. It’s a laughable challenge in many ways, clearly impossible. How could anyone feel they’ve adequately “done” an entire city, one of the world’s greats, in the time it takes to get through a single workday? But sometimes this is all you have. Your cruise ship arrives, it deposits everyone onto the dock, and at some point in the evening you will all pile back on again and depart. The Church of La Sagrada Familia, designed by Catalan architect Antoni Gaudi, is undoubtedly a Barcelona highlight. iStock So how can you feel you’ve experienced a place in such a short time? How can you enjoy yourself, while also coming to know a city and its culture and its heart, and maybe even checking off a few big-ticket items, in the space of eight hours? First piece of advice: do not, under any circumstances, attempt to do it all. You just can’t. Even attempting to do a lot of things will be a nightmare, an unenjoyable rush from one place to the next, with no time to take any of it in.



You could look at Barcelona and think: OK, I have to do all the Gaudi stuff. La Sagrada Familia, up to Park Guell, call past Casa Batllo. Whip through the Picasso Museum, walk around the Gothic Quarter, eat tapas for lunch, stroll Las Ramblas, have a dip at the beach in Barceloneta, ride the cable car across to Montjuic, take the Teleferico (another, more modern cable car) to the top of the mountain at sunset, jump in a taxi and be back at the port in time for the ship’s departure. 



The way to do that is to decide on your priorities, and this will be entirely personal. What brings you joy? Is it art, food, architecture, people, the opportunity to learn, the chance to wander aimlessly and see what you stumble upon? All of these will determine your final itinerary. You’ve only got eight hours, this is no time to be doing things just because you believe you should. Do it because you love it. So here’s how I would spend eight hours in Barcelona. Straight off the ship and over to La Sagrada Familia, Antoni Gaudí’s masterpiece. Book tickets well in advance, get there early before the bulk of the crowds arrive, take some photos from outside and then have a good hour or two inside to look around. From there I would take the metro to Passeig de Gracia, a point at which Barcelona splits into some of its most interesting and enjoyable neighbourhoods: the Gothic Quarter, El Born, Raval and L’Eixample. This is the ideal area to explore on foot, to just wander and see where it takes you, to call in for coffee somewhere that looks nice, check out a few shops, stroll with no agenda.



And then have lunch. This is a key area of interest of mine, and it’s also a lovingly observed ritual in Spain, so I’m reserving, frankly, a silly amount of time for lunch. We’re talking three hours here: sit down, relax, take it slow. Related Article Cruises Twelve of the most incredible experiences you can do from a cruise ship This is the key, I think, to exploration of this limited style. It’s far better to do a few things well than to do many things poorly. Part of the joy of a city, for me, is having the space to just sit or wander and take it all in. The chef and travel-show host Rick Stein calls it “mooching around”, the act of forgoing famous attractions and formal tourist behaviour in favour of doing very little for a while, just sitting in the sun with a beer or drinking a coffee and reading a book. The clock might be ticking but the idea of this sort of travel is to ignore that clock, to just forget about it for a while, pretend it doesn’t exist and enjoy yourself.



And so I’m off to El Xampanyet, an old-school tapas bar in El Born, with tiled walls and old wine bottles lining the shelves. I’ll drink vermouth and eat anchovies and watch as the crowd ebbs and flows and the day creeps by. Hours and hours well spent. The Picasso Museum is close, so that could be worth a wander later. Or maybe I’ll have a drink somewhere else, or walk narrow streets, or check out Santa Caterina Market before it’s time to head back to the ship. Barcelona, experienced and understood. I couldn’t be happier.

World.title: Jim in Japan: Treasurer to sell Australia as a safe bet in two-day Tokyo blitz
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalForeign investment Jim in Japan: Treasurer to sell Australia as a safe bet in two-day Tokyo blitz Nick Newling October 3, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers will hold a series of high-level meetings with Japanese investors and business leaders in Tokyo this week, as the government attempts to sell Australia as a safe harbour for middle-power investment amid an increasingly uncertain global economy. The Labor minister will market Australia as a renewable energy powerhouse and artificial intelligence leader, and highlight the $4.8 trillion superannuation system as a “deep pool” of capital, while also chairing a housing roundtable with leaders in Japanese residential development. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will make Tokyo his first stop in a three-country tour of Asia this month. Dominic Lorrimer “If investors want to make the most of the defining decade ahead, nowhere offers more opportunities than Australia. We’re making Australia an indispensable part of the transformation underway in the global economy, and we’re telling the world’s investors why they need a piece of the action,” Chalmers told this masthead. The trip comes after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last month used an address to the United Nations to declare the post-1945 international order “no longer fit for purpose”, forcing middle powers such as Australia to build new partnerships while defending the international rules-based order.



Albanese’s comments echoed those of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who in a historic rallying cry to the Australian parliament in March called for middle powers to unite or face subordination to bigger nations. During the two-day blitz, Chalmers is set to meet more than 30 CEOs, business leaders and investors from Japan’s largest firms, offering a five-pillared pitch of Australia’s “unique” investment advantages. The Treasurer will meet with Kenichi Hori, head of Mitsui & Co., one of Japan’s largest conglomerates and Juro Baba, executive vice president of Mitsubishi Corporation. Chalmers will pitch Australia as a resource leader for green energy and critical minerals, arguing that domestic renewable electricity production will be able to compete with traditional hubs such as the Middle East and Russia by 2050. The focus on Australia’s reliability and resources comes amid a time of tumult for the two nations, after the unveiling of a domestic gas reservation policy that rattled Japan as the primary importer of Australian gas. Australia provides around 40 per cent of Japan’s LNG, which supports a significant portion of the country’s energy generation.



Following the policy’s announcement, officials from Japan, South Korea and Malaysia – major consumers of Australian LNG – lodged appeals through the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade seeking certainty over contract protections. A modified version of the reservation plan to take effect from January 2028 will require liquefied natural gas shippers face a requirement to reserve up to 20 per cent of their export volumes for local customers. The policy is designed to force a 10 per cent domestic oversupply each year to push down the cost of the fuel. The policy has since been softened to ensure the oversupply is “modest”, quelling concerns from Asian trading partners. Albanese was also caught in a faux pas after his appearance on a podcast in which he joked about melons gifted to him by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The Japanese embassy in Australia later downplayed the incident, and the leaders posed for a picture together last month at the United Nations.



Part of Chalmers’ pitch in Japan will highlight the stable investment capacity of the nation’s superannuation pool, and Australia’s embrace of artificial intelligence and data centres. Related Article Opinion

Federal budget The world is changing rapidly. Albanese needs to follow suit Peter Hartcher Political and international editor “This is all about boosting investment in Australia, bolstering supply chains and economic resilience, and strengthening our relationships in Asia. As a reliable, responsible middle power with strong economic foundations and huge advantages in areas like energy, AI and critical minerals, Australia is an attractive investment destination,” Chalmers said. “Whether it’s our resources or renewable energy, our skills or our stability, Australia has exactly what the world needs when the world needs it.” Alongside meetings with counterparts and business leaders, Chalmers will host two roundtables on Monday. The first will take in investors and asset managers from Japan and Australia, while the second will focus on residential development including novel construction methods that could support increased supply in Australia.



The trip to Japan will be the first of three stops the Treasurer will make this month in Asia, ahead of a trip to Bangkok to meet with G20 finance ministers on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings. Chalmers will also meet with Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation counterparts in Hong Kong. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Ten people injured, P-plater charged after car crashes into Newcastle Knights fans
World.content:
A five-year-old girl was left fighting for her life and nine others were injured when a teenage P-plate driver allegedly lost control of his car and careered into jubilant crowds lining a Newcastle street to wave the Knights off to the NRL grand final. One of the injured, Chris Clancy, said the car appeared to speed up as it went through a roundabout, and then lost control on the wet road. “No-one had time to move,” he said. “I thought I was going to die, it happened so fast.” Fans at the crash site rushed to provide first aid as emergency crews rushed to the scene and word of the collision spread through the tens of thousands of excited fans waiting for a glimpse of their team. The team’s bus, which had not yet departed when the crash occurred, was rerouted, and players were informed. Loading “They were shocked, it was a very sombre bus ride,” said one of those aboard. “Our fans mean everything to us. For that to happen; horrible.”



The five-year-old girl was in a critical but stable condition in John Hunter Hospital on Saturday evening. A 67-year-old patient was in a serious but stable condition, and four others, including a 2-year-old and a 5-year-old girl, were stable. Four had been discharged, including three men in their 20s and a 63-year-old woman. Police arrested the 18-year-old driver, Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, at the crash site and took him for mandatory drug and alcohol testing. He was later released from hospital and taken to a police station where he was charged with three counts each of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and causing bodily harm by misconduct in charge of a motor vehicle. He was refused police bail to face a court on Sunday. Samarasinghe’s licence has also been suspended, and the vehicle he was allegedly driving has been seized to undergo forensic examination. The two male passengers in the vehicle at the time of the crash, aged 18 and 19, were both uninjured. NSW Police Assistant Commissioner David Waddell said officers were investigating reports the P-plater had been “driving erratically” before he lost control of the vehicle. Footage posted to social media depicted the BMW careering around the roundabout moments before the crash, as shocked onlookers were heard screaming.



The crash scene. TNV Scenes at Wallsend, Newcastle, after a car crashed into a crowd of Knights supporters. Onlookers expressed anger towards the occupants of the car after the crash, police said. “We had to get the three of them out of there because the crowd did turn on them,” Waddell said. Witness Dean Liddell said he could hear the vehicle coming towards the crowd and then “all hell broke loose”. “I watched the little girl get dragged underneath the car. Seeing the whole scene unfold, it took me 10 minutes until I could say anything to anyone,” Liddell said.



He said the crowd grabbed the driver from the wreck and a scuffle began before police intervened. “If the copper wasn’t there, the driver would have had massive injuries as well,” he said. The accident came after a joyous week in Newcastle, where the city threw its support behind a team that has not won a premiership for 25 years. The Knights had been expected to be inspired by the joy of their supporters during the grand final, but will now also feel the weight of the tragedy when they take the field. Newcastle Knights captain Kalyn Ponga said on social media that players’ “hearts are with everyone affected” by the crash. “We’re thinking of you, your families and everyone in our Newcastle community.” Longtime league watchers say no other grand final has been played under such a shadow.



“It’s heartbreaking for the whole rugby league community, not just in Newcastle,” said Brad Fittler, a former Roosters captain and a member of the league hall of fame. “We’ve never seen anything like this ahead of a grand final and it puts everything in perspective.” Australian Rugby League Commission executive chairman Peter V’Landys said he was deeply saddened by the crash. When asked whether it would affect plans for Sunday night’s game, he said “we’re just concerned about the victims at the moment.” Paramedics prepare to transport the injured by helicopter. Sitthixay Ditthavong NSW Premier Chris Minns said it was heartbreaking to see fans who were sending off their grand final team involved in such a terrible incident. “My thoughts are with the families and friends of loved ones who have been involved or injured in the crash. I also want to thank emergency services, including police and ambulance, who are responding to this tragedy”, the premier said.



“We’ve seen how this grand final has brought the Newcastle together, and I hope the whole community remains united as we continue to respond.” Newcastle Lord Mayor Gavin Morris said that, before Saturday’s crash, the lead-up to the grand final had been one of the “most incredibly joyous weeks in our city”. “It’s a tragedy. It’s something that we can’t take back,” Morris said. Morris said that passing vehicles were “revving up the crowd” as they drove past thousands of Knights fans lining the roadside before the crash.



“That just should not have been occurring, but it has,” he said. Asked whether bollards or fencing should have been installed at the roadside to protect fans, Morris said securing the 20-kilometre stretch of road between the Knights’ home ground and the crash site was “almost an impossible task”. The injured Clancy said a police vehicle was stationed near the crash site and responded quickly. He said the car came at the group of supporters too fast for them to jump out of the way. He was hit by the front of the vehicle. Knights fan Jed Partridge, 29, who arrived at 8.20am to join thousands of others in waving off the team bus, was among fans who watched the celebration turn to shock. “We were on the side of the road, just waiting. Everyone was happy, and then there was a real flurry of cop cars, ambos and rescue cars shooting past.” He said word soon filtered out that there had been a serious crash. “It was eerie … such a positive thing could quickly turn to this. It’s hard to wrap your head around.”



Fans urged the Knights to press forward and do their best on Sunday night. “It will be tough for them, but do what they’ve always done and do it for the town,” said Clancy. “I believe they can win. Regardless of whether they win or lose, they’ve done the town proud.” Loading Newcastle Knights fans gathered to send off their team. Nine Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ‘It was crazy’: Tornado sweeps through Ulladulla as severe storms hit Sydney
World.content:
Updated EnvironmentWeatherExtreme weather ‘It was crazy’: Tornado sweeps through Ulladulla as severe storms hit Sydney Emily Kowal Updated October 3, 2026 — 8:05pm ,first published 4:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A tornado swept through Ulladulla on the NSW South Coast on Saturday, shocking residents, knocking down trees and damaging buildings, as intense rain, flash floods and winds lashed Sydney. Greater Sydney and the CBD were struck by severe thunderstorms about 5pm on Saturday, with wind gusts reaching up to 72km/h in Sydney Harbour and up to 30 millimetres of rain falling in less than half an hour, triggering flash flooding in parts of the city. Houses were damaged by the tornado in Ulladulla. Brad Collins The State Emergency Service rescued two people from cars in floodwaters in Moore Park and Darlinghurst. In Edgecliff, vehicles were stuck in water as flash floods covered the street, while in Merrylands a tree was struck by lightning.



The tornado that ripped through Ulladulla tore roofs off homes and knocked down trees. The Bureau of Meteorology said the region recorded wind gusts of up to 98km/h. Ulladulla mother Wishaya La Spina was in her car with her baby when she saw the tornado hit about 1pm. A tornado swept through Ulladulla on Saturday Wishaya La Spina “It was already storming, but nothing too severe. Then the wind just started to pick up and the next minute we spotted that little tornado,” she said. She whipped her phone out to film, feeling helpless and unsure if she should stay in the car or flee.



“It was pretty scary,” said La Spina, whose baby was crying. “I was trying to protect him because you never know when a tree could come falling,” she said. The Bureau of Meteorology issued a severe thunderstorm and damaging wind gusts warning for central and south-eastern parts of the state, including Sydney, Wollongong, Katoomba, Penrith, Parramatta and Bowral. The SES recorded more than 230 calls for assistance across the state, most of which were located in Ulladulla. Double rainbows are seen at Sydney Olympic Park. George Chan

World.title: Doctors on strike not the answer to health system’s problems
World.content:
Photo: Matt Golding

To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published.

Striking not the answer

Working in a busy public hospital emergency department was the most challenging, stressful part of my now-retired medical career. There was never enough time to deliver the depth of care I wanted, and the constant fear of missing an important diagnosis weighed heavily. I immensely admire those who make emergency their lifelong career; a few months was enough for me.

However, I was disappointed by hospital doctors striking for higher pay, although they certainly deserve it. While I understand the strain doctors face, striking for pay increases won’t solve the underlying crisis. What emergency departments urgently need is more doctors and nurses on the floor to ease the pressure, reduce burnout, and give patients the comprehensive, attentive care they deserve.

Dr Harley Powell, Elsternwick

It’s tulip time

I’m very confused about the anxiety in relation to house prices. For years we’ve been inundated with headlines like “The Australian dream is over”, “Housing is increasingly unaffordable” and “GenZ will be lifetime renters”.

Now it appears that house prices are finally falling a bit, and therefore becoming slightly more affordable, but this also is a cause for concern. But for whom are falling house prices a problem? Not for people, like me who own one house that they live in; if I sell my house at a time of falling house prices, I will also buy my new house at a time of falling prices – the result is more or less a zero-sum game. And not for first home buyers who will need a smaller mortgage.

The only people who are negatively impacted are investors who view housing as a means to build their wealth by relying on increasing prices and tax breaks. I’m sure some people will be worse off, but that is the nature of investments – not everyone is a winner – just ask the Dutch investors who bought into the ″⁣tulip mania″⁣ of 1634-1637.

Vera Boston, Fitzroy North

The housing divide

Your correspondent (Letters, 2/10) acknowledges the people who are doing it tough but also comments on those who are still able to spend on wants as opposed to needs. Housing affordability is impacted when interest rates rise. One cohort of people it doesn’t seem to have repercussions for, are those who buy houses to be pulled down and replaced with more expensive houses.

The land value on its own, then becomes what the house and land together were sold for. The vendor price represents the home that the owners are about to vacate. A house that served a family well. With knock down and rebuild, the overall property value increases and influences the surrounding property values. Affordability of what once was a modest suburb is now out of reach for those with reduced economic resources.

Your correspondent’s observations raise the question as to why there is a discrepancy between the relaxed spending for some during difficult times, at the same time as a capacity to knock down and build luxurious houses, while others struggle to pay rent and the supermarket bill. Are interest rates the only economic influence contributing to the social divide?

Cathie Hutchinson, Mulgrave

World.title: Path to ruin: How Victoria’s mental health watchdog was stripped of its power
World.content:
Months later, in December 2025, an act of parliament was introduced to remove the four independent commissioners, sold as a cost-saving measure.

The MHWC’s former commissioners and senior executives drafted a scathing opinion piece, in June 2025, as part of a plan to go public about their diminishing independence and fears the government was turning its back on the royal commission recommendations, but did not follow through.

The commission was also blocked from accessing vital data by the Department of Health and did not act on concerns of excessive emergency department wait times for the mentally ill, or that health service administrators may be siphoning off mental health funds to prop up other areas of their struggling hospitals.

The hundreds of pages reveal the watchdog’s roles and powers have been so extensively undermined, it cannot investigate systemic issues such as whether there are enough new mental health beds for young people, whether restraints are being illegally used, patients being discharged into homelessness, or whether poor pay is contributing to a mental health workforce crisis.

Internal Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission documents, seen by The Age , detail how it was weakened to the extent it can no longer effectively monitor the sector or track the state government’s promised reforms – the two roles it was mandated to perform.

As Victoria’s new mental health commissioner starts in her job, the records show she will be inheriting a watchdog demanded by the royal commission that has been progressively diluted over the past 18 months.

A trove of leaked documents reveal how the state’s mental health watchdog was put on a path to ruin by the state government, with its powers, budget, staff and independence slashed to such an extent it could barely perform its safeguarding and oversight roles.

Official notes from that meeting detail discussions that would be typical for the organisation. A planning day for its lived experience team, a meeting with the Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service, and Victoria Police raising concerns that it did not have funding to train recruits in how to cope with mental health callouts.

When MHWC executives gathered for a commissioners’ governance meeting on February 20, 2025, there was no hint of the carnage that would soon befall the watchdog, the mental health system and, most importantly, the Victorians who need it.

The Department of Health said the MHWC remained independent and a critical part of Victoria’s mental health oversight framework.

When contacted by The Age about the reduction of its powers, budget and staff as detailed in its confidential documents, the commission stated it had upheld its independence and was focused on its role as it “navigated a period of significant organisational and governance change”.

Victoria’s new mental health commissioner Jennifer Black started her role on September 29, after being the NSW mental health commissioner for the past two years.

Health Minister Ingrid Stitt appointed a single commissioner in their place. Former NSW mental health commissioner Jennifer Black took up the role from September 29 – but with only half the staff and budget that the watchdog had a year earlier, and with a greatly reduced mandate to hold the government to account.

“The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission has been advised by the Department of Health that it will receive drastically reduced funding in the next financial year and that plans are afoot to change the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act which will reduce and reshape the role of the commission,” the MHWC executives heard.

But when the commissioners met on June 12, 2025, everything had changed, and recruitment was now the last thing being discussed.

There were no obvious alarm bells. The executives were so confident about the budget that the meeting moved on to a discussion about salary modelling in light of a mid-year recruitment drive.

The commission was told “the process was cabinet in confidence and was not given an indication of what was to come”.

An Instagram post from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission on April 28, 2026 – the day an act of parliament eliminated the role of the commissioners.

There was also a short update to let everyone know the mental health commission had submitted its 2025-26 budget bid, and that it was seeking a copy of the government’s final budget to see what it would receive.

The department told McKenzie that, despite the cuts, they still expected the commission to hold the government to account on progress with the royal commission.

To stem the bleeding, chief executive Simon McKenzie suggested to the Department of Health that senior leaders could work below full-time to provide savings.

By the middle of July, the commission learned its operating budget had been cut in half – from $9.93 million in 2024-25 to $4,761,000.

The MHWC had been so blindsided that it noted that the government “did not outline why it was making the changes” and planned to clarify to the public, via the media, that they were not engaged or included in any of these decisions.

“The government appears to have scrapped two elements of this central reform agenda – regional boards and the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission operating as outlined in the royal commission,” the June meeting heard.

Although details were limited, the MHWC already believed their role as a watchdog was being limited just 18 months after they had been established. They aired views that, through its mottled changes, the government was shifting power back to the department, which represented “a significant change from the intent of the royal commission”.

As part of this, the organisation’s four commissioners would be pared back to just one.

But month after month, the watchdog’s concerns grew that the department was refusing to hand over the data it needed to see what was happening inside mental health services, or whether the promised reforms were being implemented.

By law, the MHWC is required to monitor and report on the quality, safety and performance of Victoria’s mental health system.

By this time, the MHWC’s total staff had fallen from 43.9 full-time roles to 27.19. Those who remained had been relocated to share an office with the Health Complaints Commission, prompting privacy concerns over the discussion of highly sensitive information.

As of January 2, 2026, there were no staff in the System, Performance and Monitoring Team whose main role entailed tracking big-picture problems and assessing how Victoria was performing against its royal commission targets.

If the chief executive believed them in July, briefing documents show that by the end of 2025, the watchdog’s senior leadership was deeply worried that its key purpose was being wound back.

It labelled the department’s obstruction as “hurdles”, though they had huge consequences.

Information the watchdog struggled to access included basic details on the number of mental health patients admitted to beds or attending emergency departments, right up to safety data detailing how many patients were being subjected to bodily restraints, compulsory treatment orders or violent attacks.

While trying to prepare its annual report in June 2025, the MHWC’s governance committee raised the issue of the department withholding vital information.

“We note that the Draft Information Sharing Agreement as provided by the Department omitted critical information that the commission requested within the data-sharing schedule, and which is required to fulfil our functions. The commission is therefore seeking these data outside of the information-sharing agreement to facilitate timely extraction and provision of this information.”

The June meeting resolved to remind the department of its obligation to hand over the data, including spelling out the relevant sections of the law demanding it “provide reasonable assistance to the Commission” and that “the Commission may collect data and information from the Department in order to perform its functions”.

It also reminded the department it was a signatory to the Victorian Public Sector Data Sharing Heads of Agreement, and requested information about mental health patients be provided within 14 days, and details of the royal commission recommendation implementation to be handed over within five days of the end of the financial year.

By August, the governance committee reported its “assertive approach” of referencing the legal obligations had seen an improved turnaround by the department, though there were concerns the resulting data would not present an accurate picture, nor would it allow it to cover the entire 2024-2025 year in its annual report.

In December, the MHWC was denied access to data on the promised mental health system reforms while trying to complete its report into the government’s implementation of the royal commission recommendations.

But there was one massive hurdle the commission refused to jump.

In exchange for access to the data, the department asked the commission to sign a secret data-sharing agreement that included terms that would effectively remove the watchdog’s ability to independently hold the government to account.

The terms, seen by The Age, would have handed the department a right to review the way the mental health commission used its data, as well as the right to review any of its reports before publication.

It also demanded the right to seek advice on any “analytical risks” associated with use of its data.

The commission refused to sign up to the agreement, citing concerns for its independence, prompting the department in December to block its access to the data needed to perform its legislated oversight role.

“Have also been advised that despite words of assurance to protect data, it will not be shared unless there is a data-sharing agreement in place,” the MHWC heard in December.

“The department cited that the decision from the MHWC to pause progression of the data-sharing agreement without acknowledging the various hurdles/difficulties presented by the department, which influenced the decision to put it on hold,” the MHWC’s December meeting heard.

Rather than cede its independence, the MHWC decided to “do the best we can” with whatever information was already publicly available, while calling out the department’s obstruction in its report.

“Agreement that, based on the previous year, if expectations and timelines have not been met, to not let the department off the hook and communicate to the public that the MHWC will endeavour to report on anything that doesn’t meet the annual report submission requirements.”

However, the withholding of information may not even be the most concerning aspect of the department’s handling of mental health data to emerge from the documents.

Confidential information provided by the department’s executive director of governance and accountability reveals it does not even record data on the number of violent incidents occurring in its mental health units, nor the number of patients dying of suicide while being treated.

Warnings not delivered

Commissioners, executives and MHWC staff uncovered a host of serious failings and issues directly harming mental health patients while conducting a series of visits inside the state’s mental health units.

A report outlining those “pressing issues”, detected in 14 visits to mental health services across the state during 2024 and 2025, was presented to the MHWC’s leaders on August 5, 2025.

A clinical en suite door from the Swanston Centre in Geelong, which cannot be locked but is all that separates patients in the acute psychiatric ward.

It detailed critical staff shortages in mental health units that were up to five times higher than in other departments at the same hospitals, inconsistent documentation on patients being restrained, discrimination faced by lived experience workers, and challenges for mental health patients in emergency departments.

The report also raised concerns that features, including shared bedrooms and bathrooms, continued to be an issue at some “outdated facilities”, where infrastructure improvements had not been undertaken.

Seven months later, on February 22, 2026 – while the report and the concerns it raised had still not been made public – Michael McKeown was found dead inside his acute room in Geelong’s Swanston Centre, which was joined to the room of Joel Steinbock, who has since been charged with his murder.

The MHWC’s service visit report was eventually published, but not until July 7, 2026 – 11 months after being presented to the executive meeting, and more than four months after McKeown’s death.

While the published report continued to flag concerns over the transparency of funding and the sustainability of the royal commission reforms, additional allegations that mental health dollars were being misappropriated, which were contained in the August version, had been removed.

“Some services reported that mental health funding was being diverted to support sub-acute care, undermining the original intent of the reforms,” the August report had stated.

Later, the watchdog also privately flagged its need to investigate systemic issues harming mental health patients in emergency departments, though there is no evidence it followed through.

The MHWC’s January 29, 2026, governance meeting raised systemic issues stemming from prolonged emergency department stays. The meeting heard its investigators had two reports available, and the attendees detailed the legal provisions that gave the watchdog jurisdiction to launch an own-motion investigation into the issue.

At that time, 20 of the state’s 21 adult mental health units were failing to meet their target for admitting acutely mentally unwell Victorians to a bed within eight hours, and a host of leading medical groups were pushing for action amid grave fears for their patients.

While discussing their need to investigate, members of the MHWC executive suggested they meet with the deputy president of Australian College of Emergency Medicine to gain background and data on the issue.

However, there has since been no evidence of any investigation having been undertaken by the MHWC despite its January discussion. When asked by The Age, the College of Emergency Medicine said it had never been contacted by the mental health commission, and that it did not even have a position of deputy president.

Backed by more than five leading medical groups and unions, The Age this month revealed the extent of issues for mental health patients in emergency departments. When asked this month whether it was investigating the emergency department issues, the MHWC initially stated it did not have relevant information to discuss, and later confirmed it had received complaints – but pointed to an ongoing examination by the Victorian Auditor General’s Office, rather than any work it was undertaking.

Blowing the whistle

After learning it was set to lose its budget and remit, the MHWC in June 2025 developed a communications plan to blow the whistle on the government “walking away” from its royal commission commitments.

It planned a stinging rebuke that would inform the public of the government’s intent to centralise power back with the Department of Health in contravention of the royal commission’s findings.

Former Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission chair Treasure Jennings. Paul Jeffers

Presented at the commission’s June 12, 2025, governance meeting, a communication plan was hatched outlining the importance of getting on the front foot with public and stakeholder messaging before the changes were imposed.

One of the main objectives was the need to make it clear the MHWC was not involved in, or even consulted about, the decisions that would water down its functions and composition.

Its proposed key messages were blunt:

“These changes represent a significant change from the intent of the royal commission – to shift power away from a central government department to involve lived experience voices in decision-making.

“As the oversight authority – highlight the government is walking away from the RC [royal commission] to decentralise control of the system and operate a new system of governance.”

The commissioners and executives discussed plans to let the public know the MHWC’s funding had been “drastically reduced”, but that the government had not outlined why.

Its resolve even saw the MHWC draft an opinion piece, penned in the name of then-chief commissioner Treasure Jennings, which informed Victorians the government was stripping the watchdog of the powers it needed to hold them to account.

“Now it appears the government has decided to refocus the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission away from system oversight and more toward service oversight and complaint-handling,” Jennings’ unpublished op-ed said.

“If government is stepping away from the central mechanisms for enabling reform, however, there needs to be openness and transparency regarding the Mental Health levy and how it is used. We encourage the government to provide details.”

Two days after discussing its plan to speak out, a June 14 front page article in The Age revealed the watchdog’s “drastic” budget cuts and Jennings’ warning that the MHWC may be rendered unable to hold the government to account for the performance of the health system.

Jennings’ comments, however, did not extend to warning the public that the government was walking away from the wider mental health reforms it had promised.

The state government provided The Age information for that article stating the commission would get $5.97 million in funding for 2025-26 – a 40 per cent cut.

But when the MHWC met again for a “Budget Reprioritisation Meeting” on June 24, it had received confidential news that was even worse than the government had led it, and the public, to believe.

“DH shared that a letter (‘the Letter’) from the minister is expected to be shared shortly [with] the commissioners which will provide the MHWC’s Budget and Ministerial Directions. The budget reported in The Age is not the figure that will be communicated in ‘the Letter’. It is less than the reported figure,” the June 24 meeting was told.

After digesting the full scale of the cuts, the MHWC’s governance team in August debated another communications strategy. Its goal was how “best to illustrate the lack of support received from the department to perform our role/functions”.

Victoria’s new mental health commissioner Jennifer Black. Kate Geraghty

As well as highlighting that its modest funding would not meet the expectations of the royal commission, the MHWC wanted to highlight the government’s retreat from the lived-experience commitments at the heart of the reforms.

“It is likely that if we ask ‘why’ the department will provide a standard response. The philosophy should be ‘what is next?’ If the government is stepping away from the RC recommendations, there should be transparency about this and ‘what is next’.”

It’s a question the new commissioner, Jennifer Black, will now have to turn her mind to alone.

World.title: Whistleblowers offer to aid Education Ministry probe
World.content:
Education Ministry whistleblowers, who contacted RNZ in the past week, plan to add their voices to an investigation by the Office of the Ombudsman.

The investigation was announced after publication of a video showing a ministry manager asking staff not to mention contact with the Education Minister's office in writing.

Nine people with inside knowledge of different parts of the ministry subsequently contacted RNZ to corroborate claims that ministry managers routinely asked staff not to write down sensitive information, least it be discovered through the Official Information Act.

Some were from the ministry's curriculum centre, which was the subject of a negative report about workplace culture published last week.

Others said that a culture of secrecy and avoidance of written records was common in other parts of the organisation.

The Education Ministry said the comments made in the leaked video did not meet its expectations, but it would not comment on claims made by the people who contacted RNZ.

It initially said it was investigating whether there was a wider problem, but told RNZ it had dropped plans for an internal inquiry in light of the Ombudsman's investigation.

Three of the sources confirmed they would contact the Ombudsman to make a protected disclosure and others said they were likely to do so.

A 10th person - former ministry staff member Claire Coleman - told RNZ she had already offered to participate in the Ombudsman's investigation.

This week, Chief Ombudsman John Allen said he had formally notified the ministry of the investigation.

"I will be looking at various practices, including whether the ministry's curriculum centre staff have either deliberately failed to make records or have been told not to do so," he said.

Chief Ombudsman John Allen Supplied

"My investigation will concentrate on administrative conduct, and whether the Ministry has met its legal obligations under the Official Information Act and the Public Records Act.

"I will not be considering any substantive advice or decision making relating to the curriculum itself."

Coleman, who has been a strong critic of the government's approach to the curriculum rewrite, said she hoped the Ombudsman "might get to the truth of things".

"I hope we can hold some people responsible and any future processes are transparent."

Coleman also hoped the Ombudsman's work might lead to a wider inquiry into the curriculum rewrite.

"There were far too many things that were done in a secretive and unethical way," she said. "Too many financial interests that have no business in that space."

Coleman previously claimed work on the curriculum was heavily politicised and several of the ministry insiders who contacted RNZ made similar allegations.

One source told RNZ the new curriculums felt like a step back in time.

"It felt like I was taken right back to the 80s of 'we don't let brown people have any rights' and 'we're going to whitewash everything,' and 'we're going to make sure that this is back to how things should be'," they said.

They said the curriculum was too directive of what teachers must teach.

"Some of the prescribed nature is needed, in order to be consistent and to make sure that children have all got equity wherever they are," they said. "I get that, but not to the extreme this is.

"New Zealand is innovative, creative... yet we're just throwing it all down the tubes."

Another source said schools could teach the new curriculums with resources left over from 20 years ago.

"It misses how young people learn today and it misses what's important for young people today," she said. "It's such a missed opportunity for what a good curriculum could look like.

"It's devastating, actually."

Another source said: "I think the public deserve to know, in no uncertain terms, that the quality of primary and secondary education in this country is being directly compromised and coloured by the government's ideological position, that the people responsible are consciously aware of it and that the minister, ministry and related parties have taken steps to circumvent proper protocol, and intentionally obscure the truth about how they have been operating."

Minister of Education Erica Standford RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Foreign influence

Several of the nine whistleblowers said the Australian firm Learning First had a major hand in draft curriculums and some ministry staff were flown to Melbourne to work with the company.

One said the primary school maths curriculum was completely rewritten by Learning First and other learning areas were heavily influenced by the company.

"The general feeling amongst internal staff was that the work being produced by Learning First was bad and unnecessary," they said. "There was a lot of confusion about why they were involved at all."

Another said Learning First wrote a lot of curriculum content, but ministry staff were told not to imply or say that the ministry was not the author of the curriculum.

"Learning First replaced everything we had done," they said.

They also said Learning First's understanding of the Treaty of Waitangi was "completely wrong".

A third source said Learning First provided a lot of content for some curriculums, but not for others, and ministry staff rewrote much of it.

"A lot of it was wrong, literally wrong," they said.

However, Learning First chief executive Ben Jensen denied the allegations.

He said the claim Learning First wrote most of the content for several curriculum drafts was not true.

"We did lots of research, benchmarking, provided advice and so on, but this is just completely false," he said.

Jensen said his company did not write the revised version of the maths curriculum

"We provided comparisons with other systems and made suggestions," he said. "We do a lot of work on how to sequence foundational learning in maths and what this means for the curriculum, but as above, we were not even doing this work when the draft was written.

"A lot of the feedback we provided was rejected by the ministry, so the idea that we wrote most of it is simply not true.

"When we finished, a lot of writing was still taking place, so just don't know how people can say it was mainly written by us."

Jensen said he was not aware of Learning First content being rewritten due to errors, and the company was up front about not having expertise on local knowledge and history, such as the treaty.

The Education Ministry also defended the process, and said it was responsible for all final content and decisions.

"Characterisations of the curriculum process based on individual recollections or particular examples do not necessarily reflect the full context of how curriculum content was developed, reviewed, and finalised," it said.

"The ministry develops and writes the curriculum, drawing on input from teachers, subject matter experts, stakeholders and external advisers throughout the process.

"As previously outlined publicly, including during the Education and Workforce Select Committee scrutiny examination, external advisers may contribute specialist expertise and international perspectives.

"For example, ministry officials have previously explained that Learning First helped identify relevant international curriculum content, while the curriculum itself was written by the ministry."

123RF

No written records

The Ombudsman's investigation was sparked by a video showing a principal seconded to the ministry to lead work on the secondary school curriculum, warning staff not to mention in writing feedback from the Education Minister's office.

The source of that video said they were outraged by the attempt to circumvent the proper processes for recording and providing information.

"These rigorous processes are put in there exactly to serve the children and to serve the schools, and us bypassing them is not okay," they said.

They said they heard similar requests almost once a month.

Other sources who contacted RNZ shared similar stories.

"Verbal instructions were given for changes that were controversial and come directly from the minister's office," one ministry insider told RNZ.

Another source said the comments made by the ministry manager in the leaked video were not an isolated case.

"This was a routine and extensive problem before she was seconded," they said. "The problem did not walk in the door with her."

Another ministry insider told RNZ: "We have been told many times not to write things down."

As RNZ reported last week, a person present at a ministry-run curriculum hui said ministry staff were present to take notes and one of those staffers revealed that they had been told to be very careful about what they wrote down.

"The things that they weren't writing down were pretty obviously things that they didn't want to be recorded as part of the feedback we were giving," she said.

She said, later at the same hui, a ministry manager instructed their staff to stop recording what was being said, because it was beyond the scope of the meeting and because it could be discovered through the OIA.

An established culture

Several sources told RNZ they witnessed repeated attempts to keep information off the record prior to the change of government in late 2023, but it became worse after the election.

One said ministry managers would respond to complaints or potentially critical queries with face-to-face meetings, a tactic that appeared aimed at avoiding a written email response.

"The whole 'have meetings, keep things off paper' is deliberate," they said.

The source said there were frequent meetings where nothing was written down.

"It didn't feel like there was any integrity."

A separate source said they commonly heard "that you shouldn't write things down, because they would then be OIA-able" prior to the 2023 election.

"Recording discussions and notes was sometimes discouraged, with people encouraged to have conversations instead," they told RNZ.

Another source said, prior to the change in government, reminders about the OIA and putting things in writing were light in tone and emphasis, but after the election, the term "OIA-able" was frequently used and, in 2024 meetings, became the preferred mode of communication.

Banned words

A learning lesson from a book for teaching te reo Māori. RNZ / Te Aniwa Hurihanganui

Most of the sources told RNZ they were told to remove Māori words from curriculum documents or noticed that others had done so.

They said the word "Aotearoa" was used as a synonym for or alongside New Zealand in original curriculum drafts, but was later removed.

"This instruction was never written down and, in some cases, senior staff made the changes themselves, rather than relay this change to the writing teams," one source said.

Another said Aotearoa New Zealand was the blanket term used in the curriculum, often shortened to ANZ, but proofreaders and editors were told to replace it with New Zealand.

One source said the push to remove Māori words began before the new coalition government had even taken office, with some managers indicating they wanted to make the change because "it was in the pipeline".

Two other sources said some English words were also apparently unwelcome, with instructions to remove words including "culture", "identity", and "wellbeing".

The Education Ministry had previously denied that it sought to remove Māori language from the curriculum.

Bullying and fear

The source of the video said ministry staff were being asked to behave dishonestly.

"We're public servants and we're being bullied, which I would say strongly, we are being bullied," they said. "The majority of people in the ministry are under a toxic environment."

They said nobody felt safe to complain.

"If you speak up and ask a professional, polite question of 'is this okay?', you very quickly have your fixed-term contract ended," they said.

Another ministry insider said staff felt they had to comply with government demands or lose their jobs.

"There was a lot of fear within the ministry that our jobs were now at risk, due to the change in government, and this contributed to what I experienced as an overall feeling that we had to say yes to everything and not question whether proper process was being followed," they said.

World.title: Cost of fixing storm-damaged Whangārei roads balloons to more than $23m
World.content:
The cost of fixing storm damage inflicted on Whangārei district roads earlier this year has risen to more than $23 million - of which almost $11m has been spent clearing one giant landslide.

The almost week-long January storm cut off coastal settlements at Ōakura and Whangaruru, swept away a bridge approach, damaged dozens of homes and destroyed others, and triggered a huge number of slips on the coastal road between Whangārei and Russell.

One section of road at Helena Bay Hill was only re-opened on Friday, after an eight-month effort to remove almost 100,000 cubic metres of soil, boulders and trees.

Further storms in March and April added more damage.

A report prepared for Whangārei District Council said the initial estimate for repairing storm-damaged roads was $16.5m, but that had now increased to $23.2m.

The report, by transportation manager Greg Monteith, sought councillors' approval for the extra $6.7m.

The NZ Transport Agency was expected to contribute $16m, leaving Whangārei ratepayers to pick up the remaining $7.2m.

The $23.2m total included $10.9m for emergency works at the massive Helena Bay Hill slip on Russell Road, the main connection between Whangārei and coastal communities at Ōakura and Whangaruru.

Almost $11 million has been spent repairing Russell Road, in the Whangārei District, after a massive slip on 21 January. Supplied / Ngātiwai Trust Board

The council previously described the slip repair as one of the biggest and most complex projects it had ever undertaken.

About 93,000 cubic metres of soil, boulders and downed trees had to removed - reduced from the initial estimate of 110,000 cubic metres - and the 35m-high slip face had to be stabilised.

The cost of fixing the slip had previously been put at $7.5m.

The council would fund its share of the extra costs by borrowing, to avoid major delays or cuts to existing roading projects.

The report stated the original cost estimate for the Helena Bay Hill slip was based on a completion date of mid-2026.

Since then, however, persistent wet weather, difficult ground conditions, giant basalt boulders, fill site constraints and further slip movement had delayed work and increased costs.

Some boulders were so big, they could not be broken up, even with a 50-tonne breaker, and instead required blasting or a specialist rock-breaking crew.

The report stated there had also been delays due to health and safety issues, such as near-misses involving trucks and local residents, and unauthorised entry into exclusion areas.

Aerial view of the cleared slip on Russell Road’s Helena Bay Hill. Supplied / Whangārei District Council

Once the slip had settled, which was expected to take about a year, more funding would be needed to repair the road below the slip and along the 2km route to the clean-fill site.

The estimated road rehabilitation cost was $2.3m.

During the road closure, the Whangārei District Council operated a convoy, via steep, narrow and unsealed Kaiikanui Road, to allow continued access from the south.

Piloted convoys left every 35-40 minutes from 6.30am to 6.30pm, seven days a week.

The cost of operating the Kaiikanui Road detour was put at $2.1m.

According to claims recorded by the Insurance Council, the total nationwide cost of the January storm, was $75.9m.

More than 5000 claims were lodged including $54.5m for damage to homes, $13.7m to commercial property and $4.6m for vehicles.

According to the Insurance Council, the most costly event of the past decade in terms of insurance claims was the 2023 Anniversary Weekend storm, which totalled $1.98 billion nationwide.

World.title: Green Party announces plan for passenger rail between major NZ cities
World.content:
The Green Party says it will connect the country with intercity passenger rail services, if elected.

The party has announced plans to introduce an overnight rail service between Auckland and Wellington, passenger rail between Christchurch and Dunedin, and to extend the Te Huia train route to Tauranga.

"Where public transport has been invested in, it's well used, saving people time and money every day. But for a lot of New Zealand, public transport options remain expensive and infrequent, especially when travelling long distances," Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said.

"We want to connect our cities and our country with alternative ways to travel that will save people money, connect our communities and give New Zealanders real transport choices."

"Aotearoa was once connected by a reliable passenger rail system, with fast, frequent services linking communities across the country. But the privatisation of the rail network led to the sale of our assets for private profit and was returned to the people in disarray.

"Now, our aging rail infrastructure is suffering from a generation of underinvestment, leaving the rail network in a state of decline with cancellations, delays and bus replacements.

"We should restore these systems so we can have an efficient, comfortable and affordable alternative to experience our country."

Green Party co-leaders Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick Tess Brunton / RNZ

Green Party transport spokesperson Julie Anne Genter said the tracks were already there, so should be used.

"Restoring commuter rail will give smaller regions and towns the benefits of more travellers stopping at their town stations, creating more economic opportunities and connecting them to main centres and other towns."

There were compelling reasons to back the services the party had set out, she said.

"The train journey from Auckland to Wellington is long, which makes it perfect for an overnight service. All that is needed is new, comfortable sleeper trains and operating funding.

"Extending Te Huia to Tauranga would connect one of NZ's fastest-growing regions. All it needs is some station, tunnel and track upgrades to give the region an affordable alternative to driving.

"With KiwiRail already undertaking significant work on the Christchurch to Dunedin track, extending it to passenger rail would only take building stations and some upgrades, making better use of existing rail infrastructure," she added.

Peters: 'Our job is to make sure it's viable'

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters was not opposed to the idea of a sleeper train between Auckland and Wellington.
